lead: A small win for the British ex-prince Andrew. A court in London agrees with him that the police made important mistakes in February when searching his homes in Sandringham and Windsor. The search warrants were based on the wrong statutory article. The court therefore declared the warrants unlawful. This does not mean the investigation against him must now be stopped, the court said. The searches were related to the investigation into whether the ex-prince, while he was British trade envoy (2001-2011), shared secret information with the American sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Errors acknowledged: Andrew (66), who now goes by the name Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor as a private citizen, went to the judge to have the search warrants declared unlawful. He presumably hoped that any evidence found during the searches could not be used against him. Whether that reasoning holds up is still the question. The police do not yet have to return the prince's seized property. The court will consider next year whether material taken during the searches may still be used as evidence. Andrew did not appear in court himself, possibly partly because he knew how this would turn out. The police had already admitted in July that errors were made in drafting the search warrants, but had not yet made this public.

title: Off, then not, now on again: rainbow flag will after all hang at the House of Representatives
lead: A majority of the House of Representatives is in favour of flying a rainbow flag in front of the House of Representatives building on Sunday, on Coming Out Day. That emerged on Thursday evening during a roll-call vote. During the late Thursday evening vote in the House of Representatives, 90 members were in favour of raising it and 36 were against. It is the first time this flag will be seen in front of the House of Representatives. The members voted individually, but it was clear that most members from D66, VVD, CDA, Pro, Partij voor de Dieren, SP, ChristenUnie, 50Plus and Volt voted in favour. The members from JA21 and the group-Markuszower were not present. PVV, Forum voor Democratie, Denk and SGP were against. Heated discussion. Whether or not to raise the rainbow flag has led to quite a heated discussion behind the scenes in the House of Representatives in recent days. Initially the presidium, the daily board of the House of Representatives, thought it was a good idea, but on second thoughts it scrapped the plan after all, RTL Nieuws reported earlier today. This happened after small Christian parties had been informed of the new flag plan. It met with resistance from the Christian opposition party SGP. Only larger parties sit on the presidium, but the intention is that the views of smaller parties are taken into account. On 24 February 2024 the Ukrainian flag was hoisted in front of the House of Representatives building, two years after the Russian invasion. The SGP believes that flags other than the Dutch flag should be hoisted with restraint. "The rainbow flag is not a national flag, but a flag of interest groups that has since grown into a symbol of activism", said SGP member of parliament Van Dijk. A number of opposition parties such as Pro, Partij voor de Dieren, 50Plus and Volt were so outraged that they submitted a motion to try to reverse the decision. "The House of Representatives must stand up for the rights of the worldwide LGBTI movement", the members stated in the motion. They also wrote in the motion that it is important that there is "an inclusive working environment" for the staff of the House of Representatives. The motion had to be put to a roll-call vote late on Thursday evening as well, at the insistence of the SGP. This meant that each member individually, not by parliamentary group, made their position known. U-turn. All members had to be called back for that roll-call vote. So various members who had already gone home on Thursday had to turn back. And that caused considerable irritation. A waste of thousands of kilometres, said BBB member Van der Plas, who had come back from her home town of Deventer. CU member Grinwis called the whole affair "sad and ridiculous", but did vote for the motion. "For the sake of the people it concerns."

title: French minister announces emergency plan after protests: 3000 substitute teachers
lead: The French Minister of Education has announced an emergency plan in response to the ongoing protests in France. In the short term, he wants to deploy more than 3000 extra teachers. According to Minister Geffray, the teachers must start work at the 514 schools where the teacher shortage is greatest. According to the minister, most of them can start by next Tuesday. In addition, Geffray and French Prime Minister Lecornu announced that money is being set aside to temporarily hire staff after the autumn holiday, which in France runs from 17 October to 2 November. 'Not very convincing' Whether the measures will calm the protests is an open question. "Édouard Geffray tries to offer reassurance....without really convincing anyone", is the headline in Le Parisien, for example. And Le Monde says it is mainly a stopgap, with the question being whether shortages will still arise later in the year. The teachers' union SNES-FSU calls it "a hasty attempt to create the appearance of a political solution, but one that is not sustainable". For further measures, the government points to the 2027 budget. Lecornu wants to make a change to it in which he can free up extra budget to further absorb shortages. 71,500 demonstrators Yesterday there were again demonstrations in many places by secondary school pupils. University students also joined. According to the ministry of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity>, 71,500 people took to the streets yesterday. Those marches and blockades were largely peaceful, but in some places there were also violent outbursts alongside the peaceful demonstrations. In Strasbourg, for example, a police car was set on fire, and in Bordeaux arson was committed at a police station. During the protests, 504 arrests were made yesterday and 48 police officers were injured. Calm in Liège The protests have also spread to Belgium. There, in recent days, protests have been held against planned cuts to education. In Liège, the protests caused damage, after which a ban on assembly took effect yesterday. As a result of this and of stricter controls, according to the Liège police it was a quiet day yesterday. No damage was done and the city centre was calm. However, 76 people were arrested, probably because they did not comply with the ban on assembly.

title: Terneuzen municipal council agrees to permit for asylum seekers' centre
lead: After a debate lasting hours, the Terneuzen municipal council last night agreed late in the evening to a permit for an asylum seekers' centre. The previous council was still against it. That was reason for then mayor <entity id="person:erik-van-merrienboer">Erik van Merrienboer</entity> to step down. The new college of mayor and aldermen, which was installed in July, adjusted the proposal to improve social safety. The focus was placed more on reception for families. The new proposal was narrowly adopted with the support of some opposition parties: there were sixteen votes in favour and fourteen against. Former office building That means the <entity id="org:zbo-centraal-orgaan-opvang-asielzoekers">COA</entity> can get to work on realising an asylum centre on Handelspoort in a former office building. Terneuzen will accommodate a maximum of 200 people. After the vote, the PVV submitted a motion of no confidence against all aldermen. This caused displeasure with mayor Weerwind, who sternly addressed the council according to Omroep <entity id="org:provincie-zeeland">Zeeland</entity>: "Difficult files are coming, and even then we must take our responsibility." The motion was rejected with 18 votes against and 12 in favour.

title: Rising French national debt and interest rate increasingly worrying for Europe
lead: Under pressure from ongoing demonstrations, the French government has promised that 3000 extra teachers will be hired. But the pressure on France to address its public finances is at least as great. France has, since the French Revolution of 1789, a tradition of mass protests that escalate into violence. And, to mention two recent examples, whether it concerns investing in school buildings or reversing pension cuts: meeting the demands of the demonstrators costs the state money. Money that does not exist. "The task of cutting spending was already very large, but because of rising interest rates it is becoming much harder still", says Rabobank economist Maartje Wijffelaars. According to a panel of economists appointed by the French government, 126 billion euros must be cut to stabilize the national debt by 2032. "That will hurt", says Wijffelaars, "because you cannot spare all households and businesses". France's debt mountain. France structurally spends more than it takes in, and also more than the EU's stability pact allows. And so French national debt keeps rising. According to the latest European statistics it amounts to just over 3500 billion euros. France's debt has risen to 119 percent of GDP (the total annual national income). A debt of at most 60 percent is considered desirable in the EU. France has repeatedly been reprimanded by the EU over its high budget deficit and high national debt. Declining confidence. Investors are also looking critically at France. Confidence that the country can repay its debts in the long term is falling. This is shown by the rising interest rate on government debt. Anyone lending money to France for 10 years now gets almost 5 percent interest per year. One and a half years ago that was still 3.5 percent. Investors demand a higher interest rate because they doubt France's creditworthiness. And so the country is not only dealing with high debt, but interest is also taking an ever larger bite out of the budget. France correspondent Saskia Houttuin: "While French debts and interest costs keep rising, <entity id="org:regering">de regering</entity> of Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu is in a tight spot. In the coming period he must get the 2027 budget through parliament. But just as in the Netherlands, the government has no majority. Last year that already proved a huge challenge, but Lecornu got through it thanks to a deal with the socialists. This year it will be harder; with the presidential elections on the horizon, opposition parties will not readily want to get burned by unpopular cuts. Lecornu does have one trump card; he could possibly push the budget through without parliament. But earlier, the use of that controversial legal provision led to a government collapse, so it is also a risk." Also other countries have a very high national debt, such as the United Kingdom and the United States. Even the Netherlands and Germany are seeing interest rates rise. But in France the rate is rising a lot faster. That interest rate difference, called the 'spread', was still 0.8 percent a year ago. It is now 1.5 percent. "That may seem little, but it is a cause for concern", says ING economist Bert Colijn. Given the size of the national debt, it concerns billions. "If that difference becomes too large, it leads to doubts among investors, banks and other countries about the strength of the entire European Union", Colijn explains. Eurocrisis. That recalls 2010, when the Greek debt crisis erupted. Greece's huge debt led to declining confidence in the euro. After lengthy crisis talks the EU provided emergency loans to the country. That ensured Europe stayed politically together and the euro did not sink further. In recent weeks too the euro has lost value against the dollar. The question is whether the situation now is as serious as it was in 2010. Colijn says the situation is still far from as pressing as it was then with Greece, but the consequences if France slides further are potentially greater. "France is a much bigger player than Greece, both politically and economically. If France weakens financially further, it will affect the whole of Europe more than Greece did back then." According to Colijn, the pressure on the European Central Bank to step in may increase, but it is really first up to France itself to solve its problems.

title: Rotterdam woman (23) was driving herself during fatal accident in Aruba, says Public Prosecution Service
lead: The Rotterdam woman (23) who died last month in a single-vehicle accident in Aruba was herself behind the wheel of the off-road vehicle. That is the conclusion of the <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity> in Aruba, based on video footage. The woman's family members told Rijnmond earlier that they could not imagine the woman was driving herself. Kimberly van Ardenne was on holiday on the island with her boyfriend. Together with a Dutch marine who lives on the island, they set off on Sunday afternoon, 13 September, in a UTV, an open off-road vehicle. For reasons still unknown, the off-road vehicle overturned. The two male occupants remained unharmed. The woman died on the spot. The men told local authorities that Kimberly was behind the wheel, but family members in the Netherlands doubted that. "She falls more into the category of scaredy-cats than daredevils," her cousin Stephanie told Rijnmond. The woman reportedly already experienced a lot of stress in the Netherlands when driving in the morning rush hour or parking in traffic jams. 'Public attention' Justice in Aruba now says that the account of the two other occupants is correct. The investigation has not yet been concluded. But because of the "public attention", justice is already making this information public now. The family's lawyer, Peter Schouten, says in a statement on X that he finds it "extremely strange" that justice is now releasing the information about the video. "The family also finds it cruel and inhuman that this video was not shown to them immediately, and that their grief was therefore unnecessarily disturbed for four weeks by the uncertainty about Kimberly's death," he writes.

title: Netherlands Dachau Committee knew camp stories of 99-year-old were not true
lead: The Netherlands Dachau Committee has known since 2024 about the untruths regarding the wartime past of Willem Wilbrink and has tried to prevent him from spreading them further. That is what chairman <entity id="person:wimar-jaeger">Wimar Jaeger</entity> of the foundation told NOS. The 99-year-old Wilbrink was regularly at commemorations of the Second World War and at schools to talk about his wartime past and his time in the Dachau concentration camp. But a publication this week in Historisch Nieuwsblad shows that it is very unlikely he was ever imprisoned there. The publication also reveals that other claims he made are probably not true. By his own account, Wilbrink was arrested at the age of 15 for resistance work and taken to the concentration camp near Munich. There he is said to have been put to work as a corpse carrier. In that capacity he says he saved forty people from death. He did this, he claimed, by bringing people who were supposed to be dead and about to be put in the crematorium, but who turned out to be alive, to the infirmary. No evidence. According to researchers there is no evidence for these claims. For example, there is no documentation of his imprisonment in Dachau and no prisoner number is known for him, while in this concentration camp, where more than 43,000 people died, everything was recorded meticulously. Wilbrink also wears decorations of which it is unknown how he obtained them. For example, Wilbrink claimed he had received a Polish heroic title, but research by RTL Nieuws shows that his name does not appear in the country's archives, and that the title Wilbrink mentioned does not exist. Furthermore, Wilbrink told stories that other Dachau survivors had no memory of and which, according to researchers, also did not take place. Wilbrink also does not appear in the accounts of and about well-known people who were imprisoned in Dachau, such as those of priest and war hero Titus Brandsma, who was murdered there in 1942. Organisations informed about untruths. Jaeger says the National Dachau Committee discovered that Wilbrink's stories were not true after the publication of his biography. The organisation found that book remarkable because they did not know Wilbrink's story. The Committee therefore conducted research and spoke with historians, after which the conclusion was drawn that Wilbrink's past in Dachau was invented. "We then tried to stop the book from being distributed and informed commemoration committees that Wilbrink's story is not true", says Jaeger. The National Dachau Committee did not actively make the news about Wilbrink public because "we know better than anyone what a war trauma can do with the stories in your head", says chairman Jaeger. "We are convinced that Wilbrink thinks he experienced this." Jaeger states that the organisation has empathy and wants to understand people with war trauma, but also that it is important that stories about the Second World War and Dachau are based on the truth. Therefore the committee now cannot do anything but make clear what the reality is, he says. "Otherwise we have nothing to gain from the lessons we learned there." Although the Dachau committee already knew about the untruths in 2024, Wilbrink was still at the National Commemoration of the Capitulations 1945 in Wageningen in 2025. <entity id="person:vincent-karremans">Minister Karremans</entity> then wrote on LinkedIn that he "had the honour of sitting next to Wilbrink". The organisation of the Wageningen commemoration did not know about the untruths in the 99-year-old's story, a spokesperson says. He says Wageningen45 was not informed about this by the Netherlands Dachau Committee. According to him, the organisation relies on expert bodies when recognising veterans and their stories. "Wageningen45 has taken note of the Historisch Nieuwsblad article and takes this very seriously", he tells NOS. For the organisation, "it is paramount that the stories we tell and the change-makers we honour are reliable and authentic", the spokesperson says. "So that we can keep veterans' stories alive with great care and respect for a wide audience." Second World War newsletter Interested in the Second World War? Subscribe to our newsletter here.

title: A2 in Limburg closed all weekend, significant delays already this morning
lead: The A2 in Limburg will be completely closed in both directions this weekend. Last night the section between St. Joost and Roosteren was already closed. That was clearly noticeable during the morning rush hour: motorists faced significant delays. Tonight at 21.00 the A2 will close between junction Het Vonderen (Echt) and junction Kerensheide (Urmond) due to roadworks. The A2 is being widened: an extra lane will be added in both directions. The total works will last for years. This weekend <entity id="org:rijkswaterstaat">Rijkswaterstaat</entity> is running a liveblog about the so-called WeekendBreek . With such a full closure, work can continue day and night for a whole weekend. This weekend, among other things, two wildlife culverts are being built. Less traffic The first night of the works went smoothly despite the rain, Rijkswaterstaat tells L1 Nieuws. The motorway runs through the narrowest part of the Netherlands and there are no good alternative routes. Traffic today is being diverted from the St. Joost exit via Echt over the N276. Rijkswaterstaat urges people not to go on the road if it is not necessary. "There was somewhat less traffic heading north compared with other Fridays," said Rijkswaterstaat. Hundreds of people are working day and night on the A2 this weekend. It is the second weekend closure in a series of seven weekend closures over the next five years. The closure lasts until Monday morning at 05.00.

title: France warned about non-visible military aircraft near Curaçao
lead: France warned during the American attack on Venezuela on 3 January about military aircraft that were not visible to civil air traffic control in the Caribbean region. Because they were not visible, air traffic controllers could not always inform other aircraft about the presence of military aircraft. That is evident from documents that the Dutch <entity id="org:ministerie-van-buitenlandse-zaken">ministerie van Buitenlandse Zaken</entity> released following an appeal to the Open Government Act (Woo). NOS reported on 14 December already about a near-collision between a passenger aircraft and an American military tanker aircraft above Curaçao, in which the military aircraft was not visible on radar. The danger of military aircraft that are not visible to civil air traffic control is that air traffic controllers cannot warn other aircraft in time. Without information about the position of those aircraft, they also cannot ensure sufficient separation between aircraft. Pilots of passenger aircraft can therefore unexpectedly encounter a military aircraft and may then have to intervene themselves to prevent a collision. That risk also played a role in the near-collision NOS reported on in December. The French warning makes clear that during the American attack on Venezuela, military aircraft that stayed out of sight of civil air traffic controllers were again taken into account. Listen here to part of the conversation between air traffic control and the pilots during the near-collision: The French warning related to the flight information regions of Curaçao, San Juan and Piarco. Pilots were also advised to take extra fuel, within operational possibilities, so they could divert if necessary. The documents do not show that such aircraft actually flew in the Curaçao flight information region on 3 January. Emergency consultation after near-collision. The incidents NOS first reported on led to emergency consultation between airlines, the American aviation authority FAA, Curaçao air traffic control and international aviation organisations. KLM subsequently tightened its safety measures for flights through Curaçao airspace. Aircraft had to carry extra lighting throughout the entire flight through that area from then on. On 18 December, the governments of Curaçao and Aruba reported that agreements had been made with the United States about American military aircraft switching on transponders. American flight ban. Just over two weeks later came the American attacks on Venezuela, in which President Maduro and his wife were captured and taken to the United States. On 3 January the FAA issued a flight ban for American civil aviation operators in the Curaçao Flight Information Region (FIR). This applied at all flight levels due to safety risks from military activities. American military and state aircraft were exempt from the ban. The Curaçao FIR covers a large part of the southern Caribbean and borders the Venezuelan flight information region Maiquetía. Air traffic services are provided by Curaçao air traffic control. The American ban applied to American aviation operators and did not mean that airspace was closed for all aircraft. Other airlines had to assess for themselves whether they could operate their flights safely. See our special on the near-collision here: KLM cancelled flights to the ABC islands, Sint Maarten and several other Caribbean destinations on 3 January. TUI and Corendon also cancelled flights. According to Buitenlandse Zaken, around 2600 KLM passengers were affected by the cancellations. The Curaçao <entity id="org:regering">regering</entity> said at the time that the airspace was not completely closed, but that there was heightened readiness. Airlines had to assess for themselves whether they could fly. On 4 January the American restrictions were lifted and airlines resumed their flights to the islands. Crisis consultation in The Hague. The Dutch government held crisis consultation on 3 January about the American attacks and the consequences for the region. Among those involved were the ministries of Buitenlandse Zaken, <entity id="org:ministerie-van-defensie">Defensie</entity>, <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity>, <entity id="org:ministerie-van-infrastructuur-en-waterstaat">Infrastructuur en Waterstaat</entity> and <entity id="org:ministerie-van-justitie-en-veiligheid">Justitie en Veiligheid</entity>. Representatives of KLM, TUI fly and Corendon also received information about the security situation. On 4 January it was announced that a steering group for the Caribbean region, chaired by Binnenlandse Zaken, would convene. Defensie and Buitenlandse Zaken would share information there. The released documents do not show when the Curaçao aviation authorities were informed about the international security warnings, or which agreements were made with the United States about military flight movements during the attack. Crisis phase scaled down. On 6 January the Dutch crisis consultation convened again. The consultation decided to return the crisis approach to the pre-crisis phase. A next consultation was planned for 13 January, unless the situation gave cause to convene earlier. The scenario analyses on which the decision-making was partly based have been largely redacted. The documents made public do not state what information the Curaçao air traffic control had about military aircraft movements during the American attack. It also remains unclear whether the agreements that Curaçao and Aruba announced in December with the United States about the use of transponders during the operation were still in force and were being observed.

title: Rotterdam files a police report against employees for fraud in connection with the childcare benefits scandal
lead: The municipality of Rotterdam suspects that several employees committed fraud with money meant for victims of the childcare benefits scandal. The municipality has filed a police report against two people, the regional broadcaster Rijnmond reports. Five others have been put on leave. The municipality is still investigating them. The employees helped victims of the childcare benefits scandal, for example with buying new furniture or equipment at the municipality's expense. They had access to a municipal payment card for this. The victims received help from the municipality because they had run into financial problems after the <entity id="org:belastingdienst">Belastingdienst</entity> wrongly accused them of fraud with childcare benefit. Spending for themselves The municipality of Rotterdam believes that at least two civil servants also bought items for themselves or others. These concern expenses where it is not clear what the money was spent on, and expenses where it is not clear why they were made. "As far as we know, the victims simply received their items. They did not lose out, but that does not change the fact that it is fraud," says alderman Diederik van Dommelen (VVD) to Rijnmond. The possible fraud was discovered more than a year ago following a report about one of the employees. A hundred people Van Dommelen does not yet know how much money is involved. That is currently being investigated. "What happened is truly unacceptable. I want to know what happened and how much went wrong." Around a hundred people had access to the municipality's credit card. The alderman considers it justifiable that so many people had the freedom to make purchases for the victims. "Let's not forget: we did this to help the victims, and then you need speed, because those people need help," he says. "Speed and care sometimes clash." To prevent fraud, the spending limits have since been adjusted. "We have also reduced the number of people who can use the credit card," said alderman Van Dommelen. Fingers in the sugar bowl "We cannot prevent people from having their fingers in the sugar bowl. But we must be able to detect it as quickly as possible," said the alderman. "The checks therefore need to be faster. At the same time, we want to be able to help the victims quickly. It will always be a search for balance."

title: Hobby fishers also deployed to remove harmful crayfish
lead: Hobby fishers, sport fishing clubs, contractors and muskrat control officers may in future also catch invasive American crayfish on a larger scale. Currently the water boards do this, but they do not have enough people to push back the harmful crayfish population. So a new regulation for fishing invasive crayfish is coming, <entity id="person:silvio-erkens">staatssecretaris Erkens</entity> told <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity> today. Tunnels and burrows In Dutch ditches, canals, lakes and pools an estimated tens of millions of crayfish are causing major damage to water quality and biodiversity. They cut water plants to pieces with their claws, eat aquatic insects and amphibian and fish eggs. They also dig tunnels and burrows, making banks and dikes less stable. The invasive crayfish reproduce quickly and it is no longer possible to remove the animals completely. But the ministry does want to do more about the so-called 'catching away' of the animals. Umbrella trap So other catching equipment may now be used, such as the slot trap and the umbrella trap. Currently the water boards mainly work with fyke nets and cubs, but the drawback is that many other fish and aquatic animals are caught too. These are then returned, but are often injured or have already died from the catch. Hiring in other fishers, such as sport fishers, members of fishing clubs, contractors and muskrat control officers is also new. Until now they were only allowed to catch crayfish on a small scale, namely with a rod. Under the new rules more is allowed, but that does not mean everyone may always catch crayfish. A water board can locally put out "an assignment", says state secretary Erkens (Fisheries), and hobby fishers, for example, can then get to work on it. Crayfish cuisine Erkens speaks of "an important step" to bring the plague under control. He does point out that once caught, the animals must not be released elsewhere. "They must be destroyed or consumed." The state secretary himself has eaten crayfish before, he says when asked. "I found them quite tasty," said Erkens. "Who knows, a very nice Dutch crayfish cuisine may be on the verge of emerging." Ruben Ariaans is a professional crayfish fisher. He is not really keen on hobby fishers also going hunting for the animal:

title: Twenty asylum seekers slept in the rain in Ter Apel: 'Fallen below the humane minimum'
lead: In Ter Apel, twenty people who want to apply for asylum slept outside on the grass in the rain last night. According to the aid organisations Vluchtelingenwerk Nederland and the Red Cross, this is a direct result of the lack of reception places in the Netherlands. According to the aid organisations, the Netherlands is falling below a "humane minimum". At the registration centre in Ter Apel there is a building with day shelter. There is room there for a maximum of 150 people. People who want to apply for asylum can go there if there is no place at the registration centre. "We now have people who have been in that shelter for ten days, people cannot wash there", says a spokesperson for the Red Cross to NOS. The limit of 150 people has been reached several times in recent weeks, the aid organisations say. By their own account, they have to "make impossible choices to keep the situation safe and manageable". That is why only the 150 people from the day shelter can go to the emergency night shelter. According to the Red Cross, there have been earlier incidents in the night shelter, such as theft. "For safety reasons, we now have to say: we will only help people in the night shelter whom we know from the day shelter. That is why people are sleeping on the front yard", says the spokesperson. Dispersal Act The aid organisations are calling on municipalities in the Netherlands to arrange emergency reception immediately. "It is the responsibility of the government, and we are doing what we can to help", says the spokesperson for the Red Cross. What is the Dispersal Act? The Dispersal Act has been intended since 2024 to ensure that the reception of asylum seekers is distributed more fairly across the Netherlands. The Netherlands structurally lacks reception places for the number of people who come here and apply for asylum. That shortage is affecting the registration centre in Ter Apel and (emergency) reception places throughout the country. After registration in Ter Apel, a person awaiting the asylum process should move on to a reception location elsewhere in the country. That often does not happen, because those reception locations are full. Places there are largely occupied by status holders; people who have applied for asylum and are allowed to stay. They have difficulty moving on to a home because of problems on the housing market. The number of pending asylum applications and the length of the asylum process have also been increasing for years. People who want to apply for asylum therefore remain dependent on asylum reception for longer than before, which leads to fuller asylum seekers' centres. According to the <entity id="org:immigratie-en-naturalisatiedienst">IND</entity> (the Immigration and Naturalisation Service), the number of people coming to the Netherlands is higher than the number of applications the IND says it can process each year. Earlier research by NOS shows that most municipalities say they are willing to cooperate with the Dispersal Act. Even so, the aid organisations say that about two thirds of municipalities do too little in practice. <entity id="org:kabinet">Het kabinet</entity> placed 24 of the 342 municipalities under supervision this summer, because they are not arranging enough reception locations. Asylum Minister Van den Brink, who is responsible for reception, calls the situation in Ter Apel "unworthy of the Netherlands". The minister says he will soon look for reception locations at municipalities. "Sometimes you have to keep persevering with what you are already doing." Since this summer there has also been temporary additional emergency reception in Ter Apel. Nieuwsuur went to take a look:

title: Cabinet apologises to Q fever patients: 'Passed from pillar to post'
lead: Twenty years after the start of the largest Q fever epidemic in history, health minister Hermans apologises on behalf of the cabinet. Tens of thousands of people in <entity id="org:provincie-noord-brabant">Noord-Brabant</entity> became infected by contaminated goat farms in the area. Various investigative committees, ombudsmen and doctors have since established that the government fell short in protecting the people in that region. The minister does not apologise for what happened during the epidemic. She does apologise on behalf of the cabinet that there was no good social safety net for people who have become chronically ill for a long time. "When you are not believed, have to keep telling your story over and over and are passed from pillar to post, that is terrible. And I offer my apologies for that," said Hermans to hundreds of patients during a meeting in the provincial house of Den Bosch. Chronically ill Two thousand people are still chronically ill to this day, have mostly lost their jobs and live a life on the margins of society. There was already hope that the minister would apologise. Her ministry had given independent experts the assignment to evaluate policy and actions regarding Q fever patients. That the minister apologises is seen by the researchers as "essential", the report states. It echoes the recommendations of three earlier reports by the <entity id="org:nationale-ombudsman">Nationale Ombudsman</entity> from 2012, 2017 and 2024. Time and again, successive ministers refused to apologise. Other important recommendations were also ignored, such as investing in medical science and setting up an expertise centre for the treatment of chronically ill patients. Also, the long-term version of Q fever, the Q fever fatigue syndrome, is still often not recognised by the <entity id="org:zbo-uitvoeringsinstituut-werknemersverzekeringen">UWV</entity>. Patients therefore cannot count on disability benefits. The loss of income has in turn led to further suffering. 'Trust in government damaged' Also, how well social support is arranged differs per municipality. Patients often experience little understanding and are passed from pillar to post for help. "As a result, trust in the government as a whole has been damaged," the researchers write. They strongly advise the minister to take the initiative herself to improve help and cooperation between various municipalities, support services and organisations such as the UWV. The new report also emphasises the recommendation to "invest heavily" in an expertise centre, medical knowledge and long-term research. The researchers see that the medical indifference towards patients "has reduced trust in the medical world and in the government." Q fever fatigue syndrome The Q fever fatigue syndrome fits in with the other post-acute infectious diseases (PAIS) such as long covid, ME, Lyme and post-sepsis syndrome. Medical knowledge about these conditions is still in its infancy. Curative treatments do not yet exist, and the few treatments that can bring relief lack sufficient scientific basis. As a result, there is almost no reimbursed care in regular healthcare. Tens of millions of euros have been invested in research into long covid and ME in recent years. But most findings are not yet concrete enough for practice in regular care. More time for medical science needed Nevertheless, the planned policy of <entity id="person:sophie-hermans">minister Hermans</entity> is not to make large follow-up funding for research available soon. In addition, funding for the existing long covid expertise centres will be stopped at short notice. The cabinet's idea is that GPs and other care providers can take on care for PAIS patients. The researchers oppose this plan and write that medical science must be given more time and space so that diagnoses and treatments with a scientific basis also become possible, so that they can be reimbursed too. "Until then, in the view of the review team, integration into regular care is not yet on the agenda." The <entity id="org:gezondheidsraad">Gezondheidsraad</entity> gave a similar warning earlier this year in an advisory report: "The estimated large numbers of people with long covid and other PAIS cannot simply be absorbed into regular care." One-off 2.5 million euros During the meeting in which minister Hermans apologised, patients from the audience asked whether tens of millions of euros would be invested in scientific research into PAIS. For now, that will not happen, the minister said. However, a one-off 2,5 million euros will be freed up in 2027 to improve the quality of life of Q fever patients. Proposals for spending this budget have been drawn up in consultation with the Q fever ambassador, patient organisation Q-uestion and Q-support. The funds will be used to help Q fever patients who have become stuck, for example at the UWV, but also in care. Not all Q fever patients can be helped with this budget, but the minister hopes the lessons learned from this approach can lead to a better standard of support for all PAIS patients.

title: US announces sanctions against International Criminal Court in The Hague, wants to 'paralyse' the court
lead: The American government has announced sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague. These are to take effect largely in April next year. "President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans", says minister Rubio of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-buitenlandse-zaken">Buitenlandse Zaken</entity> in a video message on X . "That is why the US is imposing sanctions on the ICC. We will ban transactions with this runaway court, cut it off from resources and paralyse its ability to function." Microsoft Earlier, the American government already imposed sanctions on individual prosecutors and judges. For example, an affected jurist of the court would no longer have access to Microsoft, and financial services via American companies were cut off. Now the US is expanding the package of measures and threatens to cut off the entire court from such services. "We do not need the Criminal Court", says Rubio. "Americans do not fall under the jurisdiction of this 'fake ICC'." The American government believes the court has no authority to prosecute American citizens or citizens of American allies. 'Not stopping' Acting ICC prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan says in a response that the American sanctions against the Criminal Court must be condemned, and promises that they will not prevent the work of the tribunal. "The sanctions are intended to undermine the international legal order and the work of an independent judicial institution. Our work will continue in all our files, in our investigations and in our prosecutions." US does not recognise the Court. The ICC, based in The Hague, is an international court established in 2002. It can prosecute people suspected of genocide, crimes against humanity and war crimes. The United States, like Russia, China, India, Israel and Iran, is not a member of the ICC and does not recognise it either. These sanctions do not come unexpectedly. Trump has a profound dislike of the ICC, and sanctions against the Criminal Court had been in the air for some time. In his speech during the UN General Assembly he called on all member states of the ICC to withdraw. The direct reason for the sanctions is the arrest warrant against Israeli prime minister Netanyahu. Israel is an ally of the US. American personnel were also investigated for involvement in war crimes in Afghanistan. Support for the ICC was also limited under Democratic presidents. When the International Criminal Court issued arrest warrants in 2024 against Israeli prime minister Netanyahu and former defence minister Gallant, Biden called that "scandalous". Nobel Peace Prize Today, not entirely by coincidence, ICC president Tomoko Akane had coffee with <entity id="person:willem-alexander">koning Willem-Alexander</entity> at Huis ten Bosch. What was discussed there has not been made public. And today of all days, former ICC judge Navi Pillay also received the Nobel Peace Prize. The system of international law is currently "under enormous pressure", the jury said about the appointment, "and its institutions are being attacked".

title: Podcast De Stemming: Waving cyclists, water pistols and the Jetteritus
lead: There was once again old-fashioned consensus building (polderen) this week, because at the Catshuis the trade unions, employers' organisations and <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> discussed the future of social security. But whether they have actually made progress is the question. Furthermore, <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">de Eerste Kamer</entity> debated the budget of the Jetten cabinet. And there too, it proves difficult for the prime minister to win over a broad majority enthusiastically. And there is again disagreement within the coalition over box 3. The VVD and the CDA are not on the same wavelength regarding the 'paper gift tax'. What does that do to relations within the coalition? Podcast De Stemming This episode of De Stemming by Vullings and De Rooy can be listened to at <entity id="org:zbo-nederlandse-publieke-omroep">NPO</entity> Luister. You can also find all previous episodes there. Just like all other well-known podcast channels. About this podcast Political journalists Joost Vullings (EenVandaag, AVROTROS) and Marleen de Rooy (NOS) go through the week in The Hague every Friday, with sharp analyses, rumours and predictions. Want to respond? Email destemming@nos.nl.

title: Netherlands returns twenty stolen objects to Indonesia
lead: The Netherlands is returning twenty objects to Indonesia. These are cultural objects that were looted during the colonial era, or acquired under duress and brought to our country. Among the objects being returned are the Banjarmasin diamond, a handwritten Quran and several gravestones. Eighteen objects were until now in the possession of the Wereldmuseum, two were from the Rijksmuseum. "We are always pleased with a restitution", says Marieke van Bommel, director of the Wereldmuseum. "We feel that when objects have come into our collection improperly, it is only right that they go back to the country of origin." The handwritten Quran from Aceh: "With some objects you know they come from a certain war", says director Van Bommel. "Then you already have a suspicion that they were acquired in the colonial era." According to the director of the Wereldmuseum, there was often an unequal balance of power and violence involved. "Sometimes we really know for sure, and some things we research further after a request." In returning them, <entity id="person:rianne-letschert">minister Letschert</entity> of Culture is following the advice of the Commissie Koloniale Collectie. It investigated the provenance and concluded that these twenty objects involved "involuntary loss of possession". "These objects have great cultural and historical value for Indonesia", says Letschert. "They should never have been in the Netherlands. We are now putting this injustice right." First, packing still to do The objects will remain in the Netherlands for the coming months. "Today is the legal transfer", says director Van Bommel. Minister Letschert and her Indonesian counterpart are signing an agreement today in Amsterdam. "In the coming months the objects will be packed and all the paperwork put in order for transport to Indonesia", says Van Bommel.

title: Disappointment over 99-year-old's 'camp lies': 'The truth is already bad enough'
lead: "It is important that the stories told and the people we honour are reliable and authentic", says the Nationaal Comité Herdenking Capitulaties about the news that claims made by the 99-year-old Willem Wilbrink, who until now passed as a war hero, are not correct. A publication in Historisch Nieuwsblad this week revealed, among other things, that Wilbrink was not held in the Dachau concentration camp . Also the NIOD Institute for War, Holocaust and Genocide Studies says his name does not appear on the list of Dutch people who were held there. NIOD researcher Kees Ribbens says in a response that stories like this harm the truth about the Second World War. Malicious people can seize on them to sow doubt about what happened in the Holocaust. 'He really believes it' Although the Nederlands Dachau Comité has known about the untruths since 2024, it is only now going public. Chairman <entity id="person:wimar-jaeger">Wimar Jaeger</entity> does so "because it is important that the stories about the Second World War and Dachau are based on the truth", he says. Jaeger says he understands the 99-year-old, and Jaeger is convinced that Wilbrink believes he experienced this. "We know better than anyone what a war trauma can do with the stories in your head." Carolien Brugsma, journalist and daughter of Dachau survivor Willem Brugsma, also assumes that Wilbrink has a war trauma. She too thinks he truly believes he was in the concentration camp. She herself was interviewed last year for Andere Tijden about the concentration camp and her father's time there. Her father was a resistance fighter and was arrested in Paris. He was held in three camps before ending up in Dachau. Unlike camps such as Auschwitz, which were set up for the extermination of Jews, Dachau was mainly intended for heavy forced labour. It mainly held resistance members and political opponents of the Nazis, such as priest and war hero Titus Brandsma . Checking claims At first Brugsma thought when she heard the news: "How sad for him and his children", she says. "But now I'm starting to get angry. Not at him, but at the person who wrote his biography." As far as she is concerned, that person should have verified Wilbrink's claims. She herself did so with her father's wartime past when she went to Dachau for Andere Tijden. Although she was certain her father had been there, she double-checked whether she knew his camp number correctly. Brugsma finds it especially objectionable that in times when knowledge of the Holocaust is declining , untruths like Wilbrink's are being spread. Precisely now, stories told about the Second World War must be true, she says. "The truth is already bad enough." Biographer on Wilbrink: 'He is himself responsible for his statements' The biography of Wilbrink was published in 2023 and was written by Laurens van Aggelen. He says he checked everything he could check. "But Wilbrink is himself also responsible for what he says", Van Aggelen believes. The story he wrote in the biography had already been told in other media, he says. "Only mine is more detailed." Even so, the biographer left out claims by the 99-year-old from the book because they could not be correct, says Van Aggelen. That Wilbrink said things that were presumably incorrect may be related to his advanced age, in his view. But, as Van Aggelen puts it: "I am a biographer, it is not a scholarly book." Family does not want to address the issue The Wilbrink family has told other media that they stand behind his claims. They do not want to go into the substance of the matter with the NOS. NIOD researcher Ribbens agrees with this. He states that people know the general story of the Second World War as it appears in history books, but that personal stories make the war easier to imagine and empathise with. "Precisely because these stories have emotion, they are appealing and valuable." The problem with personal stories like these is that they are scrutinised less critically than historians normally do, says Ribbens. Few comparable cases are known at the NIOD. "But if there are more examples like this, people become critical of stories that are in fact well supported and factually correct." "Towards the end of his imprisonment my father weighed only 40 kilos", Brugsma concludes. "He barely survived his time in Dachau. Those are the real stories." Newsletter Second World War Interested in the Second World War? Subscribe to our newsletter here.

title: Ice rinks open despite high temperature: 'Otherwise in a bind with competitions'
lead: Despite temperatures around 20 degrees, many Dutch artificial ice rinks reopened last week. Skaters could not wait to get on the ice, but others often look on in amazement. The question often arises whether the skating season could not start later. Because the higher the outside temperature, the more energy it takes to lay down an ice surface. Ice master Frank Zuurendonk of the rink in <entity id="org:gemeente-haarlem">Haarlem</entity> sees some merit in starting later. "You can ask yourself: shouldn't you just start in November?" But other ice rinks do not see this as an option because of the competition calendar of the Dutch skating federation KNSB and the international skating federation ISU. "As long as the ISU calendar does not change, the skating season does not change either," says ice master Tonnie Horstman of ice rink De Scheg in <entity id="org:gemeente-deventer">Deventer</entity>. 'Laying the best ice' The Netherlands has 22 permanent artificial ice rinks. These decide for themselves when they open. Most do so at the beginning of October. The ice rink in <entity id="org:gemeente-rotterdam">Rotterdam</entity> always opens later than the rest: in November. The rink in <entity id="org:gemeente-alkmaar">Alkmaar</entity> does not open at the beginning but halfway through October. "We sail our own course," says location manager Roy Lennings. "We want to lay the best ice for our skaters." For the quality of the ice, it is indeed better to start later, says ice master Zuurendonk of the rink in Haarlem. Not only because of the temperature but mainly because of the wind. In October, the strong autumn wind often makes it difficult to make good ice, the ice master says. Less energy In the discussion about the length of the skating season, sustainability is also a theme. Because ice rinks are energy guzzlers. Commissioned by the <entity id="org:gemeente-amsterdam">gemeente Amsterdam</entity>, research was carried out in 2020 into the consumption of various ice rinks. The rink in <entity id="org:gemeente-leeuwarden">Leeuwarden</entity> would consume 49.3 kilowatt-hours per day for every cubic metre of ice. That is roughly as much as a household uses in electricity in a week. Opening later in the year could mean less energy consumption. In November, outside temperatures are indeed lower than in October, so less energy is needed to make ice. But opening later is not the only way to save energy, says Joris Wouters, director of the Jaap Eden Baan in Amsterdam. "We should not have to choose between skating and sustainability, but look at how we can make skating more sustainable." The KNSB and the ice rinks are, according to him, actively working on this. The so-called Team Duurzaam IJs, of the KNSB, Essent and Daikin, was established two years ago with the goal of making ice rinks energy neutral. Ice rink De Meent in Alkmaar underwent a sustainability trajectory in 2023 that serves as an example for the other rinks. "The heat released when making ice we now store in the ground and with that we heat the sports complex," says location manager Lennings. In a bind with competitions "The most sustainable is of course not to skate, but that is very black-and-white," says manager sports participation Jurre Trouw on behalf of the KNSB. He points out that in the whole discussion about the length of the skating season you should not forget the skaters. "The rinks are open to clubs in October: they have the wish to skate and you want to offer them a decent sports offering." Moreover, "you get into a bind with competitions" if the opening of the skating season is postponed, says Trouw. The international skating federation ISU makes a competition calendar, to which the KNSB then aligns the national calendar. In a week, the IJsselcup traditionally opens the Dutch skating season. If we really want the season to start later, a change in the mindset of skaters is needed, says ice master Zuurendonk. "They are really itching to start now." Wouters of the Jaap Eden Baan says the same. "The value of an ice rink should not be expressed only in kilowatt-hours. An ice rink is more than a layer of ice."

title: Cabinet condemns US sanctions against ICC, but still hopes for diplomacy
lead: The Dutch cabinet condemns the new American sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC). <entity id="person:rob-jetten">Premier Jetten</entity> says in an initial reaction that he fully stands behind the institution in The Hague. He calls the sanctions "deeply regrettable". On the other hand, Jetten is pleased that the new measures only take effect in six months. There is then still "plenty of time" to talk with the United States about what Jetten calls "an appropriate solution". The US has already announced measures against the ICC on several occasions. The ICC prosecutes people suspected of, for example, genocide and war crimes. President Trump does not recognise the institution and finds it unacceptable that the Court issued an arrest warrant against Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu. Paralysis The Americans now want to ban transactions with the court, which in their eyes has "run amok", and also "paralyse its ability to function", said US Secretary Rubio of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-buitenlandse-zaken">Buitenlandse Zaken</entity> today in a video message on X. This could mean that ICC staff can no longer access their bank accounts or can no longer travel to the US. That has not happened yet, which is also a relief to <entity id="person:tom-berendsen">minister Berendsen</entity> of Foreign Affairs. In an initial reaction he does speak of an "undesirable and new escalation", but he also emphasises the importance of diplomatic talks with Trump. Berendsen repeatedly speaks of pursuing the "diplomatic track". He does not want to go into the question of what the Netherlands will offer to meet the United States halfway. "We are going to have an open conversation." Jetten also speaks of an "open conversation". Outside Hague politics too, the sanctions are met with indignation. President of the European Council António Costa says he will take "appropriate steps to protect the court". EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas stresses that protecting the ICC remains "a European priority". Like Jetten, she says there is room for dialogue in the coming months. The High Commissioner for Human Rights at the United Nations, Volker Türk, calls the measures "unacceptable". He calls on the US to withdraw all sanctions against the ICC and its staff. The ICC itself is also not pleased with the American decision. "The sanctions are intended to undermine the international rule of law and obstruct the work of an independent judicial body," said acting ICC prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan to news agency Reuters. Difficult position Trump's sanctions against the International Criminal Court have put the Netherlands in a difficult diplomatic position. On the one hand, the Netherlands wants to stand firmly for the international legal order and in particular for the Court, which is based in The Hague. On the other hand, the Netherlands must also avoid antagonising the United States, an important NATO ally, too much. The United States is also an important trading partner of the Netherlands. The first appearance of Jetten at the UN General Assembly in New York, at the end of September, was therefore awaited with some tension. At that time Jetten chose harsh words to make clear to Trump that his attacks on the court were not accepted. They undermine the international legal order as a whole, he said. The VVD is already letting it be known today what the party considers important. In a tweet on X, MP Rajkowski says that as far as the VVD is concerned, the "economic and security interests of the Netherlands weigh heavily in how the cabinet responds to these sanctions".

title: Three men arrested in Ghent for shooting in Overasselt
lead: In Ghent three men have been arrested who were presumably involved in the shooting in Overasselt at the beginning of last month. That is what the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> reports. The suspects are 23, 25 and 28 years old. They are suspected of murder, manslaughter, firearm possession and membership of a criminal organisation. The police are not saying what role they may have played in the outburst of violence on 1 September in the Gelderland village. The men, all three of whom live in the area of the city of Ghent, were arrested by a special police team. Three homes and a warehouse were also searched. Various data carriers and vehicles have been seized. The Dutch <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity> has requested the surrender of the three suspects. Last week RTL Nieuws reported that the men who entered Overasselt and fatally shot a security guard had been recruited via social media. They reportedly received instructions for the attack via messages on Signal and Snapchat.

title: Severe earthquake in Panama, power outage and damage to buildings
lead: Panama has been hit by an earthquake with a magnitude of 7,7. That would make it one of the most severe tremors of the year worldwide. No reports of casualties have come in yet. The epicenter of the quake was in the southern province of Herrera, a sparsely populated area. Local media report that in various regions of the country people had to leave buildings, businesses, schools and homes. "We felt it very strongly. Things fell over in the kitchen, but we are all fine, although we are really scared," 60-year-old Rosendo Domínguez from Herrera tells news agency AP by phone. "Everyone is standing outside, full of fear." Damage to buildings A spokesperson for the national civil protection service tells news channel Telemetro Reporta that damage is mainly in the provinces of Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos. In the city of Penonomé, roughly halfway between the epicenter and the capital Panama City, the cathedral, the governor's office and a hotel reportedly suffered considerable damage, among other things. Power has gone out in six provinces. The tremors were also clearly felt about 200 kilometers away in Panama City, according to people on the spot, for about 40 seconds. Buildings began to shake and people fled into the street. For now no damage has been reported in the city, which is known for its hundreds of skyscrapers. The country's international airport has been temporarily closed. Shipping through the Panama Canal continues as usual, the authorities report. Shortly after the quake there were several aftershocks. The national weather service initially issued a tsunami warning for the coasts of Panama and several surrounding countries, but this was later lifted. Panama lies along the 'Ring of Fire', the arc of fault lines around the Pacific Ocean where most and the most severe earthquakes in the world occur. Next Monday a large national evacuation exercise was to take place in the country, to test how well the emergency services function during earthquakes.

title: 110 arrests on a day full of violence in central Brussels
lead: In Brussels, at least 110 people have been arrested after a union strike day turned into riots. Only in the course of the evening did calm return to the Belgian capital, reports VRT Nieuws. The unions protested today against cuts to social security. After a while, hundreds to thousands of young people mingled with the protesters. According to various media, this was because of the planned cuts to education, but the police deny that there was any link with those cuts or with the union action. The young people were mostly dressed in black and wore masks. They threw stones, set cars and shared bikes on fire, and caused many other acts of vandalism. The police deployed water cannons and tear gas to disperse the young people. The Belgian minister Quintin van <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity> has announced that a response will follow that is proportionate to the damage caused. The mayor of Brussels has also spoken out against the violence. He calls it "absoluut schandalig" that public services were attacked during the riots. The mayor wants a forceful response against the rioters and for identified perpetrators to pay financially for the damage. According to VRT, the unions had been warned that their strike action could possibly be hijacked. After education protests earlier this week in Liège, it had been advised to possibly postpone the action. On Tuesday, dozens of activists marched past secondary schools there, where they smashed windows and set trash cans on fire. Nevertheless, the unions decided to take to the streets today. This weekend the federal government is negotiating again about the cuts to social security. That is why the unions considered it important to make their voice heard today. According to Belgian media, the federal government is looking for about 10 billion euros to balance the budget. The unions fear that cuts will be made to social security among other areas. Watch footage of the disturbances earlier in the day here:

title: Yesilgöz despite criticism: 'I am the next lead candidate of the VVD'
lead: VVD leader Yesilgöz wants to become the party's lead candidate again at the next elections. In an interview with the NOS after a VVD gathering in Veghel, she clearly states her ambitions. Asked whether she is the logical next lead candidate of the VVD, Yesilgöz says: "Yes, I am." She has been party leader since August 2023, when she succeeded <entity id="person:mark-rutte">Mark Rutte</entity>. Criticism of Yesilgöz and of the course of the VVD leadership in <entity id="org:gemeente-s-gravenhage">Den Haag</entity> has been growing among the party rank and file recently. In the polls the governing party is not doing very well, and former VVD politicians are voicing their discontent through newspapers. Especially last week - when the cabinet plans of <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity>-Jetten were significantly amended at the urging of Pro and the trade unions - considerable dissatisfaction was heard among the rank and file. Concerns The party had given in too quickly to the pressure from Pro's <entity id="person:jesse-feras-klaver">leider Klaver</entity>, was one of the points of criticism. That stung all the more because during the campaign for the House of Representatives elections Yesilgöz had promised her voters not to go into partnership with this party, which in her view is too left-wing. Concerns also arose among VVD members about changes to the wealth tax (box 3). There is still no clarity on that. Yesilgöz says in the NOS interview that she does not like the criticism. "Not even as a person". She does feel that the media devote disproportionate attention to what happens at the VVD. She does not want to brush the criticism aside, but the emergence of unrest within a party "is timeless". She has experienced it as a council member, House of Representatives member and minister. "We are a party that enjoys debating, and afterwards we move on again." Today's gathering with critical VVD members from <entity id="org:provincie-noord-brabant">Noord-Brabant</entity> was, according to Yesilgöz, "very good". Together with House of Representatives parliamentary group chair Brekelmans, she answered questions for two hours in front of a room of about 150 members. In her view, the impression that the VVD "was rolling out a left-wing agenda" arose unjustly. Yesilgöz stresses that she does want to work with Pro, but then also together with the right-wing party JA21. "We do want to work with Pro, but not without the right." Afterwards she says that cooperation with Pro alone on "parts" might be possible, for example on the nitrogen plans. At the end of November there is a VVD congress. Then it will become clearer whether the VVD leadership has succeeded in reassuring the critical members about the approach.

title: Dozens of bullets fired in Overasselt: reconstruction of a night of excessive violence
lead: More than forty shots are fired at the officers who are the first to arrive on 1 September at the house of Jan G. in Overasselt. Shortly before, a large group of armed men had moved through the village and a security guard had been shot dead in his car. So far 42 suspects have been arrested for this outburst of violence, the last three only yesterday. Some perpetrators do not shrink from serious violence, others seem to have hardly any idea what they were recruited for. This is shown by a reconstruction by NOS based on documents from the criminal case file, in collaboration with Omroep Gelderland. 'Flashes of light from all sides' Shortly after 04.00 the first police car arrives on the Ewijkseweg in Overasselt. The officers are responding to an urgent report and were already warned by the control room to "put on heavy vests". As the two officers get out, they are immediately fired upon. One of them presses his emergency button and shouts in panic that he has a gunshot wound in his leg. His colleagues hear over the radio that the shooting continues non-stop. He is also hit in his other leg, and his colleague is shot in the foot. A second police car arrives at the scene. These officers see "many silhouettes of people" who are "running helter-skelter". They too are fired upon; there are "flashes of light from all sides". At risk to their own lives, the officers run to their seriously wounded colleague. Behind the police car he lies on the ground. Blood is pouring from his leg and the officers immediately know that his artery has been hit. They fear he will die on the spot. The shooting still continues; in total about forty shots are fired. The officers try to lift their injured colleagues into the car. The windscreen has been shot through, and there is no time to close the doors. While the lower body of the seriously wounded officer still hangs out of the car, they drive off at high speed. A colleague holds on to him so that he does not fall out. 'Dead man in the car' The officer behind the wheel wants to drive to a safe location, but has to stop on the way first to apply a pressure bandage. While officers rushing there cordon off the area in Overasselt with tape, a man comes walking toward them. In English with a French accent he says: "There is a man dead in the car." He points to the Ewijkseweg. The man who speaks to the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> is himself arrested a little later. He is one of the 42 suspects, 39 of whom are in custody. With one exception, they are all suspected of murder, attempted murder and a series of other offences. The youngest suspect is 16 years old and they come from all over: some from the Netherlands, others from Belgium, still others from France. A French suspect says after his arrest that he is homeless and sometimes steals food. Another still lives with his mother and has a debt of 25,000 euros. He is not allowed to come to Marseille anymore because he dealt drugs there. Some of the suspects were lured through intermediaries or via social media with the prospect of a "well-paid job". Many men say they had no idea what that job entailed. One said he assumed he had to steal cars; other suspects were told they had to beat someone up for 15,000 euros. "Is 15k, we get 7.5 today, the rest over 2 days max", reads a message on his phone. The French suspects gather in Brussels and at the start of the evening, on 31 August, are taken to an unknown warehouse. There their phones and identity papers are taken away. They are also handed heavy weapons and pistols. The group is split in two: people who can handle a weapon, and people who have never fired a shot. The first group must go in front, the second group forms the rearguard. Refusing the job is no longer an option. One suspect says he was threatened in the warehouse with a firearm because he wanted to leave. Another says he was beaten, after which his phone and the 85 euros he had with him were taken. One of the leaders seems to be someone called "the Chechen". Whoever does not listen will pay for it, he is said to have threatened. According to one of the suspects, it was said in the warehouse that someone had been shot dead the week before for refusing to cooperate. The group with weapons experience is told: "Everyone must die. Whether it's the goldfish or the cat: everyone must die." Afterwards the men in the back are driven to Overasselt in a truck or minibus. The police investigation also shows that several cars drove from Amsterdam to Overasselt. These are presumably the Dutch suspects. A number of them have extensive criminal records, from violent offences to bank helpdesk fraud. Futile warning On surveillance footage you can see two minibuses arriving on the street. A large group of men gets out. Some carry automatic firearms, others hold a pistol. A few minutes later the vehicles drive away again. In a car in front of the house of convicted drug criminal Jan G. sits security guard Berry. By chance Berry is on duty that night; he swapped a shift with his employer. When the two minibuses drive past his car, he gets out to see what is going on. Afterwards he calls his boss. The boss shouts that he should "bloody well get out of there". The connection is cut. This is how the minibuses arrived: The owner of the security company texts him several more times: "Get out of there", "Are you gone?" and "Let me know something". He also calls him four more times, but Berry no longer answers. He has been shot dead. The footage shows that 'the Chechen', a 30-year-old man from Ukraine, walks ahead on the Ewijkseweg. From the same footage investigators conclude that he may be the one who killed Berry. He was recognized by his Lacoste shoes. Other suspects may also have shot at the security guard. Not everyone in the group of suspects has an appetite for this violence. When the first shots are fired at 04.05, some of the men immediately take flight. Others shoot at the police, who arrive a few minutes later, and then run off. The moment the security guard is shot through: With suspects having fled in all directions, a large search immediately begins in the wider area around Overasselt. Some suspects are arrested fairly quickly in the village. A small group hides in a cornfield less than two kilometers from Jan G.'s house, which is surrounded by the Dutch Special Intervention Service. With thermal imaging cameras, drones and a helicopter the police manage to locate several suspects. 'The Chechen' is also picked out of the cornfield. The suspects try to escape the area in all sorts of ways. A truck with a Polish license plate, used with three suspects inside, is forced off the road on the A50. Three other suspects who fled in a car with a Belgian license plate are arrested at a petrol station in Nijmegen. Someone is arrested at a bus stop in Mill, another tries to order a taxi in soaking wet Malden. Three suspects get away with a lift but are still noticed elsewhere because they are covered in mud. Two suspects were even caught on stolen bicycles on a dike. The furthest two suspects get are those arrested on the A76 in Limburg, just before the Belgian border. They took a taxi from Cuijk, but the police still manage to find them shortly after 12.00. Also in the weeks after the incident, the police continue to arrest new suspects who may have played a role in the events in Overasselt. Yesterday three young men were arrested near Ghent. Client The investigation into the client behind the violence is ongoing; no one has been arrested for this yet. The first hearing in the case is in December. Target Jan G. is now also in custody. He managed to escape the violent outburst at his house, but was arrested more than two weeks later in Germany because he is allegedly involved in a large cocaine shipment.

title: Podcast De Dag: waiting for the surrogacy law
lead: In the Netherlands, around thirty to fifty families a year have a child with help from a surrogate mother, and that number is increasing. <entity id="person:rob-jetten">premier Jetten</entity> also says he has sometimes thought about it himself. But nothing has been legally regulated for this group, and that leads to problematic situations for both intended parents and surrogate mothers. Annemiek van Tilborgh, also known from B&B Vol Liefde, was a surrogate mother twice for a good friend. She does not want to raise the children herself, but she does regret how quickly she gave up legal parenthood. Want to listen? You can listen to this episode of De Dag via <entity id="org:zbo-nederlandse-publieke-omroep">NPO</entity> Luister and all other podcast apps. Do you like it? Then don't forget to subscribe. A new surrogacy law that <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> wants to introduce keeps being postponed in the meantime. Why? What are the dilemmas? Nieuwsuur journalist Fleur Damen spoke with surrogate mothers, intended parents, child judges and others. She saw how sensitive and emotional this dossier is for everyone. The need for clarity is great for many, but there are also objections and criticism of the draft law. Reactions? Email dedag@nos.nl Presentation and editing: Elisabeth Steinz Editorial team: Rosanne Sies Final editing: Judith van de Hulsbeek

title: Not burning but recycling: manufacturers must start collecting old furniture
lead: Many discarded sofas and other furniture still end up in incinerators. It is a shame, says <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity>. Furniture must be better recycled and reused. Just like plastic bottles and cans, within four years manufacturers and importers of products such as sofas, kitchen cabinets and beds will also become responsible for the collection and reuse of their products. The cabinet expects to have a first draft plan ready this autumn. A growing number of municipalities is already anticipating this and has started recycling furniture itself. At this recycling center in Geldrop they show how that works: In total, around 2 billion kilos of new furniture are sold per year in the Netherlands, according to the research agencies Tauw and Rebel. Each year, 260 million kilos of discarded furniture get a second life through, for example, online sales platforms or thrift shops. But most of it ends up at the recycling center. "Furniture doesn't last as long anymore," says Jacolien Eijer, director of the NVRD, the interest group for municipalities on waste collection. "Most of the furniture that comes to the recycling center ends up in the incinerator." And that is a shame, because materials such as wood, metal, textile and foam can often be reused very well. That is why producers and importers of furniture will be made responsible by 2030 at the latest for the collection and recycling or reuse of the items they put on the market. Barbecue aprons and animal leashes More and more municipalities and public waste companies do not want to wait for that and have set up dismantling halls themselves. By now there are six of them across the Netherlands. Often people with a distance to the labor market take the furniture apart. One of the waste companies involved is Cure Afvalbeheer, which handles collection in <entity id="org:gemeente-eindhoven">Eindhoven</entity>, <entity id="org:gemeente-valkenswaard">Valkenswaard</entity> and <entity id="org:gemeente-geldrop-mierlo">Geldrop-Mierlo</entity>. "We take apart all box springs and sofas that we receive through the recycling centers," says Twan de Waal of Cure. "Sofas without staples and with a lot of cardboard are taken apart in 20 minutes. Others are harder and take half an hour." Box springs are even harder. "There is a hard wooden side nailed on. You almost can't get those staples out." Cure partly does this from the perspective of sustainability. The materials from the furniture are reused. For example, the plastic is used to make beer crates and shopping baskets, the wood is used for new bathroom furniture, and the leather is used for animal leashes and barbecue aprons. In addition, cost savings are an important motive. The more waste is incinerated, the more incineration tax has to be paid. And that hits furniture hard, precisely because it forms such a large and heavy waste mountain. "That tax is already very high and will become much higher in the coming years," says De Waal of Cure. Citizens feel that in their wallets through the waste charges they pay. That is why it pays to extract reusable materials. "The less we have to incinerate, the lower the waste charge." Better to repair Furniture manufacturers and importers will now pay the costs. "This creates an incentive for producers to make furniture that is easier to take apart, better to repair and reuse, and lasts longer," says NVRD director Eijer. A number of companies have already started themselves. For example, IKEA has a buy-back service and customers can repair their furniture with spare parts. Office furniture company Ahrend refurbishes office furniture to sell again. Mandatory reuse According to Eijer, it is mainly important that clear targets come with the introduction for more sustainable design and reuse of materials in furniture.
