It has also not been established that she killed the child "with intent", but the court does hold that she should have known that the violence would be fatal. The fact that the child was only ten months old also weighs with the court. "He was completely defenceless and dependent on the suspect." The court also holds it heavily against the woman that she was unwilling to be open about the case, "as a result of which the relatives still do not know what happened". Child born in detention The sentence is somewhat lower than the nine years in prison that the Public Prosecution Service had demanded . In determining the sentence, the court took into account that the woman has been in pre-trial detention since 2024, while her husband cares for their two other children. One of the children was born while the woman was in detention and was taken away from her shortly after birth. "Under those circumstances it is understandable that the detention weighs very heavily on the suspect," the court said.

title: Man (23) arrested over death of Amsterdam woman Hajar (29) found dead
lead: The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> has arrested a suspect in connection with the death of 29-year-old Hajar. She was found dead last week in <entity id="org:gemeente-amsterdam">Amsterdam</entity>, after being missing for almost two weeks. The suspect was arrested today and is in custody, the Amsterdam triangle of mayor, police and justice announced this evening. The suspect is a 23-year-old man with Somali nationality, with no fixed residence, who has lived in the Netherlands since he was six and has a residence permit for an indefinite period. The suspect was initially seen as a witness and was questioned by police yesterday. This morning he was named as a suspect, because additional investigation made it clear to the police that he is "presumably involved in the death of Hajar". The police then actively searched for him. Arrest after violent incident This morning the police received a report of a violent incident in a house in the North Holland <entity id="org:gemeente-koggenland">gemeente Koggenland</entity>. At the home, officers found an injured man and arrested another man. That arrested man turned out to be the 23-year-old suspect in the investigation into Hajar's death. <entity id="person:femke-halsema">Burgemeester Halsema</entity> called for restraint at the press conference: Yesterday the police reported that the body of the woman had been found on 16 October in a suitcase in the water in the Amstel, near the Amsteldijk. Earlier it was already known that she had died as a result of a crime. No indications Hajar was reported missing on Sunday evening, 4 October, by a family member. The woman was last seen that day near the RAI event complex in Amsterdam. She then cycled together with an unknown man in the direction of the Buitenveldert neighbourhood, the police said earlier. The police report today that this man is the arrested man. The chief public prosecutor said this evening that there are no indications that Hajar and the suspect knew each other. The suspect has previously committed criminal offences such as shoplifting. Amsterdam mayor Halsema said at the press conference that the information currently available about the suspect may provide input "for an ongoing social and political debate about the background of perpetrators". Halsema said that for that, "this is not the place and not the moment". "Violence against women is a major, deep-rooted social and cultural problem that has plagued our society for a very long time and that occurs in all parts of our society." In deep mourning The organisation Namens de Familie, which speaks on behalf of Hajar's family, says it is "very glad" that a suspect has been arrested, but also that the family "is still in deep mourning over the loss of their daughter, sister, family member". "The family therefore attaches great value to being able to say farewell to their loved one in peace, anonymity and full privacy."

title: Infighting within ShinyHunters, an FBI hack and murder commissions: the Pepijn van der S. case
lead: The 24-year-old Pepijn van der S. was recently arrested on suspicion of participating in the notorious hacker group ShinyHunters and of inciting two murders. RTL Nieuws reconstructs how the Dutch hacker came back into view of the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> and became entangled in a conflict within the international cybercriminal world.

title: With a child via a surrogate it can take two years until you are officially the parent
lead: <entity id="person:rob-jetten">Premier Jetten</entity> and his partner Nicolás Keenan are expecting a child next spring, they announced yesterday. Two friends are the egg donor and the surrogate. That is first and foremost a private matter, but when it concerns the prime minister of the Netherlands, it is also public and political. Surrogacy is indeed a topic high on the political agenda. A surrogate carries a child for someone else, here for a male couple. That can be done with an own egg or with a donor egg. In this case a donor egg was fertilised via IVF and placed in the surrogate, who goes through the pregnancy and gives birth to the child. Jetten and Keenan shared this on Instagram. They have not disclosed who the biological father is. Clear agreements Being a surrogate is a major decision, emotionally, physically and legally. If you have found someone willing to be a surrogate, clear agreements must be made. The law does not help with that, because the bill for the Act on child, surrogacy and descent has been waiting since 2023 for <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity> to deal with it. It is now on the agenda for December. "I hope this wonderful news for the prime minister will make the House step on the gas a bit more for the legislation", says Arnoud Breitbarth, chairman of the Stichting Meer dan gewenst, to the NOS. "Surrogacy must be arranged properly, the child must be able to trace how it came into the world, a careful process is needed", says Breitbarth, who himself is the father of twins with his partner. He points out that intended parents, surrogates, but above all the children, must be well protected. Long road Although there is no law yet, there are rules. Surrogacy is not prohibited, but a surrogate may not ask for money for carrying someone else's child. She may receive a compensation for expenses, however. Often people who wish to have a child look for someone in the family or circle of friends. Once the child is born, it can take up to two years before the intended parents are also recognised as parents by law. The surrogate is always on the birth certificate, and if she is married to or in a registered partnership with a man, he is also listed. The court must 'deny' this fatherhood and the biological father must recognise the child. Then the second intended parent must adopt the child, and only then does the surrogate lose her legal parenthood. All of this is recorded in a deed that is added to the birth certificate. Only then do the intended parents have the rights of parenthood. Until that is arranged, the actual parents are highly dependent on the surrogate. "In practice you run into the fact that you cannot get a BSN number, cannot take out health insurance, that you cannot register the child for the crèche, or that the surrogate first has to give consent for vaccinations", Breitbarth says from his own experience. Also in hospital you have no parental authority and cannot make necessary decisions. "That lies with the surrogate, and she is often not waiting for that either. She has to make decisions she does not want to make." "If the surrogate dies while parenthood has not yet been transferred, that child suddenly gets a child's share of the inheritance, while that was not the surrogate's intention. Those are serious problems. Fortunately that happens quite rarely." Breitbarth hopes the law comes quickly. Law still to be adjusted But not everyone agrees with the bill that is on the table. It regulates, among other things, that the intended parents have custody from birth. Judges think some major problems will not be prevented by it. They want it to be possible to check after birth whether everything went well and whether the agreements made are kept. That is why they want the proposed period of three months before intended parents receive parental custody to be extended. A majority in the Tweede Kamer is also not yet certain. As a result, it could well happen that the law is not yet in place before the prime minister's child is born.

title: Vinted removes listings of items stolen during French protests
lead: Vinted has removed listings of products offered for sale that are presumably stolen during the large-scale protests in France last Saturday. The secondhand sales platform also says it has tightened its checks on suspicious listings, French media report. Among others, cosmetics chain Sephora reported that stores had been broken into. Footage also shows shop windows smashed and looting at branches of luxury fashion brands such as Céline, Louis Vuitton and Hermès. Some resellers of the stolen products explicitly state in the listing description the day protests took place across France, 17 October, or that the goods are stolen, French media report. Minister's call French Minister of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-diza">Digitale Zaken</entity> Le Hénanff has called on online sellers such as Amazon, eBay and Vinted to take the listings offline. "We expect these platforms to remove the relevant listings immediately, without delay." Le Hénanff also says the platforms must cooperate with the government so that sellers can be prosecuted. Vinted says it is cooperating with the French authorities, news agency Reuters reports. The company says it has taken "immediate action" and that accounts that violate the rules may receive a permanent ban.

title: 16 years in prison for shooting with automatic weapon at football club in Zwolle
lead: A 28-year-old man from Zwolle has been sentenced to 16 years in prison for shooting a man at a football club in Zwolle. In September 2024 the man opened fire with an automatic weapon on the Zwolle criminal Emin Y. The perpetrator and the victim knew each other from the criminal milieu. According to the <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity>, the shooting was part of a long-running conflict. The trigger was the possible theft of the customer database of a courier service by a rival drug gang. The 33-year-old Y. is seen as one of the main players in the conflict. In June he was sentenced to 10.5 years in prison for, among other things, organised drug trafficking and a violent kidnapping. 25 bullets fired The conflict led to incidents in 2024, several of which took place on the day of the shooting, writes RTV Oost. For example, there was reportedly a fire in the car of Y.'s father, and a friend of the suspect was then allegedly taken hostage. According to the regional broadcaster, this happened in response to the car fire. Later that day, the suspect and the victim had a brief conversation about the conflict at the canteen of the Zwolle football club Ulu Spor. After the conversation the perpetrator went home, where he fetched an automatic firearm, two pistols and ammunition. He then drove back to the football canteen, where he walked in armed. Panic broke out there. Emin Y. escaped outside through a window. The shooter also went back outside and fired a total of 25 bullets at the victim from a few metres away. The victim was hit by three bullets and was wounded. Several other bullets went through the facade and landed in the football canteen, where at least three other people were present at that moment. Attempted murder The court rules that the shooter is guilty of attempted murder of both the victim and the other people present. According to the judges, the man had enough time after the conversation with the victim to think about the consequences of his act. Also, by shooting in the direction of the canteen, the man took the risk that other people present would be hit by the bullets. "Such a shooting in a public space not only impacts those present, but also causes social unrest and feelings of insecurity," the court ruled. No case of self-defence The lawyer for the perpetrator stated during the hearing that the victim had threatened the man before the shooting and that the shooter was reportedly on a death list. There would therefore allegedly be psychological duress and self-defence, meaning the shooter could not act otherwise. The court did not accept this. All in all, the court arrives at an unconditional prison sentence of 16 years. In determining the sentence, the court took into account that the shooting was part of a conflict in the criminal milieu, "in which the suspect took the law into his own hands". The sentence is lower than the demand of the Openbaar Ministerie. The prosecution demanded a prison sentence of 20 years two weeks ago.

title: First ebola case in Nigeria since new outbreak in Africa
lead: The health authorities in Nigeria have confirmed an ebola infection in the capital Abuja. It is the first case of ebola in the West African country since the recent outbreak of the virus in the centre of the continent. The patient is a woman who had been in Uganda. The authorities there stated at the end of July that their country was ebola-free, after twenty cases had been confirmed. Most of these reportedly involved people from the severely affected Congo who sought help in Uganda. "She is in isolation and receiving good care", health minister Pate said in a TV interview about the woman in Abuja. The source and contact investigation is ongoing, he also said. So far, 44 people with whom the woman had contact have been traced. Thousands dead The ebola outbreak mainly affects the Democratic Republic of Congo. There, since mid-May, at least 9500 infections have been confirmed. More than 4600 ebola patients have died. That makes it the deadliest outbreak ever in the country. The virus has also been confirmed in nine people in Kenya, which borders Uganda. Ebola is a highly contagious infectious disease caused by the ebola virus. Most people develop serious symptoms, such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea and bleeding. More than half of people with ebola die.

title: 4 years in prison demanded against man who planned an attack on a proposed asylum centre in Doetinchem
lead: The <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity> (OM) has demanded a four-year prison sentence , one year of which is suspended, against a man from Doetinchem because he is said to have planned an attack on a proposed shelter for asylum seekers in that city. The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> responded in the night of 8 to 9 December last year to a report of vandalism and trespassing at the home of the 37-year-old suspect's ex-partner. The man fled, but was eventually arrested at a friend's home. His ex-girlfriend told the police that the man had been asked to place cobras at a future asylum centre in exchange for payment, the OM writes. That same night in December, the police found an explosive in a garage box. According to the OM, it concerned four cobras taped together and fitted with a fuse. The Explosive Ordnance Disposal Service <entity id="org:ministerie-van-defensie">Defensie</entity> (EOD) had to dismantle the package. Demonstrations. A few months before the explosive was found, a protest took place in Doetinchem against the arrival of an asylum centre in the city. Riots also broke out. Last summer, a little over a year after the protest, the reception location opened. According to the OM, the suspect was busy "preparing an attack with a terrorist intent" at the upcoming asylum centre. The judiciary concludes that the man "wanted to instill serious fear in part of the population, namely the asylum seekers who are to be housed". "He also wanted to force the local government in this way not to house asylum seekers in the municipality." Reconnaissance. The OM is convinced that the suspect actually wanted to carry out an attack because last September he scouted the possible location for the shelter. He took photos of the place and sent them to a group chat. In addition, he attended protests against the arrival of the shelter last year. According to the OM, the statements of, among others, his ex-girlfriend and the discovery of the explosive also prove that the suspect wanted to carry out an attack. "If there are objections or differences of opinion, these must be expressed and resolved through peaceful and democratic means," said the OM. "Using potentially violent force with a heavy explosive, as in this case, is therefore completely incompatible with and unacceptable." The court will rule in two weeks.

title: Two suspects arrested again over incident at English air force base
lead: British police have re-arrested two men over the incident at the Fairford air force base at the end of September. They are suspected of helping the Iranian intelligence service. The counter-terrorism unit of the police arrested a 24-year-old Briton who had already been arrested at the air base on 27 September. The second suspect is a 25-year-old British-Iranian man who was arrested in London on 1 October. Both were released after their first arrest. Bombers removed. On 27 September, five Britons were arrested near the Royal Air Force base in the English county of Gloucestershire. They were suspected of preparing a terrorist attack. The group of five was later released under conditions. The RAF base is used by the Americans in the war against Iran. American military personnel are stationed at the base. After the incident at Fairford, the US removed twelve bombers from the air base in October. This reportedly happened because of a threat that, according to the British authorities, comes from Iran. The US also points to Iran, but that country denies being involved.

title: Fire brigade rescues people from roof at house fire in Hengelo
lead: At a house fire in the Overijssel town of Hengelo, the fire brigade rescued people from the roof this evening. The fire is now under control. The fire broke out around 19.00 hours in a house on the Oelerweg. On arrival, the fire brigade saw that the roof of the building was on fire. People were standing on the roof at that time. They were brought down with a cherry picker. The people involved were checked by ambulance staff because they had inhaled smoke. No one had to go to hospital, the safety region reports. Lots of smoke The fire caused considerable smoke development. The area was therefore cordoned off and residents were advised to stay out of the smoke and, in case of nuisance, to close windows and doors. Around 19.30 hours the fire brigade declared the fire under control. How the fire started and how large the damage is is not known.

title: Hackers obtained over 400,000 AfD emails, including those of party leader Weidel
lead: The German political party AfD has fallen victim to a hack. According to the newspaper Bild , which first reported the news, unknown persons have obtained more than 400,000 emails, including emails from party leader Alice Weidel and founder and honorary chairman Alexander Gauland. The AfD confirms the hack. According to a spokesperson, the unknown perpetrators copied data from a limited number of email accounts at a hosting provider. Most of these reportedly have not been in use for years. The party is still investigating exactly what data was stolen. 49,000 documents According to the opinion magazine Stern, the 421,000 emails date from the period 2014 to 12 September of this year. Of these, 39,000 have one or more attachments. In total this involves 49,000 documents, including photos of identity documents, bank statements and membership lists. According to Stern, the hackers put nearly 60,000 emails online that can be searched by keyword. A category system has also been created, ranging from documents about minor misconduct to documents that reportedly involve "criminal offences or violence". Extremist According to Stern, an email exchange between two AfD members from the state of North Rhine-Westphalia concerns the subject "Sale of swastika flags and drugs at an information stand in Bottrop by a branch chairman". Another email reportedly shows that a branch chairman from the municipality of Lippe sent a Christmas card with a swastika and the Nazi salute "Heil Hitler". The domestic intelligence service BfV considers the party partly far-right . Xenophobia, racism and antisemitism are reportedly widespread within the party.

title: 'Suspect in Hajar case arrested after assault on foster father'
lead: The man who was arrested for the death of the 29-year-old Hajar used violence against his foster father on Tuesday morning. Hart van Nederland reports that this is based on a neighbour . Also NOS spoke to a neighbour who said it concerns the suspect's foster father. The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> has not confirmed this, but says the two know each other. The violent incident took place on Spierdijk, in the North Holland <entity id="org:gemeente-koggenland">gemeente Koggenland</entity>. The victim was found injured by the police and has been taken to hospital. According to the neighbour who spoke to NOS, the suspect lived in the foster family until he was sixteen. The man is now 23 years old, has Somali nationality and has no fixed residence or place of stay in the Netherlands, the police announced at a press conference. He came to the Netherlands at the age of six and has a residence permit for an indefinite period. The suspect was initially seen as a witness and was still questioned by the police on Monday. On Tuesday morning he was designated a suspect, because the police's additional investigation made clear that he is "presumably involved in the death of Hajar". The police then actively searched for him. The report about the violent incident in Spierdijk came in at 08.20 hours. Shortly before, just before 08.00 hours, the description of the suspect had been circulated to all police units in the Netherlands. An officer who had responded to the report in Spierdijk recognised the suspect's description. Found in the water: Hajar was reported missing by a family member on Sunday evening, 4 October. That day she was seen near the RAI event complex in <entity id="org:gemeente-amsterdam">Amsterdam</entity>. The police reported yesterday that research has shown she cycled with the Somali suspect towards the Buitenveldert district that day. They reportedly did not know each other before that. Last Friday Hajar's body was found in the water at the Amsteldijk in Amsterdam. By then it was already clear she had died as a result of a crime. Earlier this week the police reported that her body had been found in a suitcase. The police suspect that Hajar was killed shortly after she went missing.

title: WSJ: Musk behind Starlink restrictions for Ukraine
lead: Elon Musk personally ordered restrictions on Ukraine's access to the Starlink satellite network. That is what The Wall Street Journal reports, based on American officials and other sources "who are familiar with the matter". According to the American newspaper, Musk's intervention not only caused panic in Kyiv, but also confusion within the administration of President Trump. Due to the restrictions Ukraine experienced, drones could only be deployed at the front at a much lower speed, which made them vulnerable. This applies to drones used for attack, but also to drones used to defend the country. The satellite system is crucial for communication within the Ukrainian army. Musk and Trump reportedly discussed the intervention in advance and also held consultations after the restrictions were imposed, the paper writes. Yet both have publicly stated that they have nothing to do with it. Musk said that only the American military or President Trump can make such a decision. Betrayal Yesterday Ukrainian President Zelensky had a meeting in Oslo with the American envoy Witkoff. Norwegian Prime Minister Store and Finnish President Stubb were also present, in an attempt to "stimulate the dialogue between Ukraine and the US but also with Russia". In recent days Zelensky has criticised the US and Trump. The American president concluded a diesel agreement with Russia, lifted sanctions and demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries. Trump also remarked that it is time the Ukrainians got a different leader, and falsely claimed that Russia recently "has not done so much" against Ukraine. In reality Russia has stepped up its attacks on Ukraine, many civilian casualties continue to fall, and it deliberately hits Ukraine's energy infrastructure hard ahead of winter. In a reaction to the American rapprochement with Russia, Zelensky said it felt like betrayal. Witkoff goes to Saint Petersburg today, reportedly with proposals to end the war. That war began in February 2022 with a large-scale invasion of Ukraine by Russia.

title: Pakistan arrests man for large-scale fraud against US postal service
lead: In Pakistan a man has been arrested in a fraud case that reportedly cost the US postal service more than 126 million dollars. The 33-year-old Faheem Akram was apprehended after an intensive manhunt lasting a week, according to Pakistani authorities. Akram was charged in Florida, as became clear at the end of September. The man ran a website on which he sold fake labels for parcels to thousands of customers. For these they mostly paid 2 dollars, regardless of the weight of a parcel, its size or destination. With the fake labels, Akram's customers could send mail far below the regular price of the U.S. Postal Service. According to American investigators, the Pakistani's website was online from August 2023 to September of this year. Akram reportedly used sixteen different bank accounts for the dubious practices. Some of these were in the name of his brother, his wife and an aunt. The American news agency AP writes that it is unclear whether the Pakistani will be extradited to the United States or will be tried in Pakistan.

title: Guatemalan gets 30 years in US prison for role in deadly people smuggling case
lead: A man from Guatemala has been sentenced in the US to 30 years in prison for his role in a people smuggling case. In that case 53 migrants died in 2022; they suffocated in a trailer during a three-hour journey between the Mexican border city Nuevo Laredo and the Texan city San Antonio. The Guatemalan (50) had admitted that he arranged travel documents and accommodation for two of the migrants who died, as well as for two migrants who suffered serious injuries. The migrants, from Guatemala but also from other Central and South American countries, paid up to 15,000 dollars for the crossing. The prosecutor in the case said the migrants in the trailer suffered unprecedented agony in their final hours. Judging by traces in the trailer, it became clear that people "tried to claw their way out". The air conditioning in the trailer was not working, so it had become blisteringly hot. When the abandoned trailer was opened on a deserted road in San Antonio, 48 bodies were inside. Sixteen migrants were taken to hospitals, of whom five later died. 'Very harsh' More suspects are still awaiting their sentences in the case. Last year two people involved received life imprisonment and 83 years in prison for their part in the people smuggling case. Over the past decades thousands of migrants have died in their attempts to cross the Mexican-American border. The lawyer for the Guatemalan called the sentence his client received "very harsh". He stressed that the man was at the time himself staying in Guatemala and therefore had no influence over the type of vehicle used; as a result he would also not have known that the air conditioning was not working. According to the lawyer, high sentences serve no purpose and immigration reforms are needed instead.

title: 'A lot of what is said in the House of Representatives also comes from AI'
lead: That politicians use AI for their social media posts or for asking parliamentary questions was already known, but now it turns out that much of what members of the House of Representatives say in the House is also thought up with the help of chatbots. Opinion weekly De Groene Amsterdammer and platform Investico write that 68 members of parliament last year had speeches written with artificial intelligence tools such as ChatGPT and Claude. The investigative journalists ran all the speeches of the 150 members of the House of Representatives through Pangram, a program that can scan texts for the use of AI. Almost certainly even more members used chatbots, because texts that were written for less than 50 percent with AI were excluded from the study. It concerns the texts with which members begin their contributions in the House. Interruptions and motions do not count. This ultimately produced a list of 68 members. At the top is former member of parliament Lahlah of Pro, who is now alderman in <entity id="org:gemeente-amsterdam">Amsterdam</entity>. After her follow Van Meetelen (PVV), Belhirch (D66) and Van Eijk (VVD). Popular across parliament: The top 4 already shows that chatbot use is popular across the whole width of the House of Representatives. According to De Groene Amsterdammer and Investico, extreme right-wing factions such as the PVV and Groep Markuszower are overrepresented. Only the SP, Partij voor de Dieren and Volt do not use them at all. Former member Lahlah took part in five debates last year on, among other things, poverty policy and the Participation Act. In four of them she consulted chatbots. In a written response she says her contributions to debates were always based on conversations with citizens during working visits. "Those stories are sometimes difficult to capture in a few minutes of speaking time, so I used AI." The research shows that some members also used AI for their maiden speech. That is the first time they speak in the House, and it is usually a personal story. Furthermore, it stands out that the top of the list is mainly backbenchers and less prominent representatives who are also often new to the House. In the big debates where faction leaders speak, for example the General Political Considerations after Prinsjesdag, hardly or no AI texts are heard. In committee debates in back rooms, more than half of the speeches are sometimes drafted with the digital tools. Shortening arguments: All 'caught' members admit they use artificial intelligence for their speeches. They add that they only use it as a tool, to make sentences flow better or to shorten their argument. "I will never deliver a text I don't stand behind," says PVV member Van Meetelen. Of the contributions of the three BBB members, about 30 percent largely comes from ChatGPT or Claude, the analysis shows. According to <entity id="person:hendrik-vermeer">fractievoorzitter Vermeer</entity>, that is not strange for a small faction with a lot of work. "We also use calculators, mobile phones and even coffee machines." CDA member Krul is shocked that he is at number 5 on the list. He acknowledges that he sometimes uses AI to shorten texts, while the content must be preserved. "I would find it very bad if the image now arises that his contributions come entirely from Chat." Krul's <entity id="person:hendrik-bontenbal">partijleider Bontenbal</entity>, by contrast, attaches great importance to authenticity. According to him, the CDA faction is working on guidelines for AI use. "I would find it very bad if my faction members used search queries like 'make up three Christian democratic ideas on topic X, Y, or Z'." Jetten on social media: Earlier it turned out that <entity id="person:rob-jetten">premier Jetten</entity> regularly uses AI to draft social media posts. And research by the NOS showed last month that a quarter of the written questions from members were drafted with AI help. The AI detection program Pangram mainly looks at sentence constructions that chatbots like to use, such as contrasts, arguments in threes (the so-called triad) and the dash that often signals a turn in a sentence.

title: Wake-up call 21/10: DSW announces health insurance premium • ADE begins in Amsterdam
lead: Good morning! As is tradition, insurer DSW has the scoop on the level of the new health insurance premium, and it is the first day of the Amsterdam Dance Event . First, the weather: today it is cloudy in many places with some rain here and there. The wind is coming from the south and southwest. It will be around 13 to 15 degrees. Are you going out today? Here you can find an overview of traffic jams and roadworks, and here you can see the situation on the railways. What can you expect today? What did you miss? At the German political party AfD, possibly more than 420,000 emails have been taken by a hack. German media report this. The emails of party prominents are also presumably in the hands of the hackers. The emails reportedly contained Nazi statements, including "Heil Hitler". The AfD itself confirms the hack. According to a spokesperson, the unknown perpetrators copied data from a limited number of email accounts at a hosting provider. Most of those reportedly have not been in use for years. The party is still investigating exactly what data was stolen. Other news from overnight: And then just this: There is an enormous new Beatles museum coming to Liverpool, the English port city where the band was formed in 1960. The current Beatles Story museum will move in 2028 to a former shopping centre. A vacant tower will also be put into use, which will become a special Yellow Submarine attraction. The two surviving Beatles, Ringo Starr and Paul McCartney, made the plans public yesterday. "I find it incredible and feel honoured that people are still interested in our story", said McCartney. "Liverpool was the music city and still is", said Starr. Have a great day!

title: UN report: warming of more than 1,5 degrees Celsius unavoidable
lead:
It is unavoidable that the Earth will warm by more than 1,5 degrees Celsius. That is the conclusion of the UN in an annual report. The figure has been central to the approach to climate change for more than ten years. Breaching the 1,5 degree limit illustrates how stubborn efforts to curb climate change are. There are several reasons why it has not succeeded in staying below that limit. In recent years, less oil, coal and natural gas should have been burned, because the greenhouse gases released when they are burned warm the Earth. In practice the opposite happened. "Emissions have kept rising and we have once again lost a number of years," says Michel den Elzen, researcher at the <entity id="org:planbureau-voor-de-leefomgeving">Planbureau voor de Leefomgeving</entity> and the Vrije Universiteit, who contributed to the UN report.

Changed plans

The climate target is also no longer achievable because several countries did less than expected. For example, the United States under President Trump scrapped virtually all of its climate policy, and new climate plans from other countries have only marginally reduced emissions. Almost all countries agreed in Paris ten years ago to keep warming well below 2 degrees Celsius, and preferably below 1,5 degrees. In recent years, fewer and fewer experts expected that the latter was still feasible. This autumn the United Nations also acknowledges that the world will overshoot 1,5 degrees. They wrote that in September and now again in the annual report on progress in tackling climate change. In November countries will discuss this at the climate summit in the Turkish city of Antalya.

Temporary overshoot?

The highest achievable goal, according to the UN, is now to keep the overshoot as limited and brief as possible. That requires far-reaching steps. It is not only about using less coal, natural gas and oil, because even if people stop those emissions, there are already more greenhouse gases in the air than before. Some of those would have to be partly removed from the air to cool the Earth, so that warming falls back below 1,5 degrees. "That can be done with technology to store CO2, or also through more reforestation," says Den Elzen. Technically this is possible, but it would have to happen on a very large scale. You would have to plant enormous areas of land, or enormous numbers of 'CO2 vacuum cleaners' would be needed. It is an open question whether support, space and money can be found for this.

Why 1,5 degrees?

A group of islands in the Pacific Ocean launched the goal of keeping global warming below 1,5 degrees Celsius at the 2009 climate summit in Copenhagen. A strong rise in sea level threatens the survival of these low-lying countries, so they wanted more action against climate change. The summit in Copenhagen was a failure. But six years later, almost all countries agreed in Paris to keep warming well below 2 degrees Celsius and preferably below 1,5 degrees. Doubts about feasibility were also raised then. The Paris summit asked for research into the difference in consequences between 1,5 and 2 degrees of warming. Three years later the climate panel IPCC published the outcome. It showed that there are significant differences. For example, at 1,5 degrees of warming part of the coral reefs survive, while with more warming they almost entirely disappear. A rise below 1,5 degrees also limits sea level rise and the chance of extreme heat, which can also be dangerous for people. Time is also running out for limiting the overshoot. "There is a chance that we will also have to say goodbye to these scenarios," says researcher Den Elzen. If emissions rise or stay high in the coming years, global warming will continue. "It is now or never."

Growing technologies

To stay below 2 degrees Celsius of warming, countries must pull out all the stops in the coming years. With current policy the world is on course for more warming. Many countries promised to bring their emissions down to zero, but concrete plans on how this should happen are often lacking. Remarkably, wind and solar energy have grown faster than researchers had expected. Like other technologies, such as electric cars and batteries, which emit no CO2 during use. "That is indeed going faster than expected," says Den Elzen. But so far it is not enough to bring down the use of oil, coal and gas.

title: Fire in three homes in the historic city centre of Gouda, three injured
lead: Three people were injured in a fire in the city centre of Gouda. The fire raged in three homes. The surrounding houses have been evacuated. Around 03.45 hours a fire broke out in a home on the Regulierenhof. It spread to two neighbouring homes. According to Omroep West, the fire started in a home more than 120 years old. The cause of the fire is not yet known. The home where the fire broke out has been completely destroyed, the fire brigade says. The three injured were taken to hospital with unknown injuries. Around 05.30 hours the fire was under control, according to the Veiligheidsregio Hollands Midden. The fire brigade is still carrying out demolition work and mopping up. Measurements for carbon monoxide are being taken. If the readings are negative, residents of the surrounding houses may go back home. It has not been announced how many people this concerns.

title: Colombia intercepts 7600 kilos of cocaine bound for the Netherlands
lead: In Colombia, the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> has seized around 7600 kilos of cocaine intended for the Netherlands. In the port of the Colombian city of Cartagena, according to the authorities, the largest batch of cocaine in the past ten years was seized. The drugs were discovered during an inspection. Images show packaging of powdered sugar in which the cocaine was hidden. The president of Colombia, Abelardo de la Espriella, speaks of a "historic blow to drug terrorism". According to the president, the police have taken around 75 million lines or dots of cocaine off the street. The Colombian police worked together with the American drug enforcement agency DEA. The president says his country will continue to act strictly against criminal and armed groups.

title: US envoy Witkoff with Putin in St Petersburg, first oil tanker to the US tomorrow
lead: US envoy Steve Witkoff is speaking with President Putin in St Petersburg about proposals to end the war in Ukraine. Witkoff will, among other things, make a proposal for a meeting between Presidents Putin, Trump and Zelensky. Trump's son-in-law and adviser Jared Kushner is taking part in the talks via a video link. He is not in Russia, because he is ill. Witkoff was received at St Petersburg airport this morning by a confidant of President Putin, businessman Kirill Dmitriev. Alongside the talks about ending the war, an oil agreement is also being discussed. Oil tanker to the US Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak announced via Russian media a short while ago that the first tanker with Russian diesel will set off for the US tomorrow. "Subsequent shipments will certainly follow," he said. According to the deputy prime minister, the signing of the contract is "in the final phase". The New York Times reported earlier this month on the expansion of the peace talks with an oil agreement. This would involve billions of dollars and would benefit businessmen from the Middle East with ties to Witkoff and Kushner. The deal would revolve around Lukoil, one of Russia's largest energy companies, which is still on the sanctions list. Hubbard released Reports from Russian media also show that 74-year-old Stephen Hubbard has been released. He was captured by the Russian army in 2022. Russia accuses him of having fought as a mercenary in the Ukrainian army. According to Russian media, Hubbard is already at St Petersburg airport. Witkoff's mission to get Zelensky to the table was discussed yesterday at a meeting in Oslo with Kushner and Zelensky himself. Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre and Finnish President Alexander Stubb were also present. "You cannot talk about the future of Ukraine without Ukraine sitting at the table," Zelensky said at a press conference afterwards. Prime Minister Støre said that Europe will also have to sit at the table "if you want a lasting and fair peace". Russian reaction A spokesperson said yesterday that the Kremlin "greatly appreciates" the American peace efforts, but that "a final settlement is impossible without the participation of someone from Kyiv who is prepared to take responsibility". US Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters in India today that the meeting between Witkoff and Zelensky went positively. "Let's see whether we can make some progress," he added. Russian attacks have continued without pause since last night, Ukrainian Prime Minister Koretskyi writes on Telegram. In Kyiv, a drone hit a 24-storey residential building, killing two people. And in Kharkiv, two people died in attacks on homes. Eleven others were injured, including two children. What do you think of the NOS app and website? What do we do well? What could be better? We are keen to hear your opinion. Fill in the survey via this link.

title: More employees working past retirement age, especially in the real estate sector
lead: A growing share of all Dutch employees are older than the AOW retirement age, reports the <entity id="org:zbo-centraal-bureau-voor-de-statistiek">CBS</entity>. In the second quarter of 2026, 1.7 percent of employees were older than the age at which they are entitled to AOW. The CBS measured this percentage over the past years. In the first quarter of 2018, 1.2 percent of employees kept working after their AOW age. Proportionally, most people keep working after their AOW age in the real estate rental and trade sector: 4.3 percent. This is followed by the transport and storage sector with 3.6 percent. In the public administration and government services sector, the percentage is lowest at 0.6 percent. In government, employment often ends automatically when people reach the AOW age. Men keep working after their AOW age more often than women. Of all male employees, 2.3 percent were older than the AOW age in the second quarter. Among female employees this was 1.1 percent. Combating boredom: Last year it already became clear that people are working past their AOW age more often. The CBS then reported that of all working people, a quarter million are AOW recipients. Reasons to keep working are, according to the demographic institute NIDI, among others enjoyment of the work, combating boredom and feeling useful. To a lesser extent, earning money also plays a role, research by that institute showed. For 10 percent of people, that is very important.

title: Fishing out millions of kilos of waste wins Boyan Slat a Qatari prize
lead: Couch sets, shop window mannequins and even human remains. The Dutch inventor Boyan Slat comes across the craziest things in his fight against plastic pollution. His organization The Ocean Cleanup has, by its own account, already fished 65 million kilos of waste out of the sea and rivers. Last night Slat (32) received a prize in Qatar for his work: in the capital Doha he received the International Young Energy Leader Award. This happened at the presentation of the Abdullah bin Hamad Al-Attiyah International Energy Awards, prizes in the field of energy and sustainability, named after the godfather of the Qatari gas industry. In the ballroom of the luxurious Sheraton Hotel he addressed some 400 high-ranking officials from the oil and gas industry from the stage. Not impossible The contradiction is not lost on Slat: Qatar is considered one of the largest exporters of fossil fuels in the world, which also supply the most important raw materials for the production of plastic. At the same time, the wealthy country is precisely the place to raise funds. In his speech of thanks, Slat looked back on the beginning of his adventure. "When I was 16 and came up with this idea, most people thought it was impossible, but now we are doing it." One of the most remarkable finds of Slat and his organization was a water bottle from the American army from the Vietnam War. "It was still intact", says Slat in conversation with the NOS in Doha. "That shows how long that junk keeps drifting if you don't remove it." Regularly, unusual objects are found at sea, from golf balls to shop window mannequins. In rivers, staff sometimes come across gruesome finds. "Also bodies", says Slat. "Unfortunately that is something we sometimes deal with, especially in countries with a lot of crime." Kilos of plastic per second The Ocean Cleanup, based in Rotterdam, is now active in twelve countries and employs some 350 staff. According to Slat, the organization currently intercepts almost one kilo of waste per second and thereby prevents up to 5 percent of the global inflow of plastic into the oceans. Slat became known for his plans to clean up the plastic soup in the Pacific Ocean, but his company now focuses on rivers. Research by The Ocean Cleanup showed that only 1 percent of all rivers are responsible for about 80 percent of the plastic that ends up in the sea. That is why the company developed special installations, interceptors, that catch waste before it reaches the ocean. "If you can choose between cleaning up plastic at sea or intercepting it before it ends up there, the latter is of course much cheaper", says Slat. Over the next three years he wants to tackle pollution in some 250 rivers in thirty cities. That could prevent up to a third of the global inflow of plastic into the sea. Cheaper than Halloween decorations That requires a lot of money. The Ocean Cleanup received 121 million dollars pledged this year from The Audacious Project, a philanthropic club that includes Bill Gates and MacKenzie Scott, the ex of Jeff Bezos, among others. Still, there is a shortfall of 40 million dollars per year, says Slat. "It is the cheapest world problem to solve", he says. "Those 40 million are just 2 percent of what Americans spend annually on Halloween decorations." The funding for 22 new interceptors is still lacking. If that money does not come in by the end of the year, the project threatens to be delayed. In Doha Slat appealed to the wealthy executives in the room: "Qatar has shown the world what is possible when ambition goes hand in hand with investment and a long-term vision. That is an opportunity to apply that same mentality to one of the biggest environmental problems of our time." 'Not an environmental activist' Slat does not see himself as an environmental activist, but rather as an inventor and entrepreneur. "For me it is simply a technical problem. What is the fastest and most effective way to solve it?" He has little time for the idea that environmental problems should mainly be tackled by consuming less. According to him, the solution lies in technological innovation. "People simply have needs and wishes. The question is how we can shape our society so that those can be met without harm to the environment." Does he never get angry about the mess he encounters? "For me a problem is simply something to be solved. Getting angry doesn't help."

title: Actress Christina Applegate does not have MS after all: 'I'm back to square one'
lead: Actress Christina Applegate does not have MS after all. The 54-year-old American says this in a podcast. Applegate says that, according to her doctor, she was not given the correct diagnosis. "I'm back to square one", Applegate says in the podcast MeSsy, which she makes together with actress Jamie-Lynn Sigler about living with MS. Sigler, known from The Sopranos among others, has had MS for 25 years. Applegate, who broke through in the late 1980s as Kelly Bundy in the sitcom Married with Children, announced in 2021 that she had been diagnosed with the autoimmune disease. She says she still has "all the symptoms of someone with MS". "I'm back at the very beginning and don't know what is wrong with me." MS is a chronic condition of the central nervous system, in which inflammation occurs in various places in the brain and spinal cord. Because of the inflammation, brain areas may communicate less well with each other, and the body may not be properly controlled. People with MS may have problems with their vision, movement, speech and memory. The disease is in principle not curable. Wrong diagnoses MS is known to be difficult to recognise, because symptoms differ from person to person and there are different types of MS. According to the Dutch Brain Foundation, the diagnosis is often made only years after the first symptoms. Research shows that misdiagnoses occur fairly often. This is also confirmed in the podcast by researcher Marwa Kaisey of the neurology department of a hospital in Los Angeles. "It is strange, because I feel I am disappointing everyone", Applegate said. "It is very disturbing and for me also very confusing." MS in the Netherlands According to the Dutch Brain Foundation, around 38,600 people with MS were known to a GP in the Netherlands in 2023. The disease occurs 2.5 times more often in women than in men. More than 75 percent of people who receive an MS diagnosis are under 65 years old. In 2021, 258 people died from the consequences of the disease.

title: Fighter jet crashes in northeast France, at least one dead
lead: In France, north of Nancy, the body of a military pilot has been recovered after his fighter jet crashed last night. There were two people on board. The other is still being searched for, the French air force reports. It speaks of an "exceptional accident". The aircraft came down near the village of Rogéville, a few tens of kilometres from the air force base near Nancy. On board were an experienced weapons systems officer and a young pilot in training, says an air force spokesperson. The crashed fighter is a Mirage 2000D, a two-seater designed to support air missions. The aircraft was returning from a routine training mission and approaching the military base when radio contact and then radar contact were lost, French media report. Search operations underway. The aircraft then crashed. Residents reportedly heard an explosion and saw a fireball. Search operations were launched immediately. According to the prefect of Meurthe-et-Moselle, the highest official in the region, there were "difficult weather conditions". Because of the darkness and fog, deploying helicopters was impossible. The first wreckage of the aircraft was discovered around 04.00. It is unclear which of the two occupants has now been found, the officer or the pilot. A helicopter has meanwhile been deployed in the rescue operation for the second victim. The cause of the crash is not yet clear and is being investigated.

title: Government and education websites offline due to leak, risk of hacks
lead: Various companies and organisations are taking websites offline as a precaution in connection with two major leaks in the PHP programming language. These include MijnOverheid.nl, DigiD, the website of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>. The news site and app of RTL and the popular tech website Tweakers are also affected. Liveblog Follow the latest developments on the leak in our liveblog . The <entity id="org:nationaal-cyber-security-centrum">Nationaal Cyber Security Centrum</entity> (NCSC) of the government has also taken its website offline, as has the <entity id="org:zbo-autoriteit-persoonsgegevens">Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens</entity>. Various systems in higher education have also been taken offline, news agency ANP reports, although it is not immediately clear which sites are involved. Notubiz was already taken offline this morning, a system with which a hundred municipalities hold meetings. News agency ANP has also taken systems offline as a precaution. Back doors The fear of many organisations is that the major PHP leaks could be used to break into systems. Because of these leaks, it is much easier for hackers to find and exploit back doors in websites. The American company Cloudflare, which acts as a kind of firewall for many popular websites, is now seeing the first attacks come through. Cloudflare's firewall intercepts attempts to exploit the leak, the company promises, but that is not watertight. The NCSC has not yet seen active exploitation of the leak, but urges companies in the Netherlands to update PHP as soon as possible. "As long as that does not happen, any system that contains PHP and is reachable from the public internet is presumably vulnerable", the agency writes. Updating is not possible yet. A permanent solution comes this afternoon at 16.00. Yesterday the organisation behind PHP already announced a solution to the problem, but in the meantime hackers appear to have found a way to exploit it. Declining popularity PHP is one of the most used programming languages. Although PHP's market share has been declining for years, the vast majority of websites still use the language. The discovered leak is one of the most serious categories. Attackers who find the leak can run their own program code on the attacked system. This allows them to penetrate further into a website and, for example, even steal user data. Ethical hackers find security problems in software on a continuous basis. These are usually fixed before hackers can exploit the problems on a large scale. If things do go wrong, the consequences can be serious. For example, the <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity> was forced offline in 2025 after such a so-called zero day -lek.

title: Biggest health insurance premium increase in years, DSW announces monthly amount for 2027
lead: Health insurer DSW is raising the premium for basic insurance by 14.75 euros per month. In euro terms, it is the biggest increase so far. The cost of basic insurance with DSW will come to 173.25 euros per month next year. "In the eight years that I have worked here, I have not experienced such a large increase," says DSW director Aad de Groot. As is traditional, DSW is the first health insurer to announce the new rates. Other health insurers are usually close to this new price. Although in euro terms this is the biggest increase, in percentage terms it is not a record. In 2011 the premium rose by 10 percent. Next year it rises by 9.3 percent. There are several reasons why the increase is so large this time. This year the premium could stay the same thanks to a financial windfall, but healthcare costs have risen and the insurer also has to take next year into account. "Actually, in this increase we are seeing two years of healthcare costs in one," says De Groot. Higher wage costs and hospitals with a higher energy bill also drive up costs, as does the growing group of people who need care. "Ageing leads to higher demand for care, and the number of cancer diagnoses will also rise in the coming years," says De Groot. The health insurer advocates a healthier lifestyle. "A large part of those diagnoses could be prevented if we focus on healthier eating, less alcohol and less smoking." The DSW increase is higher than the 12.50 euros per month that the <entity id="org:ministerie-van-volksgezondheid-welzijn-en-sport">Volksgezondheid, Welzijn en Sport</entity> (VWS) ministry had estimated. According to the insurer, this is because cuts are being made to the national budget that VWS has made available, mainly for mental health care (ggz), hospital care and community nursing. "The ministry did not include the cut in that calculation," says De Groot. "I think it is a first cut on healthcare costs. The government therefore pays less, but the individual premium payer pays more." Where does the pain lie? The rise in the health insurance premium is not fully offset by the higher health insurance allowance next year that many people receive. That allowance rises by 11 euros per month, less than the premium. This increase is a considerable setback especially for people who just exceed the health insurance allowance threshold. "Those people do not receive the health insurance allowance, but they now have to pay a high amount every month," says De Groot. "They feel this increase the most." The group of people who can no longer pay their health insurance is therefore also growing, according to figures from the Central Administration Office (<entity id="org:zbo-cak">CAK</entity>). If someone has not paid their health insurance premium for more than six months, the health insurer reports this to the CAK. Unaffordable: a person with a payment arrears remains insured, but pays a higher health insurance premium to the CAK. If an insured person wants to pay the normal health insurance premium again, a payment arrangement with the insurer is needed. Figures show that there are currently 200,000 people with a payment arrears at the CAK. In 2022 there were still 172,000. This is no surprise to DSW. "We are seeing an ever larger group of people who have difficulty paying their premium," says De Groot. He also sees that more people are paying their own risk in instalments, because otherwise it does not work out. "It is a painful increase, but we are obliged to do this." The other health insurers must also announce their premiums in the coming weeks. The deadline for this is 12 November.

title: Nearly a million dollars' worth of Pokémon cards stolen from FedEx van in California
lead: The rush for valuable Pokémon cards has inspired thieves in southern California: hundreds of trading cards were stolen in a robbery of a FedEx van. According to ABC News, the estimated value of the Pokémon loot is well over 960,000 dollars, converted roughly 850,000 euros. The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> says the exact value of the stolen cards has not yet been determined. In total, two pallets of popular collectible cards are said to have been stolen. Countless football stickers were also taken in the robbery. The thieves are said to have stolen the cards last week while the FedEx van was parked. The driver was not at the van at that time. The company that had handed the pallets to FedEx for delivery has deactivated the certificates of the stolen badge cards. The company has also told the largest resale platforms exactly which cards were stolen, so they can be alert when rare and valuable cards are offered on their platforms. Theft in the Netherlands as well. Trading card dealers in the Netherlands are also targets of thieves. A shop in Groningen was broken into twice a few weeks ago. How much the stolen cards there were worth is not yet clear. Pokémon trading cards became more popular and more expensive after the launch of the smartphone game Pokémon Go in 2016. In the years that followed, the popularity of the cards grew further because influencers started investing in them.

title: Increased demand for workers in transport and industry helps Randstad move forward
lead: Demand for temporary workers who work in factories, airports and distribution centres, among other places, is increasing. As a result, staffing agency Randstad has performed better than expected over the past three months. The staffing group presented its quarterly figures today. Randstad has had a few difficult years behind it. In the Netherlands, this was partly caused by stricter rules on temporary workers. Many companies therefore hesitated before hiring temporary workers, but this year Randstad is in luck. Revenue grew worldwide by almost 4 percent to more than 6 billion euros. Resilience Despite global geopolitical tensions and high fuel costs, the economy is resilient, says Randstad. "Uncertainty is the new normal", says Randstad CEO Sander van 't Noordende. That uncertainty is often precisely the reason companies expand their flexible workforce. Demand is especially higher in industry, and this can be seen in many countries. Even in Germany, demand for temporary workers rose, particularly at car factories. According to the Randstad CEO, the upturn there also means a lot for the Netherlands. "On the back of Germany, we also see extra demand for temporary workers in the Netherlands." Data centres The biggest outlier is in the United States. Randstad's revenue there rose by 9 percent last quarter compared with a year earlier. According to Van 't Noordende, this is thanks to economic growth in the US. That growth is mainly caused by large investments in the AI sector. Data centres are popping up like mushrooms, and construction is exactly the kind of work that temporary workers do. Demand for temporary workers with broad AI knowledge is also rising in all sectors. "The scenarios of our tech gurus Sam Altman and Elon Musk, that everyone will soon be sitting at home without a job, I would like to refer to as a land of fairy tales", says Van 't Noordende.

title: Long-lost Erasmus book with 1609 parenting tips back in Rotterdam
lead: A long-lost book by Erasmus from 1609 has returned to Rotterdam more than four hundred years later. The book turned up in the United States and will be on display for the first time at the Rotterdam library from next weekend. La civilité puerile by Erasmus is a thin, small book about good manners for children. "It was more a book for use than a book for keeping, and that is probably why it has not survived in libraries," says curator John Tholen at broadcaster Rijnmond. "It is very special that we can add this edition to our heritage collection more than four centuries later." The book contains practical tips on upbringing, such as "when someone sneezes, you must wish them good health (pay close attention)" and "only sit down at the table after you have washed your hands, and also cut your nails". Largest collection Desiderius Erasmus (circa 1466-1536) was an influential Dutch priest, writer, philosopher and humanist. He is considered one of the great scholars of the European Renaissance. Among others, the university and the best-known bridge in Rotterdam were named after him. In his birthplace is also the largest collection of Erasmus's books in the world: the Unesco Erasmus collection. That is more than 3000 books printed before 1900 and another 3000 books from after that year. The newest acquisition was considered lost. "Many more books have existed than survive today. We know this, among other things, from auction catalogues that list titles that can no longer be found anywhere. Such books are known internationally as lost books," the library explains. Puzzle piece An antiquarian from America, who was familiar with the Erasmus collection of Bibliotheek Rotterdam, had the book in his possession and offered it. "By finding such a lost book, we have discovered an unknown puzzle piece about the history and influence of Erasmus' ideas. This copy is the only one left in the world from an edition of perhaps a thousand," says Tholen.

title: Australian MP Haines loses both legs after car attack
lead: The Australian MP Helen Haines (65) must live without both legs. Two days ago she was seriously injured when a motorist drove into her. She is still in a critical but stable condition in a hospital in Melbourne. Haines, an independent MP from the state of Victoria, was unloading her car on Monday at her electorate office in Wangaratta when a driver in an SUV drove into her. According to witnesses, the motorist pinned her against her own car, then reversed and rammed her again. The suspect was then overpowered by a hairdresser who was working on the same street and saw it happen. After left and also right leg: Haines' husband responded for the first time today to the event. He said that on Monday his wife's left leg was amputated. Doctors tried to save her right leg, but had to amputate it today as well. "The good news is that Helen is alive and that her condition is stable. That is the most important thing for our family," said Phil Haines, visibly moved. "Helen is a compassionate, caring and loving person. We are grateful that at this moment her heart and mind are in good condition." Phil Haines expects a "long and difficult" recovery process for his wife. "But we know that she is a fighter who will do everything to recover with our support and love." The couple will be married forty years next month. They have three children and this year received two grandchildren. Suspect before the judge: the statement from Phil Haines followed a few hours after the suspect appeared before the judge. The 43-year-old Brendan Nugent from nearby Tarrawingee is suspected, among other things, of intentionally inflicting serious injury, dangerous driving and injuring a federal official. Nugent remains in pretrial detention until his next court hearing in February. His lawyer said he may have psychological problems, but that no diagnosis has ever been made. The police speak of a targeted attack, but have not yet established a motive. The suspect's father and stepmother issued a statement saying they have been friends with the victim for more than twenty years. The statement does not say to what extent the suspect knew Haines. They call the incident "devastating and incomprehensible." Accessible politicians: the collision has shaken Australia, where political violence is rare. Members of parliament are generally easily accessible to the public. Only politicians with an elevated security risk receive personal protection. Opposition politician James Paterson called on broadcaster ABC for a review of the security policy. According to him, not all 226 members of parliament should suddenly receive protection, but mainly how security at party offices, for example, can be improved. "We cannot afford a situation in which shocking attacks like this take place," he said. According to Paterson, Australian democracy changes fundamentally when members of parliament have to fear for their lives. Prime Minister Albanese, on the other hand, emphasised that politicians must remain accessible despite the growing hostility in society. "That interaction is very important in our democracy." Members of parliament are today being briefed by Australian security services. They can also voice their concerns during this.

title: EU investigation into Booking.com over fake ads and phishing
lead: The European Commission will investigate whether Booking.com has violated the Digital Services Act (DSA) by not doing enough to combat fake ads and phishing. European law requires online platforms to combat illegal content. According to the European Commission, 66 percent of all online hotel reservations in Europe are made via Booking.com. At the same time, Booking reports a five-hundredfold increase in fraud practices between 2022 and 2024. "Europeans must be able to book their holidays without fear of being scammed," says Henna Virkkunen, the EU Commissioner responsible for technological sovereignty, security and democracy. "The DSA makes clear what the responsibilities of platforms are to address these risks, and we must ensure that the leading booking platform in Europe takes that responsibility seriously," Virkkunen said. Risks of illegal advertisements The European Commission's investigation focuses, among other things, on whether Booking.com has sufficiently mapped the risks of illegal advertisements. The European Commission will also examine whether the platform has taken effective measures to limit the risks for users, including by removing fake ads. In addition, the European Commission wants to find out clearly whether Booking has properly mapped the risks of phishing, in which criminals try to steal data or money, for users. Another research question is whether the platform does enough to prevent data from being misused for phishing. Accommodation providers can pay Booking.com to get a higher spot in search results, but then it must state that it is an advertisement. The Commission will check whether this is the case. Many more people affected In the first half of 2026, nearly ten times as many people were scammed via booking platforms as a year earlier, according to figures from the Fraudehelpdesk . In just over 90 percent of the 1072 cases, it involved phishing via Booking.com. In many cases, criminals hack the account of a landlord or place a fake ad for which they use photos of existing accommodations on other booking platforms. Holidaymakers then receive a payment request via a fake website. The total damage amount from fraud via Booking.com has also risen sharply. Last year it amounted to just over 75,000 euros; in the first half of this year the counter already stood at just over 82,000 euros, Nieuwsuur reported .

title: With new North Sea drilling, the British government breaks a sensitive pledge
lead: The British government has agreed to gas drilling off the Scottish coast, despite objections from environmental groups. According to the government, the drilling benefits the energy security of the United Kingdom in internationally uncertain times. But opponents point out that the drilling conflicts with climate goals. British Prime Minister Burnham wants to be pragmatic. Energy prices are high and people must be able to heat their homes this winter. And because international energy markets are unpredictable due to the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, the UK might as well extract fossil fuels itself, from its own soil, in the North Sea, he reasons. This political justification may sound logical, but it is highly controversial. With his decision, Burnham breaks with Labour's 2023 pledge not to drill for new oil and gas fields in the North Sea. The party promised instead to invest in jobs in the sustainable energy sector and to meet the agreed climate goals. Yield The Jackdaw gas field, which the government has now given the green light, lies about 240 kilometres from the Scottish city of Aberdeen. According to the industry, the gas field can heat 1.4 million homes and the drilling can help preserve hundreds of jobs in the fossil fuel industry. The field could supply about 6 percent of British gas demand. Alongside Jackdaw, the British government is also considering approval of another North Sea project: the Rosebank oil field, about 130 kilometres west of the Shetland Islands. This is the largest unused oil field in the United Kingdom and could yield much more. A decision on this controversial project has not yet been made, but is expected in the short term. The permit for these two gas and oil fields, Jackdaw and Rosebank, has been a source of debate for years. The projects received the green light in 2022 from the then Conservative government, but a judge overruled the government. The reason: insufficient account had been taken of the climate impact of tapping new fossil sources. Now, new environmental research is said to have been carried out and taken into account. According to Adura, the gas and oil producer that wants to pump the gas and oil, the climate damage of this project is limited. But Greenpeace and other environmental organisations disagree. Drilling new fields runs counter to the Paris Climate Agreement. To meet the goals agreed there, the world must quickly reduce its use of oil and gas. In 2019, the United Kingdom became the first major economy in the world to legally commit to being climate neutral by 2050. Until then, a transition period applies in which oil and gas are gradually phased out. But opinions are divided on how that should happen. Gas imports Currently, about 63 percent of British gas is still imported. As a result, international conflicts, such as those around the Strait of Hormuz, and the ban on Russian gas, directly affect British energy prices. The British gas price is already twice as high as last year, and it is expected to rise further this winter. To soften the criticism of the new drilling, the British government wants to invest the tax revenue from the gas field in sustainable energy. The British Chancellor of the Exchequer wants to announce a new Energy Wealth Fund next week, inspired by the Norwegian sovereign wealth fund. Norway has been putting its revenue from oil and gas into a national fund for decades, which is now worth about 2.4 trillion dollars and is therefore the largest sovereign wealth fund in the world. The British fund starts with 2 billion pounds, about 2.4 billion euros, of government money and must be topped up with tax revenue from gas production at Jackdaw. This is meant to finance green energy projects. In this way, the government also hopes to address climate concerns within the Labour Party. Politically charged Prime Minister Burnham knows that high energy prices are preoccupying people. According to polls, the high cost of living tops the list of concerns of Britons. If Burnham is seen as the prime minister who does nothing about high energy prices, he can kiss his re-election goodbye. At the same time, climate ranks lower and lower on that list. The political debate about the United Kingdom becoming climate neutral is also changing: right-wing opposition parties such as the Conservatives and Reform are increasingly openly questioning the high costs of the energy transition for the ordinary Briton. Burnham therefore defends drilling for fossil fuels as pragmatic: people struggle to pay their bills, so we must make maximum responsible use of our own energy sources. We will still need oil and gas for decades to come, before we can fully rely on sustainable energy, he writes in a press release. Burnham stresses that his government remains committed to the goal of achieving net zero emissions by 2050.

title: What we know so far about the Hajar case and the man suspected
lead: Little by little more is becoming known about the suspect in the case surrounding Hajar, the 29-year-old woman whose body was found last week in a suitcase in the Amstel in <entity id="org:gemeente-amsterdam">Amsterdam</entity>. Yesterday the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> said at a press conference held by the mayor, justice and police in Amsterdam that the suspect is a 23-year-old man. He is of Somali nationality, has lived in the Netherlands since he was six and holds a permanent residence permit. Today Het Parool reports that it concerns Abdi A., who was adopted in 2009 and grew up in a foster family in the North Holland village of Zuidermeer. Later the family moved to the neighbouring Spierdijk. A. has not lived there for some years now. Even so, he was arrested there yesterday morning, when officers responded to a report of a violent incident at his parents' home. What preceded his arrest and the death of Hajar? No indications of threat On 4 October Hajar was seen for the last time, near the RAI congress centre in Amsterdam-Zuid. She was cycling with what is now revealed to be the suspect in the direction of the Buitenveldert neighbourhood. As far as is known, he and Hajar did not know each other, but investigation must show to what extent that is correct. On Sunday evening 4 October a relative of Hajar reported her missing, as she was worried about her wellbeing. The 29-year-old had left home with a suitcase and reportedly had run away more often. The police initially assumed a disappearance. At that time there were no indications of a threatening situation or a crime. After detectives had searched for Hajar for several days and she had still not been found, the police, in consultation with the family, decided to share a photo of the woman online. This led to tips from people who may still have seen her. Found in the Amstel On Friday 16 October a body was subsequently found in the water of the Amstel at the Amsteldijk, not far from where Hajar was last seen. Police investigation showed that it was the body of the 29-year-old woman and that she had died as a result of a crime. 'Everything points to the young woman having lost her life violently, at the hands of another,' police chief Peter Holla said at the press conference. 'Afterwards she was hidden away in degrading circumstances.' The police say they assume Hajar was killed shortly after she went missing. 'For the sake of the investigation' a spokesperson does not wish to say whether the suitcase in which she was found is the same one she took from home. From witness to suspect The 23-year-old man was questioned as a witness in the case on Monday. After additional investigation it emerged that he may have been involved in the woman's death, whereupon he was named a suspect on Tuesday morning and the police went looking for him. That same morning the North Holland police received a report of a violent incident in Spierdijk. Officers found the 23-year-old man at his parents' home. An officer recognised him from the search order in the Hajar case that had been distributed among all police forces that same morning. He was arrested and has been held since then under all restrictions. That means he has contact only with his lawyer. Foster father attacked Last night it emerged that the victim of the violent incident in Spierdijk is the suspect's foster father. Neighbours tell a NOS reporter that he went there to 'get an explanation' and that this was accompanied by loud noise and violence. According to a guest at a nearby neighbourhood campsite, the 23-year-old had fallen out with his foster father and struck him on the head with a hammer. There are still many questions about what happened; for example, it is still unknown where Hajar was killed, police chief Holla said yesterday. The police ask people who have information about the case to come forward.

title: Former head of Hungarian central bank arrested in fraud investigation
