"The danger is that repetition makes Philippine territory sound disputed." Diplomatic row Meanwhile the diplomatic outbursts are increasing. Philippine Defence Secretary Teodoro called China a "regional troublemaker". Early this summer China already put Teodoro on its sanctions list, because of earlier statements. In response, Ambassador Quan said: "If China were to use military force, we could easily win. But China loves peace, which is why we do not choose violence." The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs also chipped in, saying "the Philippines should curb such irresponsible behaviour by those politicians". The Filipinos were shocked and, by their own account, deployed the strongest diplomatic tool available. The ambassador has been summoned by President Marcos. "To me this sounded like a threat, and not a very diplomatic statement," the president said. "I think it deserves a discussion between the ambassador and me." The meeting has yet to take place. But Ambassador Jing Quan now denies that his words were meant as a threat. Still, it is no coincidence that China is speaking out so firmly. Since Marcos took office, his government has moved closer to the US. Three years ago his government gave the Americans access to three military bases in northern Luzon. That is the largest island of the Philippines, and the island closest to the Batanes Islands and therefore Taiwan. His army also holds military exercises with Japan in that area. That is a thorn in China's side. Over the past year relations between China and Japan have cooled sharply, after Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi said that a Chinese attack on Taiwan "could create a situation that threatens Japan's survival". But China is also steadily expanding its military exercises and activities in the South China Sea. Last month the Chinese navy and air force held exercises around Scarborough Shoal, which drew fierce criticism from the Philippines and the US.

title: Voices from besieged Taiz in Yemen: 'Our city is gasping for breath'
lead: The Yemeni city of Taiz is completely surrounded by Houthi rebels. All access roads have been closed, and people and goods cannot enter or leave the city. Because of its strategic location, the country's third city has for years been an asset for the warring parties. Once again it is an important front in the recently flared-up war between the Houthis and the Yemeni government army. The United Nations and international aid organisations cannot reach the city and last week sounded the alarm. Four residents of the city describe the steadily worsening situation below. Ghada Nabil, works for an aid organisation: "My city has turned into an open-air prison. Residents are deprived of all basic necessities. There is constant danger. A systematic policy of starvation and isolation prevails here. The situation has deteriorated very quickly. It is no longer just the limited freedom of movement. The entry of food, drinking water and fuel into the city is being systematically blocked. The fighting is getting closer. I hear the sound of random shelling of residential neighbourhoods and civilians alongside the roar of explosions, mortar fire, the rattle of machine guns and the buzzing of drones. These sounds constantly remind us that we live in the middle of an active front line. I am afraid the world will forget us, while Taiz sinks into a humanitarian disaster. Crushed under the weight of this siege and the deafening international silence." Latifa Abdullah, accountant: "Our city is gasping for breath. We want to live, but we have to weigh every step we take carefully. It feels as if we have been completely cut off from the rest of the world. People who could afford it fled the city before the siege. Those who had nowhere to go stayed, rooted in their homes, their land and their memories of better times. Only at home do I feel safe. Together with my children and my family, far away from the stress on the street. I wonder what the future holds for our children, given the current state of education and the overall worsening situation. My hope is that a solution will come and the roads to Taiz will open again. My dream is that our children will know peace and safety and can experience the normal life they deserve, far removed from the fear, oppression and exhaustion we are going through now." Khaled Naggar, university professor: "Universities and schools are closed, a great challenge for our students. This war quickly led to the collapse of our infrastructure. Waste lies everywhere on the streets. Because of the fighting it is not being collected, because they cannot reach the rubbish dumps. The amount of waste on the streets affects the health of residents. Diseases are spreading quickly. We are worried about basic necessities. The flour supply is running out. There was panic and people tried to stock up as much as possible. Flour, sugar and oil were hoarded in large quantities. That means those products are now barely to be found on the market. If you do find them, they are unaffordable. I expect it to get worse quickly in the coming days if the roads do not open for food. And the petrol crisis is also growing. There is no diesel for the water pumps, so water supplies are running out. The lack of diesel is causing major problems in the hospitals. Many hospitals will have to close their emergency departments and other wards. They need help to prevent patients from dying unnecessarily." Weam Adnan, human rights activist: "There is hardly any traffic on the streets, because nowhere is safe. If you go out onto the street, you can be hit by a sniper or a bombardment. It is not only soldiers who are fighting; homes of ordinary civilians and hospitals have all been attacked by the Houthis. We hear the fighting every day and are starting to distinguish between the different types of weapons that hit the neighbourhoods. My greatest concern is that the Houthis are getting closer and closer to the city. They are not welcome here. My dream is that this war ends with the elimination of the Houthis. We want peace and want to begin reconstruction. We hope that the criminals will be punished for all their crimes in Taiz, because currently all kinds of war crimes can take place with impunity."

title: Afghans washed ashore on Texel were smuggled by convicted criminal
lead: The two Afghan men whose body parts washed ashore on Texel in 2023 were smuggled to the United Kingdom by an extensive people smuggling network led by criminal Idriss Ghazi Kareem. That is according to research by NH and Zembla. Kareem was sentenced at the end of last year in Paris to fifteen years' imprisonment for people smuggling, which he even managed to organise from prison. According to the judge he earned hundreds of thousands of euros a year from this. Shoe with foot On 6 October 2023 a shoe with a foot in it and a lower body were found on the beach of Texel. For a long time it remained unclear whose the washed-up body parts were. Police detective Fetze Venema spent 2.5 years on the identification. Together with the Red Cross he traced relatives of the missing men in Afghanistan for DNA research. Only this summer did it become clear that they were two Afghan refugees: Samiullah (20) and Ahmad Jan (27). On the night of 12 August 2023 the men boarded a rubber boat together with 66 others just north of Calais. The boat was not suitable for the crossing to England and so did not reach the coast. On open water the engine failed and after an explosion the boat tore. Sixty migrants survived, eight others did not. Of those eight, six were pulled from the water. Samiullah and Ahmad Jan went missing. Their remains washed ashore on Texel two months later. After this boat disaster, French justice tracked an extensive people smuggling network, led by Kareem. He arranged boats and other materials needed for migrant crossings of the Channel. Victims of escape attempts This year at least 26 people have died crossing the Channel in rubber boats, including two children. The actual number is probably higher because people are still missing. In 2025 there were 29 dead and missing, in 2024 83, in 2023 17. That ringleaders of such smuggling networks come from the Netherlands is, according to the Royal Netherlands Marechaussee, not unusual. Our country plays an important role in the trade: "It concerns the import, transit and storage of ship supplies that are transported to the French coast. There they are used to get migrants across to Great Britain." From intercepted conversations the Dutch <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity> concludes that the traders themselves know the materials are not suitable for this. "For us that is an aggravating circumstance", says public prosecutor Petra Hoekstra. "They think the money outweighs a human life. And that means they knowingly put people on floating coffins." title: Police take webshops selling dangerous fake pills offline, linked to three deaths
lead: The police have taken thirty websites offline where illegal medicines and drugs were sold. Three suspects who are said to be behind these sites were arrested this week. The police also hold them responsible for the webshop Slaappillen.net and link their sites to at least three deaths. The police suspect that the suspects simply continued selling, for example, sedatives, sleeping pills and painkillers, after Slaappillen.net was shut down last year. That happened after a woman from Voorburg died after ordering the strong painkiller oxycodone there. The fake pills contained nitazenes, a dangerous synthetic substance that carries a high risk of overdose. New webshops The suspects now arrested, according to the police, ensured that the sale of illegal medicines continued unabated via other sites. Customers of Slaapmiddelen.net were sometimes even directly invited to them. Whenever the government had websites taken offline, new variants appeared. According to the police, the three suspects played an essential role in setting up and running ever new webshops. Dangerous counterfeit medicines, possibly including contaminated oxycodone, were also sold there. Servers This time the police not only took the webshops offline but also seized the servers on which the sites ran. In this way the police hope to prevent new points of sale from being quickly set up again. "We have brought down all the technology behind the websites", says Ron van Brussel, responsible at the National Unit Investigation and Interventions for tackling serious organised crime. "This makes it harder to make a comeback." Prescription The suspects are a 35-year-old man from Kwintsheul, a 39-year-old man from Rotterdam and a 66-year-old man from The Hague. They are suspected of offering, selling and supplying illegal medicines, which led to the death of three people. The medication they are said to have sold is only available in the Netherlands on doctor's prescription and through a pharmacy. The webshops taken offline targeted the Dutch market, but sometimes also German or French customers. "The customers are often vulnerable people who need sleeping or sedative medicines that they cannot get through regular channels", Van Brussel says. "They then go looking online. Then you don't really know what you're buying." The precise composition of the medicines is often unknown, so users run serious health risks. The police call on people to report themselves if they know someone who has become seriously ill or even died after using pills ordered online. Relatives pleased Besides the arrests there were also several searches this week. The police seized, among other things, crypto wallets of the suspects. Various storage sites of illegal medicines have also already been found in recent times. Next week two men will appear before the judge who are said to have played a subordinate role in the organisation behind Slaappillen.net. The police are therefore now a step further in the investigation into the main responsible persons. Further arrests are not ruled out. Relatives of one of the victims of the fake oxycodone pills from Slaappillen.net respond with pleasure. "Congratulations to the police that there is finally progress in the search for the organisation behind the website that proved fatal to our daughter", they say. Trade not over Alongside the investigation into the group behind Slaapmiddelen.net and the replacement sites, the case against the webshop Funcaps is also still ongoing. That too sold counterfeit medicines and designer drugs on a large scale. The <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity> links more than twenty deaths to substances sold through Funcaps. The owners are still in custody. Although the police think that crucial players from the group around Slaapmiddelen.net have now also been arrested, the trade in illegal medicines is certainly not over. "There are several criminal groups keeping these kinds of sites online", says Van Brussel.

title: Rapprochement promised, but attacks on Russia and Ukraine continue regardless
lead: Two people have been killed and several injured in Russian attacks on Ukraine in the past few hours. The violence therefore continues despite Russian pledges to consider negotiations. "Russia is responding to negotiations with missiles", President Zelensky summarises. In the capital Kyiv, the air raid alarm already sounded yesterday afternoon, while in Moscow it was still unclear what US envoy Steve Witkoff had discussed with the Kremlin that day. Attacks on the Ukrainian capital also continued overnight. According to President Zelenksy, at least 34 people were injured, including children. Among the dead is a woman who died in the eastern city of Kharkiv, according to local authorities. "Russia launched the attacks almost immediately after talks had taken place again", Zelensky responded on X. "This means there is no real change in their attitude." He repeated that better air defence is crucial for his country. Civilian targets According to Kyiv mayor Klytsjko, the South Bridge was again attacked, among others, an important traffic artery across the Dnieper. In addition, an ambulance post and six ambulances were hit. Zelensky further speaks of attacks on shopping centres, railways, energy infrastructure and even a monastery. According to the mayor of Moscow, Ukraine also carried out a large drone attack on the Russian capital. He said that most of the more than 600 drones had been shot down, but that two people were still injured. Little concrete result This suggests the war violence continues unabated, although President Trump said yesterday that peace has never been so close, due to the shuttle diplomacy of his envoy Witkoff. He flew to Oslo on Tuesday for talks with Zelensky and his European allies and travelled on yesterday to Moscow to discuss the outcome with Putin. The Kremlin let him know it was "in principle willing" to hold talks with the US and Ukraine. If such trilateral talks do take place, it would not be peace negotiations at the highest level, but preparatory talks on the conditions for them. At the same time, a Kremlin spokesperson tempered expectations by saying that the Oslo proposals "have hardly any real value for resolving the Ukraine crisis". Norwegian Prime Minister Støre, host of the European talks on Ukraine, nevertheless said he hopes talks can take place in mid-November between the US, Ukraine and Russia. That would be the first contact between the warring parties since a trio of talks in the first months of this year, when the only concrete result was a prisoner exchange. New phase? Støre spoke of a new phase in the peace efforts. "I think this could be a phase in which the Russians too look for opportunities for diplomacy." Zelensky again responded favourably to every initiative to make progress and was open to a meeting. "But Russia has said several times before that it wants to talk, and then something changed again and it was called off. We will see what happens this time." "We want Zelensky to make a deal", President Trump expressed his stake. "We have already given Ukraine so much and we have got nothing back for it except sorrow, death and enormous financial loss." Trump has recently been increasingly critical of Zelensky and has cut back aid to Ukraine. At the same time he has actively sought closer ties with Putin, with, for example, a fuel deal that is meant to help him, ahead of the midterm elections in the US, reduce high diesel prices caused by the war in Iran.

title: Fire in Delft city centre under control
lead: A fire broke out in the Delft city centre this morning. The fire is now under control. As far as is known, no one was injured. The fire broke out around 06:15 in a building on Kerkstraat, close to the Nieuwe Kerk. The flames spread quickly, and the fire brigade turned out with many personnel and vehicles to fight the blaze. "This concerns the old centre of Delft. That is very vulnerable. We would rather have too much material than too little", a fire brigade spokesperson told Omroep West . Because there was a risk the fire would spread to other buildings, ten homes were evacuated as a precaution. People who were troubled by the smoke were advised to close windows and doors and to switch off the mechanical ventilation. People taken in at a café Some fifteen to twenty people have been taken in at a nearby café. It is not yet clear when they can return home. "Everyone was initially taken in at the construction depot. That was cold. I then opened up my business", says the pub owner. "I woke up and live nearby. So I went to look. It turned out an emergency location was needed. So I made my business available." Although the fire is under control, the risk of it spreading to other buildings has not yet passed, the fire brigade says. Parts of the affected building are being demolished to check whether there are still any hotspots. Nothing is yet known about the cause of the fire. "So we also do not yet know whether the fire started inside or outside the building. The fire was first seen at the rear", the fire brigade said.

title: Shark that became an attraction in South Korea swims away and returns
lead: The shark that has been swimming around a South Korean city since last month was escorted to open sea yesterday, but returned to the harbour of Busan a few hours later. The dusky shark grew into a tourist attraction in recent weeks and is said to have drawn around 1.6 million visitors. On 18 September the animal, which fans call Bukangi, was first spotted in a canal in the harbour. By the end of September, attempts to drive Bukangi out of the harbour had already failed. An attempt was also made early this month. Yesterday it finally succeeded in guiding the 3.5-metre-long shark out to open water using huge nets. Yet a few hours later the shark managed to swim back into the harbour, under the net. "The shark is now between the outer net and a second net placed 30 to 40 metres further along the canal", an official tells the news agency AFP. The shark keeps coming back to the harbour: not everyone in South Korea was enthusiastic about forcibly herding the animal out of the harbour. Still, according to the authorities, the shark's departure is necessary to ensure the animal's safety. Environmental organisations say the shark's arrival is related to climate change. According to them, warming seas drive many fish to colder waters in the north, and so they end up off South Korea. Hungry sharks swim after them. Bukangi is not the only shark that South Korea has found. In the first half of this year, 46 sharks were spotted off the east coast; that is four times as many as in the same period last year. title: Lawyer and accountant of Jeffrey Epstein before the court in New Mexico
lead: The US state of New Mexico is filing a lawsuit against the lawyer and accountant of sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Prosecutor Raúl Torrez claims that they may have enabled the abuse of girls by the businessman and should therefore not profit from his estate. "Jeffrey Epstein did not operate alone, and his death must not mean that the people who made his crimes possible get away with it," Torrez states. "People who facilitated the abuse must not profit while the victims live with the consequences." The state can bring the civil case because Epstein had a remote ranch for years, where girls were also reportedly abused. For the time being it concerns a civil case, but Torrez also seems in his press release to hint at possible criminal prosecution of the two. Hush money? Lawyer Darren Indyke and accountant Richard Kahn previously said they never knew anything about Epstein's practices. Now too their lawyer reacts indignantly to the charge. "No woman has ever accused Messrs. Indyke or Kahn of sexual abuse, or said that they witnessed it. Nor has anyone claimed that they or anyone else raised allegations about Mr. Epstein." Torrez nevertheless says the two must indeed have known what Epstein did. As his confidants they were, afterwards, to make payments totaling up to 3 million dollars to the women Epstein had abused, obviously hush money in Torrez's eyes. "Advisers, lawyers, bookkeepers and others were involved here, and they must face the consequences." Millions Indyke and Kahn are reported to have already received 16 and 10 million dollars from Epstein over the years. As co-executors of his estate they could receive between 25 and 50 million dollars more. The two arranged, after Epstein's death, among other things the multi-million settlement with several abuse victims. Epstein took his own life in his cell in 2019, after he was arrested for a second time for child abuse. In 2009 he had avoided a prison sentence by pleading guilty. New Mexico opened an investigation this year into whether any criminal offenses were committed at Epstein's Zorro Ranch. No one has been charged in that investigation.

title: Airbnb hosts may no longer require guests to do the dishes
lead: Hosts on the booking site Airbnb may no longer require their guests to do the dishes or strip the beds when checking out. That is what the new house rules, which the company has just published, show. According to the company these are "tasks of a cleaner", and therefore should not be carried out by tenants. Most hosts on Airbnb, the largest booking site for private accommodation in the world, also ask their guests for a cleaning fee. According to the company it is then unfair to also ask them to carry out cleaning tasks themselves, and this regularly leads to dissatisfied guests. Bears Other rules the company now sets: guests may no longer be instructed to take their waste outside and throw it away there, and they may also no longer be asked to stop using certain facilities in the accommodation, such as air conditioning or heating. Guests also may no longer be forced to sign a contract with the host outside the site. Reasonable requests, according to the company, are: putting dirty dishes in the sink, separating waste within the accommodation, gathering used towels and turning off air conditioning or heating when leaving. In exceptional cases guests may be required to store their waste "in an animal-proof container, in areas where bears occur". The new rules take effect in about a month. Strict rules Airbnb came under fire in recent years because the company would worsen the housing shortage in popular cities such as Amsterdam and Barcelona, or would undermine the liveability of residential neighborhoods, according to critics. Last year it received a fine of tens of millions in Spain for offering homes that should not have been rented out at all. In many tourist cities the company has therefore in recent years introduced strict rules for renting private homes, with for example a maximum number of nights per year that a home may be rented out.

title: Teacher on US school attack: 'Before I could close the door, he was already there'
lead: A teacher who was seriously wounded when a 16-year-old shooter opened fire at an American elementary school a week ago says she had no time at all to save her students. "I turned around to close the door, but he was already there. Before I could do anything, he shot me at close range." The 54-year-old Becky Drury was hit several times by the shooter. A 25-year-old teacher and three students aged 5, 8, and 11 were killed, and a 7-year-old child was seriously wounded. Drury writes in a written statement that she came running at the commotion when the shooter forcibly entered the school in the town of Bend. "When I realised something was going on outside, I ran over to see what it was. As soon as I saw the shooter, I immediately ran back to my classroom." Playing dead The shooter, a former student, had already opened fire outside on the driver of a car who tried to stop him. He then gained access to the school by shooting open a door. Drury realised she had been seriously wounded. "On the floor I saw that my left hand was almost completely blown off by the shot, and my other arm was also badly injured. I could not get up to defend myself or protect anyone else, so I did the only thing I could: pretended to be dead in the hope that he would not shoot me again." A colleague of Drury threw a phone at the shooter and managed to get him to the ground, after which a struggle over the rifle began. The perpetrator was finally stopped by the father of two students, who had come running at the shots. With his own weapon, the father killed the shooter. 'Incomprehensible' The police in Bend are still investigating how the perpetrator managed to get hold of the weapon. According to a police spokesperson it was legally purchased, but not by him. American media reported that it was a weapon belonging to his mother. A motive is not clear. Drury calls what happened in her classroom "incomprehensible." "My heart bleeds for everyone affected by this tragedy." "I think of those who were wounded, those we have lost, their families, our school and the community in Bend. I am grateful for the kindness and support we have received in these difficult days."

title: 'US and Israel prepare new attacks on Iran'
lead: The US and Israel have plans ready for a new attack on Iran, which the countries want to carry out after the American midterm elections. The New York Times writes this, based among other things on conversations with American officials. The countries have recently stepped up their exercises, for example of air strikes. They are doing this over Iraq, which lies between Israel and Iran. This week the American Secretary of Defense Hegseth visited Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu to discuss this, the American newspaper reports. American officials claim that a final large-scale, three-day attack would be enough to cause sufficient economic damage to force Iran to make concessions. It is unclear how an attack, almost eight months after the first Israeli-American attacks, could bring the Iranian government to its knees. Energy and weapons The planned attacks will, according to American officials, target Iran's energy infrastructure, nuclear facilities and weapons depots. "They both do not have a convincing story about how more war adds value in this conflict region", says Dana Stroul to The New York Times. She works for the American think tank The Washington Institute for Near East Policy and previously worked for then President Biden. If the Israeli-American attacks go ahead, Iran threatens to strike back hard. The country has already attacked ships and energy infrastructure in recent months, but Iran does not shy away from extending that to data centres and undersea internet cables, it is said from Tehran. Midterm elections There were already several plans to attack Iran once more, also this month. The American and Israeli militaries were put on alert for this. President Trump cancelled the plans at the last moment. Trump is in a tight spot because of the midterm elections of 3 November. Many Americans are angry about high fuel prices as a result of the Iran war, which the US itself started. The president threatens to lose his Republican majority in Congress after the elections. Israel holds parliamentary elections next week. On 27 October Israelis can go to the polls, which could also reduce Netanyahu's power. If he loses the elections, he becomes caretaker prime minister, which according to experts could make a war more difficult.

title: Florida officer finds dead man and moves into his house, caught after expensive renovation
lead: In the US state of Florida, a 35-year-old police officer has been arrested after taking on the identity of a dead man. In July 2022 the officer had responded in the city of Lauderhill to a report to check on the welfare of a person. On arrival it turned out that 71-year-old Dennis West had died. The officer reported this, and the medical examiner then determined that West had died of natural causes, and so the matter seemed closed. The officer, Brian Louis Sguros, however presented himself to the medical examiner as a close friend of the deceased and said that West had no family members left. He would therefore handle the death himself. Using the police database, the officer looked up the man's date of birth, social security number and other details, and in August 2022 Sguros finally moved into West's house. So as not to arouse suspicion with the local authorities, he simply paid the property tax and energy bills in the name of the deceased. New front door and windows He also forged West's signature to obtain a permit to renovate the house. A contractor who came in 2024 to replace the front door and some windows remembers his meeting with Sguros, according to American media reporting on the basis of the police report. The officer told the contractor that West was "not available". That the man had been dead for years was not mentioned. A year later, in 2025, the officer attempted to put the property permanently in his own name and contacted the local <entity id="org:zbo-dienst-voor-het-kadaster-en-de-openbare-registers">kadaster</entity> for this purpose. In the end it did not get that far: the fraud came to light when the heirs of the deceased man were traced by a property firm that wanted to buy the house. Renovation of more than 2 tons After that company bought the house, staff were surprised to find Sguros in the house. Confronted with the situation, he handed over the house keys, although he also started a civil case to recover the renovation costs of 214,000 dollars. The lawsuit that followed, however, raised so many questions that the authorities started a criminal investigation into Sguros. He is now suspected of fraud, identity misuse and unlawfully taking possession of the home. His defence is that he moved into the house to prevent it from being squatted. The Miami Herald reports that the officer has been placed on leave without pay. Yesterday the judge set the bail at 25,000 dollars. After paying it, he left the prison running and wearing two face masks. A local TV station has the footage:

title: Number of women in top positions lags behind: 'Only in 2044 will one third be women'
lead: "I had hoped that we would have reached the goal by now with which I started the list twenty years ago", sighs Mijntje Lückerath-Rovers. As professor of Corporate Governance, she has been compiling the Dutch ranking for 20 years on the representation of women and men in top positions: the Female Board Index. When she started the list in 2006, she set the goal that a third of supervisory directors and a third of executive directors would be women. Meanwhile, the number of female executive directors at the 81 listed companies in the Netherlands has risen to 18 percent. But Professor Lückerath-Rovers sees no acceleration in new appointments. The number of female supervisory directors is above a third. For those supervisors a statutory limit has been introduced; for executive directors that is not the case. Mixed picture According to Lückerath-Rovers, this year's list gives a mixed picture. "On the one hand there has been an increase in the share of female supervisory directors for a number of years, but on the other hand the increase in the number of female executive directors remains disappointing." At the current trend, a third of executive directors would only be women in 2044. There are now 21 companies with at least a third women on both the management board and the supervisory board, up from seventeen companies last year. In addition, at four companies (PostNL, Triodos, Fastned and Hydratec) both the management and supervisory seats are split fifty-fifty between men and women. At ABN Amro both boards have a majority of women. When the professor started the list, only 2 percent of executive directors and 8 percent of supervisory directors were women. Those percentages have now grown considerably to 18 and 44 percent respectively. Statutory quota: how does it work? Since 1 January 2022 a statutory quota applies to the supervisory board of listed companies. At least a third must be women and a third men. This year 71 of the 81 companies in the Female Board Index meet this standard. The ten companies below this limit are mainly smaller listed firms. Falling below a third does not automatically mean that a company is breaking the law. There is currently no statutory quota for the management board. For her research, Lückerath-Rovers has ranked all listed companies in the Netherlands since 2008. After each publication, the professor noticed that public debate on this flared up. And that companies made changes. "For example, I noticed that companies at the bottom of the list appointed more women the following year". Although after 20 years it is a good moment for Mijntje Lückerath-Rovers to pass the baton of the Female Board Index to someone else, she remains involved. "The importance of women at the helm must be continually emphasised. Companies should be ashamed if they have a top that consists only of men." According to the professor, staff also have a role to play. "Employees must continue to speak out for more women in executive positions." 'Missing opportunities' State Secretary <entity id="person:judith-tielen">Judith Tielen</entity> of Emancipation feels that the number of women in top positions is not growing fast enough. "Since the introduction of the statutory quota the number of women in top positions has been rising, and that is good. But it is slow. Especially when you look at the number of executive directors, it really is not fast enough. Organisations are missing opportunities." Next year she will evaluate the statutory quota. Tielen: "I am also going to talk with companies, organisations and women about what is needed to make more progress on the number of women at the top and in the management layers below that."

title: Most important EU human rights prize for Court, which is under heavy US pressure
lead: The European Parliament has chosen the International Criminal Court (ICC) in The Hague as the winner of this year's Sakharov Prize. The court is under heavy pressure from the United States . President Trump wants to paralyse the court with sanctions. "With the award of the prize to the Court, the European Parliament recognises the important work of the court in upholding international law and international jurisprudence," says Parliament President Roberta Metsola. What does the International Criminal Court do? The Court investigates, prosecutes and tries persons accused of human rights violations, and serves as a complement to the national courts of member states. Among other things, the court investigates genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. All countries in the European Union are obliged to carry out decisions of the Court, because of the Rome Statute. The court is not recognised by all countries in the world. For example, the United States, Israel, Russia and Iran do not recognise the court. The Court, which next year will face sanctions from the United States, is grateful for the prize. "With that in mind, the Sakharov Prize takes on a special meaning," says president Tomoko Akane. "It confirms the importance of an independent judiciary and of those who uphold international law," she says. Nominated candidates The award of the Sakharov Prize is a political decision. The group leaders of the political groups in the European Parliament decide who receives the prize. The Court was nominated by the Socialists and Democrats, the second largest group in parliament. The social democrats, part of which belongs to Pro, received support for awarding the prize to the ICC from the liberals (VVD, D66), the Greens (Pro) and the far left (Partij voor de Dieren). The largest political group, the Christian Democrats (CDA), did not vote for the Court. They had their own candidate, Tanzanian opposition leader Tundu Lissu. The far-right Patriots for Europe (PVV) also had its own nominee, the Iranian twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi. The twins were imprisoned and tortured after taking part in protests in Iran. Thijs Reuten (social democrats, Pro) considers the prize for the ICC "a powerful signal". "It is essential that the Court can keep functioning to prevent impunity, despite Trump's absurd threats." Raquel García Hermida-van der Walle (liberals, D66) is also pleased with the winner. "The Court protects us from perpetrators of the most heinous crimes against humanity. And now they need our protection." Other winners Earlier today, the Nobel Peace Prize winner Navanethem Pillay spoke in The Hague. She is a former judge of the Court. "At a time when the principles of international law are being tested worldwide, the work of those who commit themselves to international jurisprudence is more important than ever." An earlier winner was the late Russian opposition leader Aleksej Navalny . The population of Ukraine and the Iranian women's movement Women, Life, Freedom have also won the prize. What is the Sakharov Prize? The Sakharov Prize is awarded to people, groups or organisations that are committed to human rights or democracy. The first prize was presented in 1988. The prize is named after Andrei Sakharov, a Russian physicist and inventor of the hydrogen bomb. In 1975 he received the Nobel Peace Prize because he drew attention to the nuclear arms race during the Cold War. In the Soviet Union Sakharov was regarded as a dissident with disruptive ideas.

title: German WWII submarine found that had disappeared due to a typo
lead: 82 years after it vanished without a trace due to a typo, a German submarine from the Second World War has been found in the English Channel. Divers from Plymouth found the U-672 32 kilometres off the coast of Devon, at a depth of 70 metres. The submarine was damaged in July 1944 by an attack from the British warship HMS Balfour. D-Day had taken place just a month earlier, and the English Channel was closely watched to prevent attacks on troop transports. A depth charge had caused the hull of the U-672 to leak, so captain Ulf Lawaetz decided to order the crew to abandon the ship. The submarine was brought to the surface, the crew boarded lifeboats, and the ship was scuttled by opening its hatches. The 52 crew members were spotted a day later by a British aircraft flying overhead and taken aboard passing ships. They remained prisoners of war for the rest of the war. Remarkably, no one was killed in the attack. Surprise and mystery For years it was not known where the U-672 had ended up on the seabed. The coordinates of the British attack had been recorded, but no wreck was ever found at that spot. This summer, deep-sea divers were therefore surprised when they dove at a wreck that was marked on charts as a steamship sunk in 1917. Underwater, however, they discovered that it was an unknown submarine, lying on its port side. "We first saw some fish and then came out right at the bow," says Dominic Robinson, who led a second dive. "The beautiful thing about submarines is that they have a lovely hull, sharp as a knife. That was the first thing we saw." The question remained what this submarine was doing at a location 74 kilometres from where it was supposed to have sunk. Robinson and his team discovered that an error had crept into the paperwork: because two digits of a coordinate had been swapped, it turned out the attack had taken place somewhere else entirely. This made the find especially exciting for Robinson. "We know the fate of by far most German submarines. Almost all of those sunk in the English Channel have been identified. So this was one of the few mysteries that remained." The U-672 was launched in 1943 in Hamburg. The Danish-German captain Lawaetz made four patrols with it, without sinking a single Allied ship. After the war Lawaetz returned to mainland Europe. He died in 2002 in Copenhagen. Second World War newsletter Interested in the Second World War? Then subscribe to our newsletter here.

title: Government pages back online after PHP vulnerability, no data leaked or stolen so far
lead: The last websites of the Dutch government that were still unreachable overnight following yesterday's major PHP vulnerability are now back online. The sites Meld Misdaad Anoniem and Overheid.nl are accessible again, as are several judiciary websites and the website of the <entity id="org:rijksinstituut-voor-volksgezondheid-en-milieu">Rijksinstituut voor Volksgezondheid en Milieu</entity> (RIVM). NotuBiz is also back online. That is a service with which municipalities, provinces and water boards publish official notices. "After thorough testing, all systems are up and running again," says a spokesperson. Many personal and smaller business websites are still unreachable, because hosting providers have temporarily shut them off as a precaution, pending the update. Hosting providers are companies that provide storage space and internet connections for customers, so that they do not have to do so themselves. Update After the vulnerability was made public yesterday morning by the foundation that manages the programming language, many business and government sites worldwide went offline. After the foundation distributed a security update, most services came back online over the course of the evening and night. Nevertheless, some government services remained unreachable until this morning, as a precaution. No cases are yet known in the Netherlands in which data has actually been leaked or stolen as a result of the PHP problems, a spokesperson for the <entity id="org:zbo-autoriteit-persoonsgegevens">Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens</entity> (AP) reports. Organisations are legally required to report to this supervisory authority if there is a possible data breach involving personal data.

title: First human infected with shamonda virus animal disease, French patient died
lead: In France, a human infection with the shamonda virus has been confirmed for the first time. Earlier this month, a patient who had contracted the animal disease died. It is still being investigated whether that was also the cause of death; the patient's health had already been weakened by another condition. French authorities speak of an "exceptional case" involving a patient who already had a weakened immune system. "Based on current knowledge of this virus, there is so far no health risk for the general population", the ministries of Agriculture and Health assure. The European health institute ECDC says it is closely monitoring the situation . It is working on additional testing capacity and offers member states help with monitoring the outbreak among livestock. European outbreak Shamonda was first identified in cattle in Nigeria in the 1960s. Since then it has appeared in Africa, Australia and Japan, but this summer an outbreak was for the first time also identified in Europe. In July the first cases were reported in cattle in southern Germany, Switzerland and eastern France. Later more countries followed, including the Netherlands and Belgium. The disease causes diarrhoea, fever, spontaneous abortions and a drop in milk production in cattle. In horses, which can also suffer from it, the symptoms resemble damage to the nervous system. Earlier this month the disease was identified for the first time in a horse in the Netherlands. Sheep, goats and alpacas can also contract the disease. The disease is transmitted by bites from biting midges, small biting flies. The ECDC points out that these mainly occur in spring, summer and autumn, and spread in these colder months is less likely. European variant It is still being investigated how the patient in France became infected. That appears to have happened in eastern France. No vaccine is available against the disease. The virus circulating in Europe is a different variant from the type already known to doctors. It is therefore officially called SHAV-EU, for European shamonda virus. According to the World Organisation for Animal Health, it is still too early to say whether this variant will behave like the others as a seasonal disease.

title: Macron bans all protests not organised by trade unions, lashes out at 'far-left groups'
lead: All protests next Saturday that are not organised by trade unions will be banned. That is what French President Macron said after an emergency meeting lasting several hours with, among others, the French intelligence services. "Wherever people demonstrate who have no right to do so, intervention will follow", said Macron. "We want calm to return." He also admitted that there were "shortcomings" in the preparations for last Saturday's demonstrations. Protests spread across the country got out of hand at that time. Thousands of people took to the streets in Paris, Lyon, Lille, Nice, Bordeaux and Marseille, among other places. At least 1,500 shops were looted, there were arson attacks, and confrontations took place between masked youths and the police. In the end, more than 2,300 people were arrested for the riots. A day later Macron, live on French television, lashed out hard at the rioters and said that everyone who wanted to bring down the Republic would be held to account. Meanwhile the riots in Paris continued on Sunday. Macron acknowledged " a lack of foresight" in the violence that broke out on Saturday and Sunday. He also again explicitly referred to " organised far-left groups who want to overthrow the Republic with extreme danger, a very high level of violence and careful planning." That he now chooses to ban all demonstrations not linked to a trade union is therefore, he says, the use of "common sense". Large-scale protests are expected again on Saturday. The yellow vests have also announced that they will take part. That protest movement arose in 2018 out of discontent over the announced rise in fuel prices. It developed into a broader protest against the high cost of living and income inequality. Prime Minister Lecornu has announced that demonstrators can expect a huge police presence. To relieve the police at certain moments, the army will also be deployed on the streets. Macron said this would be discussed further tomorrow, since the security services are, in his view, "under immense pressure". It was precisely the harsh police action during the school student protests that caused social outrage in France even before the weekend riots. The Paris city council has urged its residents and shopkeepers to be "extra alert" on Saturday for rioters who "have nothing to do with the social movement". They must also have removed their bins, bicycles, terrace furniture and garden furniture from public space by 12.00 noon. Second suspect arrested for fire in Limoges Today it also became known that the police have arrested a second suspect for setting fire to the 19th-century town hall of Limoges. He is a 66-year-old man. On Tuesday a 34-year-old man had been arrested for the fire in which the town hall tower collapsed. This man is now also suspected of attempted murder of the police officers who were in the building when the fire broke out. According to French media, this suspect belonged to a far-left group and was already known to the French security services. The investigation into what exactly happened in Limoges last Saturday is still ongoing. According to French media, it is examining the extent to which the attack on the town hall was planned in advance and which forces might be behind it. In France, people have been protesting for weeks against the deficiencies of education, the high cost of living and government policy.

title: Police get help from military police to tackle nuisance in Ter Apel
lead: Police in Ter Apel are getting help from the Royal Military Police to tackle the problems in the village, RTV Noord reports. A group of migrants, mainly 'veiligelanders', is causing a lot of nuisance in the Groningen village. According to <entity id="person:jaap-velema">burgemeester Velema</entity>, it involves shoplifting and arguments, among other things. "We are dealing with a very high number of shoplifting incidents", he tells RTV Noord. On average it goes wrong twenty times a week. There are also, according to the mayor, regular incidents on and around the grounds of the reception centre, such as stabbings. The nuisance has now become so great that the <entity id="org:gemeente-westerwolde">gemeente Westerwolde</entity> has asked for extra deployment of the military police. Talks with the asylum minister Last month the mayor announced that the ministry would come up with new measures to tackle the nuisance in Ter Apel. A good month later, too little of that has come about, Velema said last night in the council. The mayor has a meeting this evening with minister Van den Brink of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-am">Asiel en Migratie</entity>. The asylum organisation <entity id="org:zbo-centraal-orgaan-opvang-asielzoekers">COA</entity> is also present. Velema wants to make clear in that meeting that the agreements to reduce the nuisance must also be kept. "I hope results will be achieved in the coming weeks. Actually, this nuisance should never have arisen at all", says the mayor. The military police will in any case help the police in Ter Apel in the coming months. Between 2022 and 2024 military police also stepped in in Ter Apel. "It is regrettable that this is necessary", says a COA spokesperson to RTV Noord. The ministry has not yet responded. Reception centre overcrowded The reception centre in Ter Apel has been overcrowded for months. Two weeks ago twenty asylum seekers were forced to sleep outside on the grass in the rain, because there were too few reception places. Last summer asylum seekers repeatedly tried to enter a residential care centre looking for a place to sleep. The care home has since hired security. "These are things we have not had before, and that is why we are contacting the minister", says Velema.

title: Son allowed to speak to Aung San Suu Kyi for the first time in five years
lead: The imprisoned former leader of Myanmar, Aung San Suu Kyi, has been allowed to speak to her son by phone for the first time in five years. Kim Aris writes on Facebook that "words cannot express how much it means to hear her voice again". He was able to call her at the Myanmar embassy in London, as shown in photos the regime has released. "I am deeply grateful to everyone who has supported my mother and me. I am convinced that your attention has made this moment possible. Please keep speaking out until she is free again." The victory of Suu Kyi's party in the November 2020 elections led to a new seizure of power by the military, which is still ongoing. Suu Kyi was detained in 2021, after a period in which the military rulers had allowed cautious reforms. Sham trial In a sham trial, Suu Kyi was sentenced to 20 years in prison for electoral fraud and corruption. Independent observers say there is no evidence for these accusations, and human rights organisations speak of a political process. The 81-year-old Suu Kyi is currently under house arrest in an unknown location. In August she received a visit from the Red Cross for the first time in five years. Earlier this week the regime released photos of her for the first time in months. They showed her receiving two books and correspondence from the British king, Charles. With this cautious openness about Suu Kyi, the regime hopes to build goodwill with the international community. The junta has long sought ties with neighbouring countries, because the country became internationally isolated after the coup. Aris believes that despite these modest gestures, the ultimate goal must not be forgotten. "Do not let the illusion arise that everything is normal", he responded to the photos of his mother. "My mother's fundamental rights are still being violated." Also after the phone call, about which he shared no further details, he said that Suu Kyi "must not be held hostage or used as a bargaining chip for diplomatic recognition, the easing of sanctions or political gain". "Freedom is not a bargaining tool", he stressed in an appeal to the United Kingdom, the former colonial ruler of Myanmar. "My mother and all other political prisoners must be released immediately and without conditions."

title: Record fine of 37 million euros for illegal gambling provider
lead: The <entity id="org:zbo-kansspelautoriteit">Kansspelautoriteit</entity> (Ksa) has imposed a record fine of 37 million euros on a gambling company. It concerns the illegal gambling company EOD Code SRL, registered in Costa Rica. The company offers gambling on all kinds of websites in our country without a licence, such as Instantcasino and Skyhills. The regulator had already established in 2024 that the company was in breach. EOD Code was then warned that it could receive a fine for the misconduct. The Ksa's first investigation focused on Instantcasino, but it later turned out that at least eleven other illegal gambling sites were active. The sites lacked visible age verification, and visitors could pay with crypto and anonymous payment methods. As a result, the company has now received a fine based on an estimate of the revenue it generated. "We have several instruments we can deploy, and we are deploying all of them, including imposing a fine," says the KSa. The regulator often sees that these kinds of parties, which operate from abroad, do not pay the fine. No response EOD Code was repeatedly given the opportunity to respond to the Kansspelautoriteit, but no response came, the regulator reports. To block access to the illegal sites, it has other options as well. For example, the Ksa works with hosting providers and payment service providers to block access to gambling sites.

title: Podcast De Dag: the vulnerability of PHP, 'the underpants' of the internet
lead: From DigiD to the French government, and from RTL Nieuws to Schiphol. Websites of all kinds of agencies went offline for a few hours yesterday. There were leaks in PHP, a language for programming websites. Because those leaks were out in the open, websites were vulnerable to hackers. And so it was safer to take websites offline for a while. What does this leak say about the vulnerability of our internet? Listen here: You can listen to this episode of De Dag via NPO Luister and all other podcast apps. Do you like it? Then don't forget to subscribe. According to NOS tech journalist Joost Schellevis, you can compare PHP to underpants. Everyone uses it, it is important, but normally it remains invisible. With the help of AI, the leak in those underpants has now been found. Artificial intelligence is both a curse and a blessing for the vulnerability of the internet. On the one hand, more leaks are being patched that a human would find hard to find. On the other hand, hackers who have bad intentions can strike more easily. Tech site Tweakers also went offline. That was unfortunate, because that was exactly where they wanted to write about this leak. Normally, it is only written about once the solution, a patch, is available. But now that order was turned upside down, so half the internet went dark. Tweakers editor-in-chief Wout Funnekotter fears this will not be the last time. Respond: Email to dedag@nos.nl Presentation & editing: Marco Geijtenbeek Editorial: Wouter Sloekers

title: Ukrainians who lost everything demand compensation from Russia via the Netherlands
lead: "I want nothing at all from Russia, but they destroyed my house. And they have to pay for that." Oleksandr Tereshchenko regularly wipes the tears from his cheeks as he describes how he lost his home in the Russian invasion of Ukraine. "I am not a soldier. My house was not a military base." Tereshchenko is one of many Ukrainians demanding compensation from Russia for the damage they have suffered from the violence in their country. Courts in their own country mostly rule in their favour, but the Russian authorities pay no attention to this. That is why various Ukrainian citizens and companies are now trying to pursue it through a Dutch court, as several ongoing lawsuits show. Chance in the Netherlands The aggrieved parties choose the Netherlands for various reasons. Tereshchenko does so out of hope, he explains: "Because of the history and the case over the shooting down of flight MH17. If there is a chance anywhere, it is in the Netherlands, the capital of global justice", he refers to the International Criminal Court in The Hague. Tereshchenko and his family lived in Horenka. This small sleepy town north of Kyiv turned into a war zone in February 2022, when Russian troops tried to take the nearby airfield before the attack on Kyiv. "Our apartment was hit by tanks, rockets, everything", says Tereshchenko. "We had to flee to the cellar. When it became quiet for a while, we crept outside. Nothing was left of our apartment." Tereshchenko, a lawyer in his own country, is realistic about his chances at the Dutch court: "I give myself a 0.1 percent chance, but I am trying anyway. If it succeeds, more people who have lost their homes to Russian violence may get something back." 'Alter ego' There is also another reason why Ukrainians try to fight out their lawsuits against Russia in the Netherlands. A lot of Russian money is still present in the Netherlands, for example from Dutch subsidiaries of gas giant Gazprom. The <entity id="org:hoge-raad">Hoge Raad</entity> ruled this year that Gazprom, as a state company, may be regarded as an 'alter ego' of the Russian state. For that reason, a claim against Russia via Gazprom may now be handled by a Dutch court. For example that of Farm Syu Zhnyva. This Ukrainian agricultural company had grain silos in the regions of Zaporizhzhia and Kherson. Those silos were partly looted "by Russian-speaking persons in Russian military uniforms", according to an interim ruling of the The Hague Court of Appeal from June. The rest of the grain has spoiled. Because of the disaster, Syu Zhnyva has now gone bankrupt. In Ukraine a court had ruled that the grain company is entitled to 75 million euros in damages. But because Gazprom does not pay, assets of Gazprom in the Netherlands were attached in 2024. Difficult, not unique Enforcing compensation from a State through the courts is not unique. However, it is difficult to sue a State, emphasises Mathijs ten Wolde, professor of international private law at the University of Groningen: "Certainly in another country." Ten Wolde points to Article 431 of the Dutch Code of Civil Procedure. It states that rulings of foreign courts cannot be enforced here. For this reason, Russia also disregards compensation awarded by Ukrainian courts. Exceptions are made for rulings in countries where the justice system meets international standards, Ten Wolde says: "If the procedures have been carefully followed, if a defendant has had sufficient opportunity to defend themselves and it does not conflict with public order." Money in the Netherlands If that is the case, a resident or company from Ukraine has a chance to recover the damage through a Dutch court. For example by having assets attached of the many Russian holdings that are here, including those of Dutch subsidiaries of Russian companies. Legal experts the NOS spoke with call the ongoing lawsuits very interesting, also because this is legally uncharted territory. However, they emphasise that this could become a matter of a long haul. The NOS asked the lawyer of Gazprom Nederland for a response to the ongoing lawsuits. The lawyer says that, due to the duty of confidentiality, they cannot respond on the substance. Claims commission in the Netherlands Late last year, the Netherlands announced it wants to become the host country for a special commission where Ukrainians can claim their war damage suffered during the Russian invasion. At that time, more than 80,000 damage claims had already been registered. This claims commission is not yet operational, according to the <entity id="org:ministerie-van-buitenlandse-zaken">ministerie van Buitenlandse Zaken</entity>. That can only happen when at least 25 states that have signed the founding treaty also ratify the treaty. In addition, these countries must guarantee at least half of the required total budget of 7.4 million euros. For now, ten countries, including the Netherlands, and the European Union have ratified the treaty for the claims commission. The ministry of Foreign Affairs expects that by mid-2027 the remaining sixteen countries will have signed.

title: Cabinet promise to cap student loan interest under pressure: plan turns out to be far too expensive
lead: Capping the interest rate on student loans at a maximum of 2.5 percent is risky and expensive. That is what <entity id="person:rianne-letschert">minister Letschert</entity> of Education (D66) writes to <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>. The minister "baalt ervan", but concludes that the plan is many times more expensive than thought. The coalition had reserved 40 million for it, but it will cost at least four times as much. That would have consequences for the rest of the education budget and the treasury. Letschert wants to discuss the problem with the Chamber soon, she writes. Amount could quickly rise Many students borrow money from the government so they can pay for their study time. Most have to repay that borrowed amount after their studies, and they pay interest on it. For a long time that interest was 0 percent, but in recent years the percentage has been rising. As a result, the amount that (former) students have to repay can quickly increase. For this reason D66, VVD and CDA agreed in the coalition agreement to introduce an interest cap of 2.5 percent. They reserved 40 million euros for this. Interest already above 2.5 percent The discussion about capping interest at 2.5 percent has become topical again in recent weeks. At the beginning of October the interest on student loans rose again, for hundreds of thousands of students even by one percentage point, to 3.28 percent. As a result, the interest is now higher for many (former) students than the coalition parties consider desirable. Letschert says she understands students' concerns, but says that the money now reserved for the maximum interest is not enough to work out the plans. Interest rises have regularly led to protests in recent years: That the plan for an interest cap poses a major risk to the government's treasury has been known at the ministry for years. In 2023, then education minister Dijkgraaf warned that an interest cap could 'drain' the Ministry of Education entirely. This is how it works: to pay out the student loans, the government itself also has to take out loans. If the interest on that loan rises sharply, the ministry has to cover the difference itself. That can quickly add up to tens of millions of euros per year. Moreover, students with an interest cap are likely to borrow much more than they need. For the money they thereby free up, they get a much higher savings rate at the bank or elsewhere. The ministry can reduce this risk by introducing the interest cap only for the current generation of students. However, according to the Ministry of Education this is difficult to implement, because <entity id="org:dienst-uitvoering-onderwijs">DUO</entity> would then have to distinguish between different generations of students. How many (former) students pay interest on student loans? According to the <entity id="org:zbo-centraal-bureau-voor-de-statistiek">Centraal Bureau voor de Statistiek</entity>, there are currently just over a million former students with student debt. There are also 400,000 people who are studying now and have student debt. The total student debt is currently around 28 billion euros. 145,000 people have student debt of more than 50,000 euros. Despite the earlier warnings, the current coalition parties nevertheless included the plan for an interest cap in their agreement. Student organisations want the coalition to keep that promise. They call on students to sign a petition. The anger is especially strong among former students who studied under the loan system. Then minister Bussemaker said, when that loan system was introduced, that students should not have to fear debt. Now the consequences of that high loan turn out to be greater for them than expected. The interest on student loans is always much lower than on other (commercial) loans. The repayment rules are also flexible: anyone with little or no income does not have to repay. Students can also temporarily pause repayment.

title: Swiss (69) and Austrian (76) released 1.5 years after kidnapping in Niger
lead: Two women who were kidnapped more than a year and a half ago in the West African country of Niger have been released. The 76-year-old Austrian Eva Gretzmacher and the 69-year-old Swiss Claudia Abbt were taken hostage in January and April last year in Agadez, a city in the centre of the country. Both the Austrian and the Swiss government have confirmed the release today. After both women were taken to the Libyan city of Benghazi and medically checked there, they flew back to Europe. Armed men Gretzmacher was kidnapped in January by armed men from her home in Agadez, where she had lived and worked for more than twenty years as a development worker and humanitarian aid worker. A few months later Abbt was also kidnapped in Agadez. She too had worked for many years as a social worker in the Nigerien city. During their captivity the women were taken to neighbouring Mali. Ransom and people smuggling According to African media it is still unclear why and by whom the women were kidnapped. No group has claimed responsibility for the kidnapping, although African media point to IS or groups linked to it. It is known that violent gangs are active in the Sahel region that earn a lot of money from people smuggling and kidnapping foreigners. Whether a ransom was paid in this case is not known. Libyan general Rumours that the women had been freed came out last week. Yesterday news agency Reuters reported this, and today the official confirmation came. Christoph, Gretzmacher's son, earlier told RTL Nieuws about his efforts to get his mother freed. He sought contact with, among others, Libyan general Haftar, who successfully mediated in other kidnappings. Footage shows Abbt speaking directly to him. "I am very happy that I have been released. I thank Haftar and his son, General Saddam Khalifa Haftar, for everything they have done to free us. Thank you very much."

title: Signals at National Cyber Security Centre of misuse of PHP flaw
lead: The National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) has received signals that the major flaw in the PHP programming language has now been misused. "We see attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities and we are receiving the first signals that this is successfully happening," says a spokesperson. Earlier, the NCSC said it did not yet see such signals. The NCSC advises companies to update systems quickly. "Attempts to exploit the flaw have been circulating since yesterday. We are in contact with all kinds of organisations at home and abroad, and through that channel we are receiving signals that exploitation is taking place." The NCSC does not want to say exactly what the concrete signals entail. The agency is conducting research, but that may take months. Protected At the same time, many websites have now been protected, research by NOS shows. At least 113.000 Dutch websites have demonstrably installed a newer version of PHP. As a result, those websites are no longer vulnerable to the flaw. However, around 145.000 Dutch websites may still be vulnerable. That cannot be said with certainty from a distance. These concern sites that run an old PHP version but which may nonetheless be protected through another route. Many problems The flaw in the PHP programming language, which many websites are built with, led to many problems yesterday. For example, the RTL Nieuws website went offline, as did a number of government sites. Municipalities using the Notubiz meeting system also could not log in, nor could accountants working with Exact software. This happened as a precaution, to prevent hackers from exploiting the flaw. At that moment there were no patches available yet, digital patches with which server administrators can protect their websites. Shortly before 16.00 the solution became available, after which many websites came back online in the course of the afternoon and evening.

title: Suspected Russian spy arrested in the German state of Brandenburg
lead: In Germany a Ukrainian man has been arrested who allegedly spied for Russia. He is suspected, among other things, of passing on military information about NATO. The man was staying in the eastern German state of Brandenburg, which borders Poland. The arrest was first reported by German media and later confirmed by the Public Prosecutor's Office of Brandenburg. The age and place of residence of the man have not been disclosed. The suspect allegedly had contact since July 2025 with an unnamed Russian intelligence service. The Ukrainian is accused of sharing information about the production of armored vehicles, ammunition and explosives. Military installations on NATO's eastern flank were also reportedly being monitored. Attacks and sabotage In recent years people have regularly been arrested in Germany on suspicion of spying for Russia or even of plotting attacks and sabotage. Two months ago a Ukrainian was sentenced to fifteen months in prison for preparing arson attacks on behalf of Russia. Two other Ukrainians were acquitted due to lack of evidence. The German authorities also hold Moscow responsible for the drone with explosives found in August near Leipzig airport. The Kremlin has consistently dismissed the accusations as nonsense. According to researchers and Western intelligence services, however, it is certain that Russia is increasingly escalating its hybrid war against European countries because of their military support for Ukraine.

title: No free bike bus on the Afsluitdijk in winter due to lack of passengers
lead: The free shuttle bus that lets people transport their bicycles across the Afsluitdijk will temporarily stop running on 1 November. In recent winters the service was barely used, which is why <entity id="org:rijkswaterstaat">Rijkswaterstaat</entity> has decided to save the money. For years it has not been possible to cycle along the 32-kilometer-long flood barrier. In 2019 the bike path was closed due to the reinforcement of the dike and the renewal of locks and pumps. The path has been largely open again since 2024, but cycling all the way to the other side is still not possible. To still get there by bicycle, people could use the free shuttle bus. Empty trips back and forth But in winter the bus often runs back and forth empty, says a spokesperson for Rijkswaterstaat to Omrop Fryslân . On average, fewer than thirty people per month used the bus, compared with 3,000 people per month in summer. "We drove back and forth empty quite a few days last year. That is a waste of money." From 1 March travelers can use the bus again. Later in the year cycling across the Afsluitdijk should be fully possible again: temporary bicycle bridges will be installed. These are likely to be put into use in the third quarter of 2027. Cheaper bicycle bridge The choice to install those temporary bicycle bridges is based on finances. Running the bike bus during the works would cost 14 million euros. Earlier this year, at the request of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>, <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> examined whether there might be a cheaper solution. That turned out to be the case: building temporary bicycle bridges. According to calculations, that would cost around 5 million euros.

title: Hajar (29) sent 'disturbing messages to an acquaintance' on the day she went missing
lead: The 29-year-old woman from Amsterdam who was found dead last week had sent "disturbing messages to an acquaintance" on the day of her disappearance. Hajar did so on Sunday morning 4 October, on the same day her parents contacted officers, the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> reports. The police will not say what exactly she sent. De Telegraaf says it has seen WhatsApp messages in which Hajar sent "Help me. Now. He is killing me" to a family member. The police say Hajar had been away for longer periods before, but always came back. That weekend too she left with a suitcase, but she never returned. The police say Hajar sent the messages in the morning. Afterwards family members had no contact with her, after which they contacted officers in the evening, according to the police. It is not clear why that did not happen right away. Urgent a day later "Based on all the facts and circumstances known at that time, the disappearance was assessed as not urgent at that time", says the police. For privacy reasons nothing further is said about this. On Monday evening, a day later, the disappearance was nevertheless made urgent, because there was still no contact with Hajar. "That assessment is made by a judicial officer", says the police. "That happens based on facts and circumstances surrounding the disappearance, such as the behaviour and personal circumstances of the missing person, the statements of the reporter and other relevant information." Family members did not give permission that day to publish her photo, according to the police. Detectives did try to find her in several ways, the police say, for example by locating her phone. A property in the Amsterdam neighbourhood Buitenveldert was searched that night, but the woman and her phone were not found there. Suspect arrested Her body was eventually found on 16 October, in a suitcase in the water at the Amsteldijk. In connection with her death, a 23-year-old man has been arrested. He has Somali nationality and has lived in the Netherlands since he was six. This Abdi A. has a residence permit for an indefinite period and at the time of his arrest had no fixed residence. The man was arrested on Tuesday in the North Holland village of Spierdijk after he assaulted his foster father with a hammer. He will be brought before the investigating judge tomorrow, who will decide whether he remains in custody.

title: Brit unexpectedly becomes a millionaire thanks to Pokémon card collection in attic
lead: He knew they were worth something, the Pokémon cards gathering dust in his attic. But that he would become a millionaire in one go thanks to his collection came as a complete surprise. It happened to a retired house painter in Great Britain, who wishes to remain anonymous. The collection started with his son, who in the late 1990s collected cards and traded them with friends at school. Pokémon had only just come out. The boy's father also got hooked. The man eventually collected 42 complete sets. Some remained completely unused and therefore in perfect condition. Such a set cost about 300 pounds at the time. The man thought it might be a good investment. Back to the attic That feeling turned out to be right, because the cards and video games from Japan became a huge hit. Later came series and even Pokémon films. But when his teenage son developed other interests, the man's interest faded too and the cards disappeared into the attic. Only after fifteen years did the box of Pokémon cards reappear. A note in the local newspaper about a valuable Pokémon card got the man thinking. He then took his collection to an auction house. There they immediately recognised the value of the collection. "When we saw what he had, everything in impeccable condition, we couldn't believe it", a card expert from Ewbank's Auctions told the BBC. 'Booming' The auction house had already attracted quite a bit of attention in advance. According to the owner, that happened without much effort, because according to auctioneer Andrew Ewbank, Pokémon is 'booming' at the moment. The most valuable was the Legendary Collection Complete Master Set. The estimated proceeds were between 15,000 and 20,000 pounds. But it turned out differently: that one set sold for 100,000 pounds, over 119,000 euros. The auction would become the most lucrative ever for the auction company. The man from Woking's entire card collection turned out to be worth 1.56 million pounds. That is over 1.8 million euros.

title: Eye condition forces British actress Judi Dench (91) to stop acting for good
lead: British actress Judi Dench is stopping acting for good. Her eye condition makes it impossible for her to take up her work again. She can no longer read either, the 91-year-old Oscar winner tells the BBC. Dench was already diagnosed with age-related macular degeneration in 2012. That condition impairs sight. The specific form Dench has mainly occurs in people over fifty. Her vision problems made it increasingly difficult for her to work in recent years. For example, she had trouble seeing well on film sets, and it became harder and harder for her to learn lines by heart. The condition is now so serious that she sees almost nothing and has trouble recognising faces. Despite her eye condition, Dench continues to appear in public. She also wants to keep talking on the radio about her life with reduced sight. About growing older, Dench says she finds it annoying, but she tries not to think about it too much. The boss of James Bond Dench has more than seventy years of career behind her. She became world famous for her role as M, the boss of James Bond. She first played that role in the 1995 film GoldenEye. In total the British actress played the role of M in eight James Bond films. As the icing on the cake, she won an Oscar for best supporting actress in the 1998 film Shakespeare in Love. Dench was also nominated for an Oscar seven more times. In the interview with the BBC, Dench also talks about her love for the work of William Shakespeare. That began when she was nine years old and her brother played the role of King Duncan in the film Macbeth. What ultimately won her over to Shakespeare were his sonnets. According to Dench, the writer expressed the feelings in these classic poems, of exactly fourteen lines, so simply that they reflect the rhythm of your heart.

title: Residents of the Euromast have for months been hearing an 'irritating whistling tone', cause unknown
lead: A 'loud echo', 'constant rustling' or an 'irritating beep': residents around the Euromast in <entity id="org:gemeente-rotterdam">Rotterdam</entity> have been complaining for months about noise nuisance from the tower. The Rijnmond Environmental Service (DCMR) is investigating the cause, but so far there is no answer. "You really hear the sound all the time," says resident Sasha to Rijnmond.
