"Since June we haven't been sleeping. You wake up from it so many times." Since June, hundreds of reports have come in to the Rijnmond Environmental Service (DCMR), the municipality of Rotterdam and the Euromast itself. This week alone there were at least 75. The sound seems to depend on weather conditions such as the wind, the complaints show. No loose cables DCMR started an investigation. At first it was thought the sound was caused by loose cables. The Euromast had been closed since January for a major renovation; possibly something came loose as a result. A contractor therefore tightened several cables. But that did not help: in July the Euromast reopened and the work was finished, but the irritating sound was not. This is what the sound is like: Now that it is autumn, the sound has become worse, says Sasha. She thinks that is due to the wind. "It's no longer an irritating whistling tone, but really a loud screech. I turn the TV up louder in the evening so I don't have to hear it." Upper part DCMR has meanwhile established that the sound comes from the upper part of the tower. But the cause is still unclear. The investigation is complex, because according to the environmental service the sound is not constantly audible. A specialised engineering firm has meanwhile been brought in to help search for the source of the sound. At the same time, DCMR cannot rule out that some reports have a different cause and that the Euromast is not the only source of the reported noise nuisance.

title: Pro-Israel AIPAC stops openly supporting political candidates due to 'challenges'
lead: The pro-Israel lobby group AIPAC says it will stop supporting candidates in elections in the United States. The policy of direct political involvement is being reversed after five years due to the growing criticism of the lobby group, American media write. Democratic and Republican candidates will no longer receive direct donations and no other support will be given to them, says AIPAC. The American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) is the most important and influential pro-Israel lobby group in the US. For more than 70 years the organisation has already worked for a close relationship between Israel and the United States. The lobby group receives money from, among others, its members and sponsors who make (large) donations. AIPAC announced the reversal of the policy in a letter to members. "We estimate that the challenges we face will continue to increase in the coming years." The letter does not state why AIPAC is stopping that support or what those challenges are. Public opinion AIPAC has in recent years increasingly come under fire due to controversial positions. For example, the pro-Israel lobby group supports the devastating war in Gaza and is in favour of the war in Iran. Political candidates openly supported by AIPAC face fierce criticism and even lose votes. The biggest defeat AIPAC suffered was in the Democratic primary between Abdul El-Sayed and Haley Stevens in the state of Michigan. Both competed this summer for a Senate seat. AIPAC put 30 million dollars into Stevens' campaign, the largest investment in a single race ever, to defeat El-Sayed. But the Israel-critical El-Sayed narrowly won that contest from the pro-Israel Stevens. More and more politicians openly criticise the pro-Israel group and distance themselves from AIPAC because public opinion about Israel in the US has changed. According to recent polls, many Americans have a negative attitude toward Israel and toward the close ties between that country and the US. Different strategy AIPAC says it is choosing a different strategy and will urge individual donors to donate directly to political candidates, American media write. AIPAC also continues to support the superPAC United Democracy Project, which is affiliated with the lobby group. A superPAC is a committee that may raise unlimited money and tries to exert influence on elections through advertising. The lobby group says that the presidential elections in 2028 call for "an even stronger commitment to a pro-Israel policy".

title: Embassy in Cairo closes after nine days of protests against the Netherlands
lead: The Dutch embassy in the Egyptian capital Cairo is closed for the time being. The closure was decided after demonstrations against the Netherlands took place for the ninth day in a row, the embassy announced on Facebook. Each demonstration required the embassy to be evacuated for safety reasons. Protesters are demonstrating against the arrest of Ahmed Nasser by the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>. Nasser is the deputy head of the 'Union of Egyptian Youth Abroad' and a mouthpiece of the government. He was arrested on 10 October and his pretrial detention has been extended by 14 days. The demonstrations at the Dutch embassy do not appear to have arisen spontaneously. Whereas demonstrations almost never take place in Egypt under the repressive government, demonstrators have now been dropped off by bus at the embassy every day in the Zamalek district. That is an island in the Nile where many embassies are located and where a large police presence is present. One day after Nasser's arrest, the Egyptian foreign minister asked his Dutch counterpart Berendsen in a phone call for Nasser's release and for clarification about his arrest. Although both ministers publicly stated after that conversation that they wished to continue the good relationship, the demonstrations at the embassy continued. Padlock at embassy in The Hague: Nasser was reportedly arrested in the Netherlands for threatening the activist Anas Habib. Habib became known last summer when he locked the gate of the Egyptian embassy in The Hague with a padlock. He filmed his action. As his reason he cited the Egyptian decision to keep the Rafah border crossing with Gaza closed for Palestinians wishing to flee. This led to a chain reaction in which Egyptians in more countries locked the Egyptian embassy. In a leaked video the Egyptian foreign minister addresses the ambassador to the Netherlands: "If anyone tries to attach a lock or anything else to the embassy, drag him inside and make his life a hell." At the time Habib's padlock action also led to a protest at the Dutch embassy in Cairo, demanding that the Netherlands do more to protect the Egyptian embassy. Habib was questioned by the Dutch police, but was allowed to await the investigation in freedom. Closed until further notice: When the embassy in Egypt will reopen is not yet known. The embassy remains reachable for consular assistance in case of emergency. The <entity id="org:ministerie-van-buitenlandse-zaken">Ministerie van Buitenlandse Zaken</entity> says the embassy has been "closed until further notice as a precaution" and that "the safety of our staff always has our highest priority". Regarding the protocols on evacuating the embassy during demonstrations, the ministry, for security reasons, would not say anything.

title: Autumn weather gets going: lots of wind this weekend, possibly with the first storm
lead: It has been hanging in the air for a few days, but whether it will actually storm in the Netherlands is still uncertain. That depends on the course of 'storm' Austen. What is certain is that it will be windy at times through Sunday. Friday morning it rains heavily. In the course of the morning it becomes drier for a short time, but stays cloudy. In the afternoon the core of 'storm' Austen arrives, bringing clouds, rain and an increasing wind. From the afternoon, the southwest of the country, but also the hills of Limburg, have a chance of severe gusts of at least 75 km per hour. In the course of the evening and night it also becomes quite windy elsewhere in the country. Whether it really comes to a storm is still uncertain. It depends on the course of Austen. If the storm moves about 100 kilometres differently than is currently most likely, that could still lead to more wind. Then there is a chance of an official storm with wind force 9. Depression train: Saturday the showers ease off temporarily, there is some sun and the wind also eases somewhat. In the evening it will rain hard again and the wind picks up again. It looks very much like we will again have a chance of severe gusts, possibly even very severe in the coastal areas. An official storm is not ruled out then either. Sunday it blows hard, especially in the north of the country. There are also showers there, while in the south the sun shines somewhat more often. In the coming days it will reach a maximum of 13 degrees. So it is fully autumn: the depression train has really built up steam.

title: Political flanks capitalise on unrest in France: 'Violence polarises'
lead: Large-scale protests, looting and police violence have gripped France for weeks. The unrest is also further sharpening political tensions, just half a year before the French presidential elections, which will also be of great significance for Europe as a whole. Almost all parties are pointing the accusing finger at the radical-left party La France Insoumise (LFI) as the instigator of the violence. The party is criticised, for example, for failing to distance itself from the anarchist anti-police slogan ACAB (all cops are bastards), which was heard frequently during the demonstrations. Prime Minister Lecornu has called the parliamentary group leaders together to calm tempers. Security around the presidential elections is also central to this. Presidential candidate and LFI leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon has announced that his party will be present, but threatens to disrupt the talks. He wants to show that he will not be summoned by the prime minister. Mélenchon refuses to go along with the view that his party has fuelled the violence. Instead, he accuses <entity id="org:regering">de regering</entity> of failing to tackle the deep-rooted social and economic problems in the suburbs. According to him, responsibility for the unrest therefore lies with the government and the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>, and other tensions such as the war in the Middle East also play a role. With that frame, he especially appeals to young people. Exhausted and weakened The radical-right party Rassemblement National (RN) is also capitalising on public anger. The unrest strengthens the position of presidential candidate Marine Le Pen, says France expert Niek Pas. For Le Pen, the ongoing unrest is an ideal opportunity to position herself as the champion of order and security against a government that is weakened and exhausted and has lost its grip on the situation. "At the RN party office they are laughing their heads off", Pas says. "Le Pen does not need to do much to win votes, apart from radiating calm." Two rounds That Le Pen has the wind in her sails is also evident from a poll published this week. It shows her not only clearly in front as the favourite for the first round of the presidential elections, but also as the favourite for the second round. She will win it, whoever her opponent is, it seems. France goes to the polls next year on 18 April for the first round of the presidential elections. Two weeks later, on 2 May, the decisive second round follows between the two winners of the first round. NOS op 3 last week made this explainer on the unrest in France: While the political flanks gain support, the social democrats and centre-right are losing ground. Raphaël Glucksmann (Place Publique), Édouard Philippe (Horizons) and Gabriel Attal (Renaissance, the party of President Marcon) are falling in the polls. "Violence polarises", Pas says. "It is precisely the political centre that is struggling to find a convincing response to it. And that uncertainty is worrying. It underlines the deep crisis France is in: a social-societal, financial-economic and political crisis." Reckoning Last Saturday, the violence completely got out of hand. Shops and supermarkets were looted, and symbols of the republic bore the brunt: the town hall of Limoges went up in flames and that of Marseille was stormed. "Le 17 octobre, Saturday, was Macron's reckoning, the evaluation of ten years of presidency", Pas says. "That it is so intense is also because the elections are approaching. Political parties are jumping on this and sharpening their strategies." The parties on the flanks are taking the clearest positions and are fighting each other, says French political scientist and pollster Jérôme Fourquet as well. "They are trying to eliminate all the other political forces that are located in the centre." Fragmentation Amid all this political violence, Macron appears powerless, analyses political journalist Solenn de Royer of Le Monde. According to her, Macron does not understand what is going on in the minds of the rioters. Nor did he, in his televised address after the riots, come up with concrete proposals to calm the unrest. Macron also has little room for manoeuvre: without a majority in the Assemblée Nationale (the French <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">Tweede Kamer</entity>), his hands are largely tied. Since the early parliamentary elections in June 2024, which he himself called, parliament has splintered into three large, irreconcilable blocs. Meanwhile, France is preparing for new protests next Saturday, or act II as the yellow vests call it. Because the police cannot handle it alone, the government also wants to call on the help of the army. On 31 October, act III follows, as the yellow vests have already announced.

title: Safe going out and getting home during ADE: extra measures again this edition
lead: Bike buddies, special hosts at the exit and a place to charge your phone before you leave. These are some examples of the extra safety measures during the <entity id="org:gemeente-amsterdam">Amsterdam</entity> Dance Event (ADE). Yesterday the largest event for electronic music in the world began. Several organisers, such as DGTL and Awakenings, deploy bike buddies at night. That way no one has to cycle alone. "These are two people who continuously cycle back and forth between the event location at NDSM and the ferry," writes the municipality of Amsterdam. "A couple was deliberately chosen so that they too travel together and are not alone on the street during the night." Empty battery At the NDSM site, a physical help post has also been set up for visitors who feel vulnerable or unsafe at night. The Safe Check-In is open daily during ADE from 19.00 to 07.00 hours. Staff are ready to offer help or a listening ear. Visitors who, for example, missed their night bus or have an empty phone can also go there. At Awakenings there is a so-called goodbye host. This host stands at the exit and mainly watches out for people leaving alone. The host can also help with the route, and you can charge your phone with the host. "Handy if you still need to order an Uber or need your phone to share your location with someone." Hajar ADE also took extra measures last year. Then the murder of Lisa, in August near Amsterdam, caused horror and unrest. Now that is the case with the death of Hajar. The body of the 29-year-old woman was found last week in a suitcase in the Amstel in Amsterdam. The municipality of Amsterdam reports that measures have been taken together with ADE. Organisers also receive presentations on safety. And with a special campaign, bystanders learn how to intervene in an unsafe situation. Lisa Shortly before the start of ADE last year, Lisa was murdered in Duivendrecht. The 17-year-old girl was killed with great violence, which caused a wave of horror. The action 'Wij eisen de nacht op' was also launched at that time.

title: Driver under the influence in Amsterdam was transporting pythons in centre console
lead: The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> in Amsterdam made a striking discovery by chance. A 51-year-old driver was found to be transporting two pythons in a storage compartment. He was under the influence. The Amsterdammer was stopped on the A4. When it became clear he was not sober, he was arrested. Goldfish in a bag The police transport team was called to move the car. When officers searched it, they found two live pythons in the centre console. On the back seat was a box of live mice and a goldfish in a bag of water. The animals have been taken to a rescue centre. Ventilation Keeping pythons is not prohibited in the Netherlands. Transporting your own python within a certain number of kilometres does not require a permit. You must, however, comply with welfare requirements. For example, there must be sufficient ventilation, which was definitely not the case here. The police come across exotic animals in the city more often, city broadcaster AT5 writes. Earlier this year, officers also found a dead, mutilated python in a rubbish container.

title: Leading game studio BioWare must close its doors after 31 years
lead: The influential game studio BioWare has to close its doors. The Canadian studio made its name in recent decades with games such as Mass Effect and Dragon Age. Parent company Electronic Arts (EA) has decided, after disappointing results, to shut down BioWare and cut 400 jobs. BioWare was founded in 1995 and focused on so-called rpgs, role-playing games, in which players can choose for themselves which direction the story takes. BioWare's first success came in 1998 with Baldur's Gate, a PC game based on the popular role-playing game Dungeons and Dragons from the 1970s. At the start of the century, BioWare became one of the most renowned studios in the sector. This was due to the successes of the Star Wars title Knights of the Old Republic, the sci-fi games of the Mass Effect trilogy and the Dragon Age fantasy games. These titles often appear on lists of the best games ever made. Mass Effect was groundbreaking. Mass Effect (2005) and its two sequels are considered some of the most influential games. Particularly notable were the deep relationships between the main character and the other characters. Through wrong dialogue choices, players can permanently lose team members, so that they do not return even in later games, which was revolutionary for the time. Players can also choose whether to enter into a relationship with someone of the same or the other gender. In 2007 BioWare was taken over by EA. Afterwards, some successful games were still released, but the latest games disappointed. Among others, Mass Effect: Andromeda (not part of the trilogy) and Anthem performed poorly commercially. According to EA, the sales figures of the latest game, Dragon Age: The Veilguard, were also nothing to write home about. That is why a round of layoffs was already carried out at the studio last year. "After more than three decades, BioWare is closing its doors and development of the next Mass Effect game has been halted," the studio writes in a statement. "Our games became so much more meaningful because you played them, talked about your choices, fell in love with the characters, and made our worlds your own. Thank you for being the most important part of our story." EA taken over by Saudi group. The closure of BioWare follows a few months after the takeover of EA, one of the largest publishers in the industry, with games such as EA FC (formerly FIFA), The Sims and Battlefield. The American EA was bought for 55 billion dollars by a Saudi investment company, which also includes Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of American president Trump. Part of the deal was that EA would take on about 20 billion dollars in debt, which also has to be cleaned up. The closure of BioWare is part of that. EA calls the developer a "legendary studio that put the role-playing genre on the map, and we have therefore not acted hastily." Furthermore, EA says it will in future produce fewer large-scale action-adventure games simultaneously, to reduce development costs. A new Star Wars game and a new Iron Man game are still on the way.

title: Frenchman who died with the shamonda virus was already seriously ill
lead: The Frenchman who died with the shamonda virus had already been admitted to hospital for a serious illness. According to the French health service, the fact that he could become infected with the virus was due to the "severely weakened immune system of the man". However, the virus did worsen his complaints. According to the local newspaper Le Progrès, he was a sixty-year-old man living near Lyon. He died at the beginning of this month. This is an exceptional situation, says the French ministry of Health. There is no reason for panic and there is no crisis. The virus normally occurs in livestock. The man reportedly was stung by a small fly carrying the virus. In eastern France the virus was already detected in animals this spring and summer. The World Health Organization (WHO), which is in contact with the French authorities, also speaks of a single separate case. According to the organisation, it is very unlikely that the virus will spread further. European outbreak. The shamonda virus was first identified in cattle in Nigeria in the 1960s. Since then the virus has appeared on various continents. This summer an outbreak in Europe was identified for the first time, including in eastern France. In the Netherlands, an infection in a horse was identified for the first time at the beginning of this month. The disease is transmitted by biting midges, which mainly occur in spring, summer and autumn. In winter, spread is less likely due to lower temperatures. An infection with the virus causes fever and diarrhoea in cattle. There is no vaccine against it.

title: Gulf states fear a new war and seek protection beyond the US
lead: In the Gulf region, almost no one seems to doubt any more that a new war with Iran is coming. The main question is when. While the Americans are rapidly moving even more military equipment to the Gulf, the Gulf states are preparing for new drone and missile attacks from Iran and Yemen. Increasingly, they rely less on security guarantees from the US. In Doha, fighter jets flying overhead kept residents awake last night, and tension can also be felt in other places. Saudi state oil company Aramco has sent employees at its headquarters in Dhahran home to work from home. In the capital Riyadh, the iconic Kingdom Centre skyscraper has been evacuated for several days and children are getting lessons at home, out of fear of attacks by the Houthis. These measures show how much the threat of war is affecting daily life and the economy in the Gulf. Diplomats leave. Meanwhile, American diplomats have been instructed to leave Saudi Arabia with their families. According to news agency AFP, the same applies to American family members and embassy staff in Qatar, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates, among others. Iran is also preparing for a new war. Iran has warned that in the event of new American attacks it will strike back hard, not only against Israel and the American bases, but also against oil installations in the Gulf states. President Trump denies that Washington is still negotiating with Tehran, and cryptically says that an outcome will come 'fairly soon'. It remains unclear whether he means military action, but in the region those words were interpreted that way. The American Iran expert Vali Nasr, affiliated with Johns Hopkins University, says that almost everything points to Washington heading towards another war. According to him, heavier American and Israeli attacks could cause enormous damage without definitively knocking out Iran. He fears a prolonged disruption of the region, with all the consequences that entails for the world economy. New alliances. The crisis exposes a fundamental problem. For decades the Gulf states relied on the American security umbrella. They hosted American bases and bought billions of dollars' worth of American weapons. Those same bases now make them targets of Iranian retaliation. Persistent warnings from Gulf leaders have found little hearing in Washington, and earlier attacks have shown that even advanced American air defence offers no complete protection. That is why the Gulf states are increasingly looking for new security partners. This week Qatar signed the so-called Badr agreement with Turkey, Pakistan and Indonesia, aimed at jointly developing weapons systems and sharing military technology. According to Qatari Defence Minister Saoud bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, the agreement is meant to bring together the military capabilities of the participating countries. Other countries may also join later. Changing relations. According to Osama bin Javaid, analyst and reporter for news broadcaster Al Jazeera, the agreement is an important step in the changing relations in the Middle East. "This will be a historic agreement that will be part of the changing security architecture of the region", says Bin Javaid. According to him, the changing nature of warfare also plays a role. Cheap drones can cause billions of dollars in damage, while intercepting them with Western missiles can cost millions. By developing and producing weapons systems themselves, the countries hope to become less dependent on foreign suppliers. The Badr agreement follows the earlier Mecca pact between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan, in which the countries agreed to support each other in NATO style in the event of an attack. That does not mean the Gulf states are turning their backs on the US entirely. The ties are too deep and too important for that. It is more about spreading risks, with dependence on a single protector increasingly seen as a potential danger. While new alliances take shape, countries are preparing for a war they do not want themselves, but whose consequences they once again risk having to bear.

title: Scorching hot summer leads to record number of heat deaths in European cities
lead: In European cities, many tens of thousands of people died last summer as a result of the extreme heat. Scientists from Imperial College London and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine arrived at this estimate. New in their study is that they also point to the role of climate change through greenhouse gas emissions: they link a large part of the heat deaths directly to it. The scientists examined data on more than 850 urban areas in 30 European countries, where together about 40 percent of the population lives. Using models, they estimate that there were about 50,000 extra deaths in those regions last summer. For comparison, for the hot summers of 2022 and 2003 they arrived at 29,000 and 28,000 extra deaths respectively. This year thus well exceeds those record years. "The past summer consisted of extreme heatwaves across the whole continent. Since May there have been severe heatwaves every month", looks back climate scientist Clair Barnes of Imperial College. Especially in Western Europe it became unusually hot: on average the summer was about 2.9 degrees Celsius warmer than the average for the period 1991-2020. The difference with earlier years is large: especially the heatwave at the end of June, when code red was declared in the Netherlands, was very deadly. The British scientists estimate that a third of all deaths fell between 17 June and 1 July. The temperature was then about 5 degrees above the average for the period 1991-2020. The health effect was all the greater because few people were yet accustomed to the heat so early in the season. Most heat deaths are among the elderly. Still, around 6,000 people under the age of 65 also died. "It was certainly not limited to the elderly", explains scientist Garyfallos Konstantinoudis of Imperial College. "In the group between 20 and 44 years old, more than 800 people also died." As a rule, young heat deaths often have chronic conditions. "It is shocking, but it is an important point", says heat expert Carolina Pereira Marghidan of the <entity id="org:koninklijk-nederlands-meteorologisch-instituut">KNMI</entity>, who was not involved in the research. "I think not everyone realizes that it also affects young people, and not only the elderly. For the past 20 years, the picture for many people has been that mainly vulnerable elderly are affected. We simply see that this is not the case." In Italy, Spain and France most people died, but Germany and the United Kingdom were also hit hard: Although it is an estimate, the researchers' figures lie remarkably close to the official mortality figures. This was clearly visible because European governments regularly reported mortality figures in connection with the exceptional circumstances. From that data it could immediately be deduced that the extra deaths ran into the tens of thousands. Barnes: "The figures were sometimes published in real time, just to show how intense it was." The <entity id="org:rijksinstituut-voor-volksgezondheid-en-milieu">RIVM</entity> in the Netherlands reported, for example, that during the heatwave at the end of June and beginning of July there were well over 900 more deaths than normal. Pereira Marghidan: "In a way that matches well with what this research shows." For the whole summer the British estimate about 1,300 extra deaths in the Netherlands. "It was a different method and a different time span, but those figures match very well." Climate change Of the 50,000 deaths, 32,000 could be attributed to climate change. The scientists establish this by comparing the measured temperatures with the temperatures that would have been expected without greenhouse gas emissions. That knowledge, combined with medical models of heat mortality, gives an idea of the impact of climate change. "It is good that they estimate climate-related mortality this way", Pereira Marghidan thinks. "That way you see the mortality and they show what part of the mortality can be linked to climate change. That connection is well founded. With other weather phenomena that is harder, but precisely with temperature-related mortality you can make that link well." Silent killer The actual mortality is probably even higher than the 50,000 in the research. "Heat-related death tolls are underreported worldwide", explains researcher Malcom Mistry of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine. "Heat is also called a silent killer." People do not notice how severely their organs suffer from the heat, and heat deaths often also stay under the radar. This summer shows that Europe must arm itself against that silent killer, the scientists warn. "It is becoming increasingly clear that our cities are not well adapted to the rising heat", says researcher Pierre Masselot.

title: New York wants to get rid of horse-drawn carriages in Central Park
lead: The New York City Council has voted for a ban on horse-drawn carriages in Central Park. American media report this. The ban is to take effect in 2028; until then opponents can still challenge the plans legally. A ban on the carriages has been discussed for years; some criticise the industry as a form of animal abuse. The issue came under the spotlight after a horse bolted this summer. An 18-year-old tourist from India died as a result. The bill for a ban was adopted by a large majority of the council. There were forty votes in favour of the ban, only seven people voted against. Pedicab driver "The mayor will sign this bill", said the spokesperson for Mayor Mamdani. She says the city wants to protect owners and workers in the carriage sector as well as possible. At present about 180 horses are used to pull carriages, cared for by roughly two hundred owners and staff. The chair of the council said the city will do everything to help the circa 150 drivers who lose their jobs. Some could, for example, work as pedicab drivers in the park, it was suggested. The horses also get a better future: they may not go to the slaughterhouse or to other carriage companies. Supporters do not want to see the carriages disappear and hold on to what in their eyes is a charming tradition. The tourist attraction is as old as Central Park itself; the park has existed since the mid-nineteenth century. For decades tourists have used this mode of transport in New York's best-known park.

title: At least 16 dead in earthquake in Tibet
lead: An earthquake in northeastern Tibet has killed at least sixteen people. That is what the Chinese state news medium Xinhua reports. At least 65 people were also injured. The earthquake struck around 22.30 local time and had a magnitude of 7. The Chinese medium CCTV speaks of the most severe earthquake in the region in the past five years. The epicentre of the tremor is 191 kilometres from Nagqu, in a sparsely populated high-lying area in northern Tibet. After the quake seven aftershocks occurred with magnitudes ranging from 4,3 to 5,2, all at a depth of 10 kilometres. Xinhua reports that more than 300 houses have collapsed, as well as twenty livestock barns. Telecommunications services were also reportedly disrupted. The earthquake caused landslides that forced a motorway to be closed. Tents More than 1600 people from the region are being deployed as rescue workers; only they may enter the area via the motorway. They are bringing tents and folding beds, and people are also being handed flashlights and warm clothing. The Chinese state news medium writes that snow is expected in the area from time to time over the coming three days. Tingri Tibet was also hit by a major earthquake last year, in the Tingri region. At least 27.000 houses were damaged, as a result of which 45.000 people had to be housed elsewhere. The quake cost 126 people their lives; 188 people were injured. In August of this year the border between Nepal and Tibet was hit by a devastating ice and rock avalanche, in which more than 1000 people died. This happened after a glacier at high altitude broke off, causing ice and rocks to tumble down.

title: Lawyer Christa Pike: 'Wrongly placed IV may have caused damaged veins'
lead: The team responsible for the failed execution of Christa Pike repeatedly failed to insert an IV into her. That is what one of her lawyers, Randy Spivey, states in a court document, which American media are reporting on. Spivey also writes that before the execution attempt, the execution team warned that some of Pike's veins may have been torn by the needle sticks. According to the lawyer, the execution team used about ten needles in the attempts to place the IV. He states that both arms were pierced. The drug pentobarbital, which should have been fatal, was later administered through the IV. After two injections, Pike was still alive. Christa Pike was sentenced to death for murder in 1996. The execution was scheduled for 30 September, but it failed. Damaged arms After the failed execution, Christa Pike was admitted to hospital, where she received medical care. A little over a week after the ordeal, her lawyers reported that she could walk a little again, but that she was still hazy. Lawyer Spivey said at the time that Pike could not move her arms. "Her arms and hands are severely swollen, and we do not know whether she will ever regain any function in her arms." Lawyer Stephen Ferrel said Pike's arms were "seriously damaged" and that she could barely use them. The lawyers had already stressed before the execution attempt that Pike had a condition that would complicate injections, various media report. Not enough in the blood Anaesthesiologist Joel Zivot, who advises Christa Pike's lawyers, had already suggested that not enough of the lethal drug had entered Pike's bloodstream to actually be fatal. Speaking to the BBC, Zivot said the drug had most likely spread into the tissue under Pike's skin. "Most of the pentobarbital, instead of circulating through her body, ended up in her arms. That is how she survived it", Zivot said on 8 October to the British broadcaster. Two weeks ago Pike was discharged from hospital and returned to prison. It is unclear what will happen now. Pike's lawyers believe she has suffered enough and want the governor of Tennessee to commute her death sentence to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole. Murder Christa Pike was sentenced to death after the murder of her classmate Colleen Slemmer in 1995. She was 18 years old when she tortured and murdered Slemmer with her underage boyfriend. According to the non-profit organisation Death Penalty Information Center, Pike is the first person to survive her death sentence by injection.

title: Big money at stake: how Abdul El-Sayed is pulling the Democrats in the US to the left
lead: 'Abdul is cool', reads the T-shirts. Abdul El-Sayed (41) is running for a seat in <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">de Senaat</entity> and draws packed halls. In the American congressional elections of 3 November, many eyes are on his race in Michigan. In this swing state it will become clear whether the new, progressive wind in the Democratic Party also reaches new voters. Rebecca stood in line for hours before a rally in Flint; the last time, she could not get in because of the crowds. "I am a democratic socialist," she says. "And I like politicians who do not accept money from big companies." El-Sayed takes aim at that money machine in American politics. "A system in which big companies and billionaires can buy politicians is a disease," the candidate in jeans shouts to loud cheers. "Donald Trump is the worst symptom of that disease." 'The big money out of politics, money in your pocket and universal healthcare' is his slogan. If the former health chief of Detroit wins on 3 November, he will be one of the most left-wing candidates ever to win a swing state, and the first Muslim senator of the US. That makes him a sought-after punching bag for the right. Republicans consistently use his full Muslim name, Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed, as Trump and other Republicans did with Barack Hussein Obama. "My name and my faith are not the reason you can no longer pay for petrol and groceries," El-Sayed tells his audience. Rise of democratic socialists Last year Zohran Mamdani (35) already surprised everyone by winning the mayoral election in New York. Mamdani is also a Muslim and a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), which wants to restrain capitalism and strives for democratic control over the economy. The organisation is on the rise. Also in the Democratic primaries, which determined who would stand for the party in the congressional elections, far-left candidates did surprisingly well. For example, both Democratic candidates for the House of Representatives in Detroit are DSA members. In a small hall in the industrial city, Ian Mark is recruiting new members. He thinks he can reach floating voters who are fed up with the influence of billionaires and Big Tech on politics, while they themselves barely make ends meet. Bartender Victor Jimenez from Detroit joined last winter. "I have finally found my political home," he says, as he sets out extra chairs. President Trump, who also visits Michigan on Sunday, consistently calls the democratic socialists "communists" and "the greatest threat to the country since the world wars, Pearl Harbor and 9/11". According to Trump, they will destroy the American economy. But communists, unlike democratic socialists, want to achieve their goal through revolution. According to Mark, Trump's framing does not work: "People can no longer be swayed by labels." Still, there is resistance within the Democratic Party as well. Moderate Democrats fear that the radical party members will scare off moderate voters. Democrat Dave Armstrong, who is walking in a No Kings protest in Detroit, shares that fear: "They are a bit too extreme." For example, the DSA wants in the long term to give all migrants a residence status, abolish private rental housing and abolish the police. "Democrats have to fight two wars," says protester Kyla Turner. "Against the far right and against the far left. And that is a difficult struggle." Now that the movement has the wind in its sails, the DSA is holding back its most far-reaching ideas. For now the DSA is aiming for goals resembling those of European social democrats, such as free childcare, stronger trade unions and affordable rent. El-Sayed himself is not a democratic socialist; he calls himself a capitalist. Still, he is regarded as highly progressive, and among the Senate candidates as one of the fiercest critics of Israel and Prime Minister Netanyahu. That goes down well with the large Arab community in the suburbs of Detroit, but within the Democratic Party it remains a sensitive issue. Despite all the headwinds, El-Sayed narrowly leads his Republican opponent. Former president Obama is campaigning with him. DSA figurehead Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez also stands side by side with El-Sayed. For a long time she was regarded as a rebel within the Democratic Party; now she is mentioned as a possible presidential candidate in 2028: a sign of how the party is shifting. In the primaries, pro-Israel and other financiers put around 60 million dollars into a campaign to keep him out of the race. El-Sayed could spend far less, but still won: a signal that big money in the US cannot buy everything.

title: Morning briefing 23/10: Suspect in Hajar case brought before court • Go Ahead Eagles play Telstar
lead: Good morning! The male suspect in the murder of 29-year-old Hajar will appear before the court today, and Go Ahead Eagles play Telstar in the Eredivisie. First the weather: today it is cloudy and wet with temperatures between 12 and 14 degrees. During the day the wind picks up considerably, and in the evening it will be very stormy. Are you heading out today? Here you can find the overview of traffic jams and roadworks, and here you can see the situation on the railways. What can you expect today? What did you miss? In European cities, many tens of thousands of people died last summer as a result of extreme heat. That estimate comes from scientists at Imperial College London and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine. What is new in their study is that they also point to the role of climate change through greenhouse gas emissions: they link a large part of the heat deaths directly to it. The scientists examined data on more than 850 urban areas in 30 European countries, where together about 40 percent of the population lives. Using models, they estimated that there were around 50,000 excess deaths in those regions last summer. For comparison, for the hot summers of 2022 and 2003 they arrived at 29,000 and 28,000 excess deaths respectively. This year thus far exceeds those record years. Other news from the night: And then one more thing: In the South Korean city of Busan a shark has returned to the harbour for the third time. The animal was freed twice before but kept swimming back. Environmental organisations say the arrival of the shark is linked to climate change. Have a nice day!

title: Explosion and fire at Canadian military base caused by grenade launcher exercise
lead: An exercise with grenade launchers caused last Saturday's explosion and fire at a Canadian military base, in which four soldiers died. A senior defence official says so. According to Canadian media, troops were practising with the C-16 grenade launcher at the base in Wainwright, in western Canada. "The fire started at the firing range for automatic grenade launchers", said Brigadier General Vanessa Hanrahan at a press conference. "It happened during regular military training that was taking place on the site at the time." Not reachable The fire brigade could not get to the fire on that specific site to extinguish it, because the area had been designated as "permanently dangerous". Unexploded ammunition could be lying there, which could still explode if someone stepped on it. When the wind picked up, the fire spread quickly and jumped to another place on the base where soldiers were training. As a result, dozens of soldiers became trapped. Four of them died. Earlier it was reported that a gas pipeline or gas well may have been hit during the exercise. According to the Canadian authorities, there are so far no indications of this. 13 in critical condition Three separate investigations into the fire are being carried out, the authorities say. The incident is considered one of the worst accidents in the Canadian military. According to the Canadian authorities, 27 people are still in hospital. Of them, 13 are in critical condition, CBC reports. After the incident the hospitals were "completely overburdened", a doctor told the same Canadian broadcaster earlier. The soldiers were preparing for a deployment to Latvia. Canada has stationed its largest foreign troop contingent there, as part of a NATO mission to strengthen the alliance's eastern flank against the Russian threat.

title: Promising shot in treatment reduces risk of skin cancer returning
lead: A new treatment, developed by the American pharmaceutical companies Moderna and Merck, reduces the risk of death and of skin cancer returning by more than 40 percent. The two pharmaceutical companies claim this after a large-scale study. The treatment consists of a new medicine that is added to immunotherapy. The combination of the shot and immunotherapy lowers the chance that a patient dies or gets the disease again by 42 percent. Researchers found that the combination works better as a treatment than immunotherapy alone. It is not a vaccine to prevent cancer, but a shot that patients receive as part of their treatment. 1100 patients The study concerns people with limited spread of melanoma, an aggressive form of skin cancer. The results also show that the risk of the skin cancer spreading is 38 percent lower. More than 1100 patients took part in the study. The researchers base their findings on data from the first two years after the participants' treatment. "Very good news", says John Haanen of the outcome. Haanen is an internist-oncologist at the Antoni van Leeuwenhoek hospital. He does add that in the Netherlands a standard treatment is now used in which immunotherapy is given before the melanoma is removed. That also produces good results. Ultimately, the debate is about which treatment leads to the best overall survival chance. "If we have those figures, we can make an even better choice about which treatment is best", he says. Presentation in Madrid Last summer Moderna and Merck already announced that the treatment was a success in the study, but did not give details at the time. The researchers are officially presenting all results today at the congress of the European Society for Medical Oncology (ESMO) in Madrid. Whether the treatment will also work for other forms of cancer is not yet clear. Those studies are still ongoing.

title: Actor Tom Skerritt (93) dies, known from Top Gun and Alien
lead: American actor Tom Skerritt has died at the age of 93. Once described as "a character actor in the body of a leading man", he became known for his rugged charm in films such as Top Gun , Alien and Steel Magnolias . Skerritt was born in 1933 in Detroit. His first film role in 1962 was in the war film War Hunt , in which Robert Redford, Sydney Pollack and Francis Ford Coppola also made their Hollywood debuts. After smaller film and TV roles, he began to make a name for himself from the 1970s onward, starting with Robert Altman's war satire M*A*S*H* , in which he had a supporting role. In 1979 he played the captain of the doomed spaceship Nostromo in Alien. He meets his end in it while trying to lure an alien monster into an ambush. The menacing beeps of a motion sensor make his death scene memorable: In 1986 Skerritt got another role that many people will know him from, Tom Cruise's mentor Mike 'Viper' Metcalf in Top Gun, who has to turn the young, arrogant pilots into experienced combat fliers. "Gentlemen, you belong to the best 1 percent of all aviators. The cream of the crop, the best of the best. We are going to make you better", he sums up his task in the film. The role was especially suited to Skerritt: before he left for Hollywood, he had served in the US Air Force. Radiating authority Besides those best-known films from his body of work, he played a self-serving senator alongside Jodie Foster in Contact , the husband of Shirley MacLaine and of Sally Field in Turning Point and Steel Magnolias, and a sheriff in the Stephen King adaptation The Dead Zone. Skerritt was often cast in roles of characters who naturally had to radiate authority. In his varied career he won one major award, the Emmy, once. That was for the TV series Picket Fences, in which he played a small-town sheriff from rural Wisconsin. The NCRV broadcast the series here under the name Small Town USA. Skerritt also received a second Emmy nomination for the series, which ran for four seasons. In his obituary, his family writes that Skerritt liked to "help others find and share their voice". "The world knew Tom for his extraordinary acting career, but we knew him for his humor, curiosity, wisdom, generosity and the love he brought."

title: 'MIVD saw on hacked iPhone how Trump's son-in-law received many millions'
lead: The Dutch Military Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD) reportedly monitored the phone of Jared Kushner, son-in-law of US President Trump and his negotiator in the wars in Ukraine, Gaza and Iran, from 2018 onward. That is what US investigative journalist Matthew Cole writes in a new book, an excerpt of which the magazine Vanity Fair has published. According to Cole, the MIVD got in with the help of a defected Russian hacker who worked for the Russian military intelligence service GROe. How long the MIVD ultimately monitored Kushner's phone is not known. The MIVD tells the NOS it does not comment on its working methods, knowledge level or sources. Nieuwsuur, in collaboration with the Volkskrant, conducted extensive research into the claim that the MIVD had access to Jared Kushner's phone and spoke with several people directly involved. No confirmation of the story was found. 750 million dollars Cole writes in the book that the Dutch spies saw through the hack that Kushner logged into a bank account in the United Arab Emirates in Dubai. The account reportedly received hundreds of millions of dollars from a bank in Azerbaijan. Cole writes that this bank account held 750 million dollars, coming from the royal families of Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The money was reportedly intended to advance political and diplomatic goals in the Middle East. According to Cole, the account was partly managed by Kushner and the Emirati president Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan (MBZ). 'Detour' "Jared was looking for a detour to achieve his diplomatic goals", Cole heard from a source who was aware of the deal between the UAE and Kushner. "Jared promised MBZ that he would look after their interests with Trump if they took part in a fund. Jared wanted normalization of relations with Israel so that trade and investment could flourish." According to Cole, the two families at the time wanted to force a breakthrough in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. This could improve their relations with Israel without losing face. Kushner reportedly agreed to raise the Saudis' plans with his father-in-law. More about Kushner's business interests in Israel and other countries in this video from Nieuwsuur: The affair reportedly came to light when the military intelligence service discovered in 2017 that an employee of the Russian military intelligence service GROe, specialized in stolen bank data, was on his way to the United Kingdom for an espionage assignment. According to Cole, the British detained the man at the request of their Dutch colleagues. The hacker reportedly was given two options: work as an informant for the Dutch government, or face a trial in the United Kingdom with a possible prison sentence of several years. The Russian employee decided to give the Dutch intelligence service access to one of the GROe's most sensitive systems, Cole writes. On a server in the Russian city of Rostov, used by the cyber and hacking team of the Russian military intelligence service, the Dutch found screenshots of Kushner's iPhone during their investigation. According to Cole, the MIVD then managed in early 2018 to gain access to the phone itself, allowing the service to watch the screen whenever Kushner used the device. While the services were monitoring Kushner's phone, they discovered that he used it to log into a bank account in the UAE. By the time the Dutch spies gained sight of the phone, hundreds of millions of dollars had already been deposited into the account. "For the MIVD hackers, the bank account became an intelligence puzzle that had to be solved", Cole writes. 'Crazy' Whether Kushner, as a White House employee, reported the account to US authorities is not known. If he did not, Kushner may have violated US anti-bribery legislation. Kushner denies all allegations on X and calls them "completely crazy". "No bank statements, transfer details, account numbers, transaction data or other details were provided to prove these extraordinary allegations." During Trump's first term, Kushner played an important role in US foreign policy in the Middle East. He was part of the diplomatic team that ultimately led to the 2020 Abraham Accords. These normalized relations between, among others, the United Arab Emirates and Israel. He also plays an important role now as a negotiator for Trump. What do you think of the NOS app and website? title: Prehistoric cave paintings in Indonesia endangered by wildfires
lead: One of the oldest cave paintings in the world is at risk from severe wildfires on the Indonesian island of Sulawesi. Due to the heat and smoke, the deterioration of the paintings may be accelerated, researchers say. The islands of Sumatra and Borneo have been hit hardest by the fires. There are also fires on Sulawesi. In South Sulawesi are caves containing the oldest prehistoric art in the world. "Even without the fire directly hitting the paintings, it can ruin them, because the temperature around the paintings changes and the corrosion process is accelerated," an archaeologist tells the news agency Reuters. Soot particles In addition, soot particles can accumulate on the rock walls. As a result, the images become covered and are barely recognizable, the archaeologist says. Since the 1990s it has been known that many ancient rock drawings can be found in the caves. The oldest found on Sulawesi are estimated at 67,800 years old. Another drawing of a Celebes warty pig, discovered in a cave on Sulawesi in 2017, was found by Australian researchers to have been made at least 51,000 years ago. Firefighters are busy putting out the fires. "If we do not act quickly here, we will lose one of the most remarkable testimonies of human history," one of the firefighters tells Reuters. Set fires Due to the El Niño weather phenomenon, temperatures are higher and there is less rainfall, which makes forests and peat areas especially vulnerable. In addition, farmers often burn patches of land bare at this time of year to clear the ground for agriculture. This is originally a traditional way of land management for small farmers. Only now it is so dry that the fires more easily spread to, for example, the neighboring forest. Large palm oil companies also set fires to clear land for new plantations. This is officially prohibited, but enforcement is lacking.

title: Israel to fully close off the West Bank after attack in Palestinian territory
lead: Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu has ordered a full closure of the West Bank, after two men, presumed to be Palestinian, reportedly carried out an attack on Israelis near the city of Hebron. According to Netanyahu's statement, the city of Hebron must be "immediately" fully closed off, and the security forces must prepare for a full closure of the West Bank. How long this will last is unclear. In a message on Telegram, the army speaks of an "offensive anti-terrorism operation", carried out by soldiers of the army and officers of the border police. As part of this, house searches are being conducted, among other places at the homes of the attackers and other suspects. The army says it shot dead the two men, who it says were responsible for an attack at a checkpoint in the Palestinian city of Hebron, in the occupied West Bank. According to Israel, a "terror attack" on Israeli civilians has thereby been foiled. The two men, presumed to be Palestinian, reportedly had links to Hamas and lived in Hebron. 'Five injured' Israeli media, including the center-left newspaper Haaretz, write that five Israelis were injured in the men's attack early this morning, two of whom are in critical condition. The newspaper further writes, based on sources within the security services, that the two men arrived at the scene with Israeli license plates and then opened fire. A "prolonged" firefight reportedly followed. According to the army, the men were carrying an M16 rifle and a pistol. The agency makes no statement about the target of the attack. Roadblocks set up The army has meanwhile set up roadblocks and closed off Palestinian locations in the area. Because of the closure, Palestinians from the West Bank can no longer travel to and from Israel. Even without this closure, Palestinians from the West Bank cannot simply travel to Israel. For that they usually need an Israeli permit and must pass through strictly guarded checkpoints. According to the Palestinian news agency WAFA, one such checkpoint in Jerusalem has already been closed. As a result, around a hundred Palestinians who were waiting to enter or leave Jerusalem are reportedly affected. Elections will be held in Israel next Tuesday. Israeli voters will be asked whether the longest-serving prime minister, Netanyahu, should get a new term in office. There is a possibility that Arab parties will play a key role.

title: Albert Heijn customers can have groceries delivered again
lead: Albert Heijn customers can once again have groceries delivered to their homes from today, almost two weeks after the cyberattack that brought the supermarket chain's services to a standstill. In recent days, a limited group of regular customers has been able to place orders, and now everyone can do so. The number of orders that can be delivered has not yet returned to its previous level. The supermarket chain can now handle a third of its normal number of deliveries. On Wednesday the supermarket began restarting its systems, which also made its customer service available again. Last Sunday the website and app were working again too. Daily groceries According to Albert Heijn, the first orders are going out and the outlook for the rest of the day is good. "The first deliveries have been taking place since 7.00 this morning", a spokesperson told ANP. Customers are now ordering daily groceries again. "Milk, yoghurt, plant-based dairy, bread, vegetables, fruit and kitchen roll are popular", the spokesperson said. The range and the number of available delivery slots will be expanded further over the course of the week. Customers whose order was cancelled after an error message will receive a store credit from the supermarket chain. No data stolen Customers were unable to place grocery orders after the cyber incident at Albert Heijn's parent company, Ahold Delhaize. Because of the incident, Ahold took certain systems offline as a precaution. As a result, the website and app of Albert Heijn, as well as those of other Ahold brands such as Etos and Gall & Gall, have been unavailable since Sunday 11 October. The company has since filed a report with the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> about the cyberattack, after the police and the <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity> called on the company to do so through a public appeal. The internal investigation into the cyberattack is still ongoing. The company says that so far it has no indication that any sensitive customer, employee or partner data has been stolen. title: 'Deliberate RSF attacks on hospitals in the Sudanese city of Al-Fasher'
lead: The paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) in Sudan have deliberately and systematically destroyed hospitals and other healthcare facilities during the siege of the city of Al-Fasher in the Darfur region. Research by the BBC shows that there were dozens of attacks on healthcare facilities. Dozens of aid workers were killed or wounded. A number were also abducted. Under international law, attacking healthcare facilities or their staff in wartime is prohibited. The UN human rights commissioner calls the BBC's research very alarming and speaks of war crimes. Earlier, the UN reported that the fighting in Al-Fasher showed "signs of genocide". A doctor who spoke to the BBC says the RSF destroy the hospitals because they know the health system is the cornerstone of every city. "Citizens therefore could not stay. It was deliberate and planned." Al-Fasher was taken by the RSF in October 2025 after a siege of more than five hundred days. Research by Amnesty International shows that civilians are being held captive and tortured. Before the civil war between the RSF and the Sudanese army began in 2023, more than a million people lived in Al-Fasher. According to Amnesty, there are currently fewer than 70,000 people left in the city. The aid organisation spoke with nineteen of them. Of these, seventeen had been arbitrarily detained by the RSF. The witnesses say that mainly people from certain ethnic groups are being held, especially the Zaghawa and the Masalit. 'They beat you unconscious' Men held in prisons describe how they were arbitrarily tortured. "They accuse you of being in the army and beat you until you are unconscious. Sometimes as many as four times a day." Prisoners also receive the minimum of food and water. Prisoners are only released once their family has paid a ransom. Many also try to escape. Women and children are held in schools. There too, accounts emerge of malnutrition and arbitrary torture. "Every day four to five people died, mostly from lack of food", a woman tells Amnesty. Forced labour The residents tell the aid organisation that access to humanitarian aid is limited. They also speak of forced labour, such as clearing corpses from the streets of Al-Fasher or cooking for the RSF. Amnesty calls on the international community to deploy a peacekeeping force. The human rights organisation once again points to the role played by the United Arab Emirates in this conflict. That country supports the RSF, among other things by supplying weapons and vehicles. The UAE denies involvement. Podcast 'War in the backyard' NOS investigated the links between the war in Sudan and the Netherlands. You can hear more about it in the podcast 'War in the backyard'. The podcast can be listened to here.

title: Man shoots at random in Paris suburb, one dead and four injured
lead: A man has shot at random passers-by near Paris. At least one person died and at least four others were injured. The shooting took place in Trappes, a suburb southwest of Paris, near Versailles. According to Le Parisien, the perpetrator used a machine gun. He fired the weapon from a vehicle, first in Trappes and then in the neighbouring La Verriere, the news broadcaster BFMTV reports. The first images of where the shooting took place: According to the mayor of Trappes, the man seemed to be "shooting randomly around him, with the apparent intention of causing a bloodbath". He calls it a miracle that more people were not hit. Motive not known Among the injured is a 12-year-old girl, according to the mayor of La Verriere. Her condition is reportedly stable. Two men aged 29 and 49 were also injured and taken to hospital. The victim who died was 26 years old. The 38-year-old gunman was later arrested nearby in the village of Coignieres. According to French Prime Minister Lecornu, the shooting is being investigated as an act of terrorism, and he says the National Anti-Terrorist Prosecutor's Office (PNAT) is monitoring the situation. No motive has been made public yet. French Prime Minister Lecornu writes on X that "all resources of the security services have been fully mobilised". 'Our thoughts are with the victims' President Macron writes on X that his thoughts are with the victims, their families and all residents of the area. Minister of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity> Nuñez speaks of "a very serious incident". He will arrive on the scene "within a few moments". title: Austria expels four Russians over espionage
lead: Austria is expelling four Russian diplomats. According to the Austrian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, they were engaged in activities "incompatible with their diplomatic status", a wording that refers to espionage. Three of these Russians work at the Russian embassy in Vienna, and the fourth is a member of the Russian delegation to the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE). That is an international organisation founded in 1973 for cooperation in the military, economic and humanitarian fields. Its headquarters are in Vienna. The Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs has announced that a reaction will "inevitably" follow. This likely means that a number of Austrian diplomats will have to leave Russia. Diplomatic hub The Austrian capital has been an important centre for international organisations since the end of the Second World War, and therefore also for spies who can work under the cover of diplomats. The Wall Street Journal wrote in 2024 that Russian diplomats are very active there, so much so that Western intelligence circles consider Vienna the "capital of Russian espionage". Espionage network In May, a former employee of the Austrian domestic security service was sentenced to four years in prison for spying for Russia. According to Austrian justice authorities, another Austrian businessman was part of the same espionage network. He is said to have fled to Russia. During the Cold War, Austria was neutral in the conflict between the NATO countries and the communist Soviet Union and its allies, and until recently had a special bond with Russia. The Austrian government condemned the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, but does not supply Ukraine with weapons, unlike many NATO countries.

title: Thousands of households in France and England without power due to storm Austen
lead: In France and England, storm Austen, which also reaches the Netherlands this afternoon, has caused problems. The storm made landfall in Brittany this morning, where local weather stations measured gusts of up to 160 kilometres per hour. Because of the bad weather, ferry services between the two countries have also been cancelled, such as those between Dover and Calais. More than 161,000 households in French coastal regions such as Brittany, Pays de la Loire and Normandy have lost power. Code orange applies until 20.00 this evening for 23 departments in north-western France. That is the second-highest alert level. Hundreds of firefighters have been deployed to respond to reports, such as fallen trees. Yesterday storm Adam moved across southern France over land. Two people died in the process. They were two women aged 86 and 26 who were found drowned in a cellar in the southern French region of Bouches-du-Rhône. The storm had earlier already claimed four lives in Spain. Images of the storm in south-east England and Normandy: The British weather service, the Met Office, has issued code orange for Cornwall and Devon at England's south-western tip. Storm Austen was accompanied there in the early morning by gusts of up to 130 kilometres per hour. In Cornwall more than 13,500 addresses are without power, including, according to the BBC, 4,600 vulnerable people. During the day, gusts of around 100 kilometres per hour are expected in the south and middle of England. The storm will move eastward along the English Channel coast. Second storm: Weather services on the island of Jersey have issued a warning for shipping around the Channel Islands. In that area gusts of up to 130 kilometres per hour are expected. The authorities there had already received 91 reports of fallen or damaged trees this morning. Because many trees are still fully in leaf, the Met Office warns of more power outages and traffic disruption due to fallen trees and blown-down branches. Along with strong wind, a lot of rain is also expected in many places in England. Later this weekend a second severe storm is expected in the UK, which will bring strong wind and heavy rain mainly in the north of the country. Both countries have taken measures to limit nuisance and problems. In France, train services in parts of Normandy have been halted and speed restrictions apply on other routes. Authorities urged people to postpone non-essential travel due to the risk of falling trees and flying debris. Belgium is also dealing with storm Austen. The Royal Meteorological Institute of Belgium has issued code orange for the west of the country, while yellow is in force in the rest of the country. Code yellow: Storm Austen is moving this afternoon from the south-west across the Netherlands with a lot of rain and wind. The <entity id="org:koninklijk-nederlands-meteorologisch-instituut">KNMI</entity> warns from the end of the afternoon of severe gusts in coastal areas and in the south-east, with gusts between 75 and 90 km per hour. From this afternoon code yellow applies to Zuid-Holland, Zeeland, Noord-Brabant, Limburg, Gelderland and Overijssel. From tomorrow afternoon the KNMI again expects severe gusts in coastal areas and South Limburg. During the course of the night the wind will ease again.

title: 31 suspects acquitted in Belgian drug trial because the proceedings took too long
lead: In Belgium, 31 suspects who stood trial in a large-scale drug case are going free because the procedure took far too long. One of them is Dutch drug criminal John H. In recent years he has been convicted several times for drug crime. The facts date back ten years. According to the judge, there were several periods in which the case file was not worked on for no explainable reason. In total this amounted to more than five years. The court also says the file is not exceptionally complex, and that the suspects did not take any actions that could have delayed the trial. Dropping a conviction is a very exceptional decision. When a trial takes longer, a court is more inclined to reduce the sentence. Over 160 years in prison sentences The <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity> had requested prison sentences for the 31 suspects totaling more than 160 years. H. faced a prison sentence of eighteen years. This already took into account a sentence reduction because the trial took too long. The OM also wanted to seize 14 million euros. The OM sees H. as one of the leaders of this criminal organization. The organization traded chemicals used to make synthetic drugs. Large quantities of ingredients were ordered through a soap factory in Lommel. The federal prosecutor's office is appealing.

title: Dead and missing after fire on cargo ship in Black Sea off Romania
lead: A fire on a cargo ship off the coast of Romania in the Black Sea has killed one person, and three crew members are still missing. The Romanian authorities have launched a search and rescue operation. Although the authorities have not yet made an official statement on the cause, various media report that it involves a drone attack. Around 10:00 local time this morning, the Romanian navy was informed of a fire on the cargo ship. The ship reportedly "was severely damaged and capsized". On board were ten Ukrainians and three Azerbaijanis. "Nine crew members were rescued by another cargo ship, one body has been recovered from the water," the authorities said. A search is still underway for the other three. Series of drone attacks The fire on the cargo ship follows a series of drone attacks on cargo ships in the Black Sea off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria. In recent weeks, several people have been killed and dozens have gone missing. Romanian President Nicusor Dan states that this incident is part of the "Russian escalation in the Black Sea". Earlier this week, NATO said it was sending additional patrol aircraft to monitor safety. The European Parliament has called for a maritime mission to protect ships against Russian attacks. Grain is the latest target in the war of attrition between Russia and Ukraine. Both sides are attacking each other's ships and ports that export grain with missiles and drones:

title: Two arrests in investigation into crash with car full of explosives in Amsterdam
lead: In the investigation into the car containing explosive material that crashed in Amsterdam last July, police have arrested two men. They are two Amsterdammers aged 25 and 36. The car crashed at the end of July near Nierkerkestraat in the Nieuw-West district after a police chase. The chase had been launched after an explosive robbery that night in Germany. Because explosives may have been in the car, the area within a 100 metre radius was evacuated. Investigation later revealed that there was indeed explosive material in the vehicle. The three occupants of the car fled after the accident. An arrest team of the police then entered homes in the area, but no suspects were found. Suspects arrested in recent weeks. The first suspect was picked up at the end of September. The second suspect was arrested at his home last Tuesday, the police announced today. Both are in custody, NH Nieuws reports. What they are suspected of has not been made public. A third suspect was arrested at Schiphol in August by the military police, but that person has since been released. The police investigation continues and detectives are still looking for a suspect. Witnesses or people with camera footage are asked to come forward.

title: Councillor does not have to retract statements about amusement park owner Wim Beelen after all
lead: Rotterdam councillor Kevin van Eikeren does not have to retract his statements about entrepreneur Wim Beelen after all. That is what the court of appeal in <entity id="org:gemeente-s-gravenhage">Den Haag</entity> has ruled in an expedited procedure. The Pro councillor had appealed against the district court's ruling earlier this week. On Tuesday the district court had still ruled that Van Eikeren had to retract several statements about multimillionaire Beelen, including those known from the Rotterdam amusement park Spelen bij Beelen. Van Eikeren had said, among other things on radio with the regional broadcaster Rijnmond, that the entrepreneur with his amusement park "plays the Samaritan" while it is "purely about the money" for him. In addition, Van Eikeren said that Beelen had tried to buy political parties in <entity id="org:gemeente-amsterdam">Amsterdam</entity> by making high donations. The judge assessed the councillor's statements as unlawful and without factual basis. He had to post a message on Instagram and LinkedIn within 72 hours acknowledging that his statements were unlawful. Because Beelen was found to be right, Van Eikeren had to pay the costs of the proceedings. These amount to over 1850 euros. Ruling overturned: But that ruling has now been crossed out. In the appeal, the court of appeal has ruled in a so-called turbo expedited appeal that Van Eikeren does not have to retract his statements. The costs of the proceedings are also awarded to Wim Beelen. Nothing has yet been made public about the court's reasoning. The substantive justification will be published later. During the summary proceedings earlier this month the judge still expressed the hope that the men could sort it out between themselves, but that did not succeed. Therefore the judge issued a ruling. Attempts at reconciliation also continued during the expedited hearing on appeal, according to Rijnmond.

title: Podcast De Dag: female DJs take the spotlight at ADE
lead: This week Amsterdam once again turns into one big dance floor during the thirtieth edition of ADE, the Amsterdam Dance Event. The dance world was long mainly a man's world, but this year hundreds of women are on the line-up. Listening? You can listen to this episode of De Dag via NPO Luister and all other podcast apps. Like it? Don't forget to subscribe. What is it like to work as a woman in the dance scene? Two DJs talk about it in this podcast: Olive Anguz, who is performing at ADE for the second time, and Isis, who has attended all thirty editions. In the podcast you hear excerpts from the documentary Her Sound, about gender inequality in the electronic music industry. Responding? Email dedag@nos.nl. Presentation and editing: Dieuwke Teertstra. Editorial staff: Judith Kutschenreuter. Final editing: Judith van de Hulsbeek

title: Gunmen open fire on church in Jordan: seven dead and dozens injured
lead: Unknown armed men opened fire on churchgoers in Jordan. 7 people were killed and 34 injured, the Jordanian authorities announced at a press conference. Earlier, the authorities had spoken of 6 dead and 28 injured. The shooting took place at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, about 180 kilometres south of the Jordanian capital Amman. The gunmen are still at large. A funeral was reportedly under way at the time of the attack. The Jordanian news channel Al-Mamlaka has shared video from a church security camera showing three gunmen. Two of them have pistols and a third a rifle. They fire while taking cover behind trees and a wall. Then they run to the church entrance. King wants revenge Between 150 and 200 people were reportedly present during the attack, both inside and outside the church. According to an eyewitness who spoke to Al-Mamlaka, the gunmen fired continuously for 5 minutes at those inside the church. Most of the victims were reportedly between 50 and 70 years old. Jordanian King Abdullah speaks of terror and says those responsible will be punished with an "iron fist". "The terrorist attack in Karak will be met with the harshest possible retribution. Those who fool themselves that they can divide Jordanians with their bullets stand no chance against our unity," he says in a statement. Attack in 2016 Attacks like this are extremely rare in Jordan. Christians form a minority of the Jordanian population. Jordan has many locations mentioned in the Bible to which Christian pilgrims from all over the world travel. In 2016 armed men attacked police officers during an attack in Karak, including at a Crusader castle popular with tourists. Ten people were killed, including seven police officers, and dozens of others were injured. After a prolonged siege, the attackers were killed by Jordanian security forces. This attack was later claimed by the terrorist group Islamic State (IS).

title: Hajar killed on first day of disappearance, suspect also suspected of attempting to kill foster father
lead: The 29-year-old Hajar was killed on the first day of her disappearance. That is what the <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity> reports. Hajar was last seen on Sunday 4 October near the RAI event complex in <entity id="org:gemeente-amsterdam">Amsterdam</entity>. From there she cycled with the 23-year-old suspect Abdi A. in the direction of the Buitenveldert neighbourhood. According to the OM, there were no indications that the two knew each other. That Sunday morning she sent disturbing messages to an acquaintance. The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> cannot say what exactly Hajar sent. De Telegraaf said it had seen WhatsApp messages in which she sent "Help me. Now. He is killing me". The OM reports that research has shown Hajar was killed that same day, early in the afternoon.
