Due to the rain of the past few days, the river level has risen and therefore the one-way traffic was lifted today, <entity id="org:rijkswaterstaat">Rijkswaterstaat</entity> reports. The one-way traffic was reintroduced ten days ago, after the measure had been temporarily lifted two days earlier. In some places the water level had dropped below 1.45 meters again. As a result, it was not safe for ships to pass each other. The measure affected inland shipping towards the Twente Canal, reports RTV Oost. Skippers could no longer sail directly to the canal from both directions and had to go around. 'Drought period not yet over' Due to the rain of the past few days, the minimum measured depth on the Boven-IJssel has reached the required 1.45 meters. Nevertheless, Rijkswaterstaat warns that the drought period is not yet over. Water levels are therefore being closely monitored. "If the water level falls again, measures for shipping may be reintroduced."

title: Macklemore at first performance after exit from Ed Sheeran tour: 'Not difficult to be human'
lead: American rapper Macklemore performed for the first time since he was dropped from the opening act of British singer Ed Sheeran in mid-September over pro-Palestinian statements. During the concert in Colorado he said, among other things, that "it is not difficult to be human". The reason for Macklemore's removal from Sheeran's tour was statements he made during the opening act. On 4 September, at a concert at MetLife Stadium in the American state of New Jersey, Macklemore called attention to the situation of Palestinians in Gaza. "One of the reasons I wanted to do this tour was because I wanted to stand here on stages and in stadiums across America and say two words that are very close to my heart: Free Palestine", he said at the time. Macklemore, whose real name is Ben Haggerty, was initially set to perform at ten Ed Sheeran concerts in the US, but after his statements in New Jersey that number was limited to two. The stadiums where the other concerts were to take place no longer wanted to offer him a stage. According to Macklemore, Sheeran was pressured by stadium owners to drop him from his programme. The American promoter of Sheeran's concerts later confirmed to music magazine Rolling Stones that the concert venues no longer allowed Macklemore to perform because of his statements. First performance On Thursday evening American time, Macklemore performed again for the first time in Colorado. "It is not difficult to be human at this moment", he said. "It is not political. It is human to have a heart, to see others suffer and then to say: this cannot go on any longer." "That is why I say: Free Palestine." He then also drew attention to the situation in Sudan, Congo, Lebanon and Haiti. In addition, he spoke out for people in the US who are affected by the actions of the American immigration agency ICE and as a result are "afraid to leave their homes". Sold-out concerts A month ago Macklemore announced his own concert series under the name 'Free Palestine'. The proceeds go to aid organisations for Palestinians. Next Tuesday, Friday and Saturday he will perform in Dublin, Paris and London respectively. The concerts sold out within minutes. The rapper said on Instagram that he was "deeply impressed" by this. According to Macklemore, the interest in his quickly organised concert series shows the power of "collective action". He sees it as a show of support for artists who use their platform to speak out for Palestinians. After Macklemore's departure, Sheeran's backing band and three acts from his opening lineup also withdrew. The British singer found a replacement for Macklemore in Isaac Slade, former frontman of The Fray.

title: Ukraine reports stable Starlink connection again after more than a week
lead: Ukraine reports that the connection with Starlink is stable again. On 14 October the Ukrainian army reported that they suddenly had problems with the Starlink satellite internet service. That caused major problems for Ukraine's defence. Among other things, the speed of attack, defence and supply drones was reduced. The drones could suddenly not go faster than 160 kilometres per hour, while Russian kamikaze drones reach a speed of more than 500 kilometres per hour. Warnings about missile launches also no longer came through, so civilians could not be warned in time. The drones can reach their normal speed again, the Ukrainian Defence Minister tells Reuters. "The connection is stable." American government Zelensky suspected that the American government was behind the problems. In the days before the problems, Trump concluded a diesel agreement with Russia, lifted sanctions and demanded that Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries. Trump also told the press that it is time Ukraine got a new leader. "These are surprises you do not expect when you are truly partners. We rely on our partnership with the United States", the Ukrainian president responded during a visit to London. Musk Trump and Elon Musk, owner of SpaceX which includes Starlink, pointed at each other regarding the Starlink problems. Musk wrote on X that Starlink is managed by the American defence and ultimately therefore by President Trump. Last Wednesday The Wall Street Journal reported, based on sources, that Musk himself had ordered limiting Ukraine's access to the Starlink satellite network. Musk and Trump reportedly discussed the restrictions in advance, and also had contact after they were introduced. 'Worrying' The European Union called those reports "extremely worrying" and demanded that Musk immediately restore full functionality. "Ukraine needs satellite internet for communication between its soldiers, to protect its citizens and to operate the drones it needs to defend its territory", said a spokesperson for EU Commission President Von der Leyen. The EU is working on a satellite network similar to Starlink, which will be called IRIS2. "Ukraine can fully join that", said Von der Leyen's spokesperson. title: Google illegally cuts down 250,000 trees, Finns call for stricter rules for data centers
lead: In Finland there is great outrage over the illegal felling of hundreds of thousands of trees. Google cut down the trees to build data centers, but had to stop the work this month at the request of the Finnish regulator. The company had not completed the necessary environmental impact assessments before the felling started. The trees were removed in two places in central Finland. Near Muhos, some 250,000 trees disappeared. Near Otanmäki, about 100 kilometers further southeast, another 150,000 trees were felled, estimates ecologist Mari Annala in The Guardian. Google apologized last week for the deforestation. However, national director Antti Järvinen said the company had acted "to the best of its understanding of the legislation we had at the time". But the unrest is not over, because 145 data centers are planned in Finland. More than 93,000 people have now signed a petition for stricter rules for data centers. They also want the affected communities to be compensated. Wolves in village. In Muhos a resident tells The Guardian that he wants Google to pay for the damage. He suggests that the company help restore the local salmon population, which disappeared decades ago because of the hydroelectric power plants. In Otanmäki a resident says that the felling of the trees has disturbed nature. Since the trees disappeared, wolves have come, says Anni Ranta (53). "They have fled." Her aversion to the data centers is so strong that she is considering moving. "I don't want them in Finland at all. I hate the whole idea of AI and the world that is changing, and the way it is happening. It is going too fast." Investing in Finland. Last month it became known that Google is making an investment of 13 billion euros in new AI data centers and digital infrastructure in Finland. Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo said at the time that attracting this kind of investment was a "top priority" and that the deal with Google would bring "lasting benefits for both parties". Finland is attractive to technology companies because of its vast space and cold climate. As a result, less energy is needed to remove the heat that data centers produce, which lowers costs. Microsoft also concluded a deal earlier this year over data center plans in Finland.

title: Confused man arrested over devastating fire at Hitler's Eagle's Nest
lead: German police believe a confused man is behind the devastating fire at Hitler's retreat, the Eagle's Nest, last night. According to the German Public Prosecutor's Office, the 33-year-old man who was arrested last night has psychological problems. Yesterday evening, around 21.15, a fire broke out at the Kehlsteinhaus on the Obersalzberg, built in 1938 as a place where Adolf Hitler could receive (foreign) guests. The dictator had a retreat on the same mountain in the Alps, as did many other senior Nazis. When the fire brigade arrived, the flames were already coming out of the building. Extinguishing the fire was difficult because of the bad weather, a lack of firefighting water and the hard-to-reach location at over 1800 metres altitude. The firefighting, carried out by around 250 firefighters from six municipalities, even had to be halted for several hours for safety reasons. Arrested immediately. The suspect could be arrested almost immediately, because he was riding his motorcycle towards the fire brigade and police on the narrow access road. He was stopped because his motorcycle had no number plate, but officers soon realised that he might have had more to do with the fire. He was injured in one hand, but it is not yet clear whether this was caused by the fire. The prosecutor says the suspect's mental problems probably played a major role in his motive. He also speaks of possible political motives, but further investigation is needed. The man has been admitted to a psychiatric institution. According to the Public Prosecution Service, he has "a connection" to the region, but does not live there. If he is convicted, he could receive 1 to 10 years in prison for arson, although the prosecutor also takes into account that the man may be declared not criminally responsible. Although the fire is now under control, the post-fire extinguishing work is expected to last all afternoon. It is taking so long partly because the fire brigade cannot enter the building due to the risk of falling debris. For this reason it is not yet clear how large the structural damage is to the burned-out building. The area around the Kehlsteinhaus will remain closed to visitors for the time being. The Bavarian Minister of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity> Herrmann has already expressed the intention to rebuild the Eagle's Nest. "We cannot simply leave a ruin standing, can we?" he replied when asked about future plans. The German state owns the building. Heritage from the Nazi era is not uncontroversial. For example, in Braunau am Inn a long search was held for a suitable use for Hitler's birthplace, out of fear that it would attract neo-Nazis. Eventually it was decided to establish a police station there. Herrmann acknowledges that "difficult" conversations will also need to be held here, but points out that it was also a place of remembrance and had been a popular tourist destination for many years. He added, however, that he could not yet present concrete plans "only 12 hours after the fire", but believes that "a suitable solution" will be found. The operator of the building supports the minister. According to him, it has been proven that providing context is precisely what allows the past to be treated respectfully. "If visitors only find a ruin here, you get exactly the kind of tourism you do not want." Herrmann further noted that the building was insured and that the costs of rebuilding need not fall on the taxpayer. The Kehlsteinhaus opened in 1952 as a café-restaurant. With 300,000 visitors a year, it is still regarded as an important tourist attraction, because of its history and the panoramic view over the Bavarian Alps. Hitler's nearby residence, the Berghof, was destroyed during the Second World War. Second World War newsletter. Interested in the Second World War? Subscribe to our newsletter here.

title: Grief after devastating fire at Limburg saloon: 'Our pride has burned down'
lead: Members of shooting club Davy Crockett in Meterik are reacting in shock after the fire that destroyed their wooden clubhouse last night. The club has barely had a day to enjoy the saloon, which the members built themselves. The morning after the fire, chairman Jan Joosten walks through the smouldering remains. "We spent seven months building it, with all our might. And now it's gone," he tells regional broadcaster L1 Nieuws. "Our pride has burned down. That hurts." Smoke from the wall. The building was constructed by the members for the club's 60th anniversary. Today an open day was due to be held to show the newly completed clubhouse to the public for the first time. But last night, during the opening party of the saloon, things went wrong. "Around 23.30 we saw smoke coming out of the wall," Joosten recalls, tears in his eyes. "We evacuated everyone immediately. There were about 150 people at the opening evening. Club members, friends and sponsors. We got everyone safely outside, but the fire was already in the walls." Hands-on with a garden hose. While the fire brigade was on its way, the shooters tried to put out the fire with a garden hose. "We soon saw that this was pointless. The insulation material had caught fire. The whole room was also full of smoke." The last glimmer of hope that the building could still be saved vanished the moment the fire brigade started work. "When the fire brigade began breaking and demolishing to get to the flames, you could draw your conclusion. The saloon could no longer be saved." The shooting club, with a huge fondness for North American history, decided to give itself a fitting gift for its anniversary in the form of the wooden saloon. The saloon was decorated with Western paintings, had a wagon wheel on the ceiling and had a passage to the shooting range. Only the swinging doors were missing, because they would make it difficult to walk through with a full tray. Rebuilding. The rustic saloon stood next to the shooting range. That stone building was spared. "It has water damage, though. We need to see what work we still have to do there," says Joosten. He does not want to speculate about the cause. "I have no expertise in that, it is the first time we have experienced something like this," he says. "Fortunately we are insured, so we hope everything will be all right. We are waiting to see what the experts say, and then we will start again. A new saloon, again made of wood."

title: Keeper at Beekse Bergen safari park injured in panther attack, condition serious
lead: At safari park Beekse Bergen in Hilvarenbeek, a female keeper was seriously injured this morning after being attacked in the panther enclosure. The woman has since undergone surgery, but her condition remains serious. How the incident could happen is being investigated. There are two panthers in the park. It is not yet clear whether she was attacked by one or by both panthers. The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> received a report of the attack around 11 a.m. The keeper was able to raise the alarm herself with her radio. The panthers were indoors because of the poor weather. After the report, the ambulance service and a trauma helicopter went to the park. The woman was given medical treatment immediately and taken to hospital. Her family has been informed. The park reports that the keeper has worked at the park for 25 years and has worked with the panthers for 8 years.

title: Nearly 1000 arrests at demonstrations in France, riots here and there
lead: Across France today, more than 400,000 people joined protest marches, according to the French Minister of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity>. The march through Paris was largely peaceful. The route was moved away from the places where things got out of hand last week to a more southern part of the city. According to the police, 110,000 people took part in the march through Paris. There was a large police presence. Demonstrators were kept away from central places such as Place de la République and Place de la Bastille. Instead, they were directed to walk the route between Porte d'Italie and Porte de Vincennes. The first demonstrators arrived there at the end of the afternoon. Afterwards, riots broke out and the police used water cannons and tear gas to disperse around 500 rioters. According to the police, the rioters tried to break into a car dealership. At the end of the afternoon, the French police intervened in various cities. In several cities, including Nice, Lyon, Marseille and Lille, the police intervened at protests with tear gas or a water cannon. In Grenoble, riot police were attacked by 400 masked people, and in Bordeaux projectiles were thrown at the police and barricades were erected by demonstrators. Across France, nearly a thousand people were arrested at the demonstrations, according to Minister Nuñez of Interior. He says he expects that "this number will rise". At the riots on 17 October, 385 people were arrested. According to Nuñez, the police intervention prevented looting. He also says that, due to the police action, no public buildings were attacked. Schoolchildren, unions, yellow vests The radical left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, one of the driving forces behind the protests, called on participants to stay within the rules. According to him, Prime Minister Lecornu tried to frustrate the demonstrators by moving the protest route in Paris 5 kilometres further at the last minute, but he asked people "not to let his provocations succeed". The protests in France stem from social unrest over the policies of President Macron. Ongoing protests by schoolchildren in recent weeks calling for improvements in education turned last Saturday into a broader protest involving trade unions, farmers and the yellow vest opposition movement. Hundreds of thousands took to the streets. Rioters and looters turned the peaceful mood of the protests into widespread looting, vandalism and arson. Damage amounting to hundreds of millions of euros was caused, and hundreds of suspects have been arrested. Pétanque balls on the way To prevent new violence, the right to demonstrate was considerably restricted today. President Macron, for example, only allowed protests by trade unions, and in various places across the country a curfew and bans on gatherings apply. Young people may not be outside in central Lille between 20.00 and 06.00, and people may not gather there until 22.00 today. In cities such as Montpellier, Nancy and Caen, no permission was given for protests. 70,000 police officers were deployed across the country, supported by the army. In various places in the country, hundreds of people were searched preventively this morning "to deter people with bad intentions". Objects that could be used as weapons were confiscated: besides knives, batons and fireworks, also a samurai sword and several pétanque balls. Clothing that can be used to withstand tear gas was also seized, such as masks with filters and diving goggles. According to Minister Nuñez of Interior, 410,000 people took part in demonstrations in France today. Last week there were 550,000. According to the unions, nearly 800,000 people went out onto the streets to demonstrate today. Many business owners had precautionarily boarded up their shopfronts. Museums such as the Louvre and the Musée d'Orsay remained closed today, as did 24 Paris metro stations. Several football matches have been postponed. In Orléans, the party congress of the radical right Rassemblement National went ahead. According to the mayor of the city, 13,000 left-wing demonstrators turned up there. The demonstration in Orléans passed without any notable incidents.

title: 'It will be an expensive vote': expats travel back to Israel specially to vote
lead: Tens of thousands of Israelis living abroad are going back to their country to vote ahead of the elections on 27 October. Not only in Israel, but also outside it, there is a sense that a lot is at stake and that precisely now every vote counts in determining the direction of the country. By law, you can only vote if you are in Israel. Only Israeli soldiers, diplomats and settlers in the occupied West Bank, the Golan Heights and East Jerusalem are exempt from this. Israelis living in the Netherlands are therefore also boarding planes. "If Netanyahu stays in power, Israel as a democratic state is finished", says Barak Oserovitz during a transfer on his way to Israel. "The chance to stop him is now. It will never come back." He is flying in from the Netherlands for a few days. "It will be an expensive vote", says Keren Hirsch. "The tickets and rental cars are much more expensive than usual." They are not the only ones who want to be in the country on Tuesday to vote. Many people come especially from the United States. There is even an organisation active there that arranges travel to Israel, to the annoyance of the Israeli government. The organisation is linked to the people who also support the often massive protests against <entity id="org:regering">de regering</entity> in Israel. Netanyahu or Eisenkot. It will be a now-or-never election, hear the groups of American and French Israelis who have come over, but also the people who live in Israel. "The government is not functioning", says Oserovitz. "The Jewish-Orthodox and Arab parts of society are not being included. They do not serve in the army. Orthodox Jews receive more money than they contribute through taxes. In addition, Netanyahu is holding back an investigation into the mistakes that were made which allowed Hamas to carry out a major attack on Israel on 7 October 2023." These are things that Netanyahu's biggest challenger, former general Gadi Eisenkot, wants to do differently. An independent investigation into 7 October, an independent judiciary and conscription for everyone. Hirsch: "Ultimately, under Netanyahu you get a kind of theocracy. And the opposition, for me, although some of them are also right-wing parties, stands for a secular democracy. That is very important to me." Palestinians. Over the past years, Netanyahu, either out of personal conviction or as a compromise to the radical and/or religious parties in his <entity id="org:kabinet">kabinet</entity>, has increasingly attacked criticism from the media, maintained an exemption from conscription for Orthodox Jews, and downplayed violence by settlers in the West Bank. Under his premiership, settlers were also armed, and the administration of the occupied territories came under radical ministers. Because the Israeli judiciary occasionally pushed him back, he made attempts to limit that power or make it political. Hirsch: "Gaza is close to my heart, let that be clear, but violence from Israeli settlers against Palestinians in the West Bank also remains too often unpunished. And yes, there is also violence from Palestinians against Israelis, and I will not deny that". Every vote counts. Netanyahu is campaigning with the slogan "Choose Eisenkot, and you get Palestine". Yet there seems to be little difference in how both candidates want to deal with the threat from Hamas and other actors in the region. For now, there is also no difference between the two camps in their approach to Palestinian voters in Israel. Israeli Arabs make up around 20 percent of <entity id="org:kiesgerechtigden-nederland">het electoraat</entity>, but a coalition with parties representing them is ruled out by almost everyone. Whether the vote of flown-in Israelis makes a difference is still an open question. Because a lot is at stake, high turnout is expected, even among Arab voters in Israel. As a result, each vote counts relatively less. That does not stop Barak Oserovitz from boarding the plane to Israel. "I'm not saying which party I will vote for, but assume it's for change!" Nieuwsuur made this video ahead of the Israeli parliamentary elections:

title: French newspaper: Paris attacker wanted to kill Black and Arab people
lead: The arrested suspect in the attack in the Paris suburb of Trappes wanted to attack Black people and people with an Arab appearance. Sources report this to the French newspaper Le Monde. Justice sees in the suspect's modus operandi, his choice of victims, his first statements and the results of the house searches indications that a racially motivated terrorist act took place. The sources also report that a copy of Mein Kampf, Hitler's book, was found on the man. The 39-year-old shooter Kevin T. opened fire with a machine gun on passersby yesterday morning. One person died and five others were injured, including a 12-year-old child. After the man was arrested, he reportedly told Le Monde that he had taken revenge on the shopkeepers whose shops were looted during last week's riots by attacking "Black people and Arabs". He gave this statement to the first officers on the scene. A 'lone wolf' As a result, the French authorities are investigating whether this involves "murder and attempted murder in connection with a terrorist motive, with the aggravating circumstance that the facts were committed because of the actual or alleged origin, ethnicity, nationality or religion of the victims". Kevin T. has been taken into custody at the headquarters of the French anti-terrorism unit. Investigators are now waiting to see whether he repeats his racist remarks during interrogations, Le Monde reports. The initial investigation shows that during his drive between Trappes and La Verrière, T. exclusively chose non-white people as targets and shot at them from his Renault Clio. Whether he had ties to far-right groups is being examined using seized computer equipment. Sources close to the investigation who spoke with the newspaper provisionally describe him as a "lone wolf". 'Racist ideology' During the house search, explosives experts and a special intervention unit of the French <entity id="org:politie">nationale politie</entity> were deployed after an improvised explosive device was discovered in the apartment. According to the authorities, it was a construction with three gas cylinders and electrical wires connected to a timer. French President Macron expressed his horror yesterday during a visit to Trappes at the intentions and deeds of the suspect: "A man was killed this morning by one of our fellow citizens on the basis of a racist ideology." And: "This is the first time a planned terrorist attack has aimed to kill our compatriots, our children, because of their skin colour or the faith they adhere to. This is a turning point for our Republic."

title: Kim Jong-un makes a flying visit to China to celebrate wartime cooperation
lead: Kim Jong-un made a flying visit to China today. It is a rare foreign visit by the North Korean leader. Kim was received by Wang Huning of the Politburo, the highest party body of China, and one of the ideological forces within the Chinese Communist Party. Kim and Wang laid a wreath at the monument commemorating the resistance against the US and China's help in the Korean War. Tomorrow the two countries will celebrate that it is exactly 76 years since China officially joined the Korean War. Chinese participation completely changed the course of the war and pushed the Allied troops far back to the south. In the afternoon Kim visited a car factory in the border city of Dandong, after which he returned home. Whereas in the past Kim mainly travelled to China by his armoured private train, according to various media he this time travelled to the northern neighbour by road. That is not without reason. This allowed him to enter China via the recently opened Yalu River Bridge, the bridge that was opened this month after more than 12 years of wrangling between the two countries. Improved relations The visit is yet another signal that the relationship between China and North Korea is on the rise. Although China is by far North Korea's most important trading partner, contact between the two countries was for a long time difficult. Last year the two leaders agreed to promote contact, and the results of that agreement are clearly visible. At the end of last year Kim stood alongside Xi during the military parade in Beijing. Shortly afterwards satellite images showed that considerable construction was underway on the North Korean side. The plan to build a new bridge between China and North Korea began in 2011. China completed its part in 2014, but North Korea kept everyone waiting, to the frustration of the Chinese. Two weeks ago the bridge was officially opened. Last summer Xi, together with his wife Peng Liyuan, visited North Korea for the first time in seven years, but more meetings are also taking place at a lower level. According to NKnews, a news organisation that closely follows developments in North Korea, two business delegations from North Korea were in China in recent weeks. This year, the train and flight connections between China and North Korea were also partly resumed, after they had been suspended during the coronavirus period. The rapprochement comes at a time when North Korea is working ever more closely with Russia. For example, North Korea is not only sending soldiers to the Russian-Ukrainian front, but trade and knowledge exchange between the two countries have also increased in recent years. Just before the new bridge between China and North Korea was opened, Russia and North Korea also opened a brand-new bridge. With Kim's visit, and in particular the celebration of what is essentially the start of pushing back the Americans on the Korean peninsula, the door to a meeting between Kim and US President Trump appears to have been closed. Trump has repeatedly spoken in recent months about a possible meeting with Kim. The APEC forum taking place next month in southern China, which Trump will attend, seemed to offer an opportunity for this. But North Korea and China, which would have to facilitate that visit, have not said a word about a possible meeting.

title: Busy scenes at Gelderland petrol station with bargain prices: an hour of refuelling for 1 euro
lead: At a petrol station in Voorst it was exceptionally busy this afternoon. The petrol station is permanently closing its doors and is staging a stunt with fuel prices on its last day. Between 16.00 and 17.00 hours visitors could fill their tanks for 1 euro per litre. That led to chaotic scenes. The petrol station is closing its doors after 38 years and will make way for homes. To give Voorst a "dignified farewell", the owner decided to lower the price of a litre of petrol on the very last day. All day a litre of petrol cost 2.13 euros, but the biggest stunt the petrol station saved for the last hour. However, a maximum of 100 litres could be pumped and filling jerrycans was not allowed. "This whole day is a gift for the village", says outgoing pump attendant Jan de Croon. The first customers were already waiting at 13.30 hours for the moment they could fill up at the bottom price. "I knew it would get busy, so I wanted to be here on time. Petrol for 1 euro per litre, you don't see that often", said one of them. "I'm going to fill up the car nicely, for 50 euros you already have a full tank." Rows of cars through the whole village. Eventually traffic towards the petrol station came to a complete standstill. By 16.00 hours the queue of cars already stretched the full length of the Gelderland village. The grounds of an unmanned petrol station across the road were also full of people waiting. "People are honking like crazy", said a reporter for Omroep Gelderland. "There are both happy and angry people. The tension seems to be rising. Someone even already called the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> because of the long queue." People from far away came to Voorst to fill up cheaply. "One euro per litre, you can't pass up an offer like that", says a motorist who drove fifty minutes for the promotion. "I'm a taxi driver, so this is brilliant." The crowds also drew many curious residents. "We just have a very boring village and now something finally happens", says a woman. "So we thought, let's go there for a bit. And it's really cosy here too." Police intervene at access roads. As far as is known, no major disturbances occurred during the promotion. The police did intervene at the access roads and stopped motorists there, as there were already so many interested people in the queue in the village that joining it no longer made sense. Shortly before 17.00 hours the gates of the petrol station were closed. The pump attendant had already announced that he wanted to close punctually at 17.00 hours: that was when the farewell drinks for staff began. Busy from early this morning. The farewell already drew many visitors early this morning. Soon, according to the regional broadcaster, it was a constant coming and going of cars. Almost everyone in the surrounding area tried to get a bargain. Besides cheap fuel, customers could also take part in a sort of 'wheel of fortune', with which a free tank of fuel could be won. "I did predict something", said owner Jan de Croon to Omroep Gelderland this morning, "but I didn't expect such a crowd this early. In the first half hour we already had four times as many customers as normal." The petrol station had prepared for the crowds. Two traffic controllers and six petrol station staff tried to guide the day in the right direction.

title: Ukrainian department stores under fire as residents prepare for winter
lead: Russia has recently been targeting not only Ukrainian power plants, military facilities and apartment blocks. Increasingly, Ukraine's economy is also a target, with attacks on warehouses, distribution centres, post offices and department stores. Such as those of retail giant Epitsentr. In the last few days alone, four branches have been destroyed. Among them in Kyiv, where several ballistic missiles hit a shopping centre in the north of the city this week. At the locations that are still intact, work continues. Operations director Maksim Sjeremet walks between the large shelves of garden tools, electronics and holiday decorations in an Epitsentr store. "It seems like a new wave", he observes, with dark circles under his eyes. Because of all the attacks he is so busy that he has hardly been able to sleep. Empty shelves The store has had to completely adjust its way of working because of the war, Sjeremet says. Goods no longer go through distribution centres because those have also been destroyed. Items stay in lorries until they have been delivered to the store. As a result, it takes longer to deliver products and the range is more limited. Sjeremet points to almost empty shelves where some gas burners are displayed. Previously they had gas burners from ten different brands, now there is only one. In Ukraine, they believe Russia wants to make life for residents completely impossible with this kind of attack. Because it is precisely in this kind of store that Ukrainians stock up on things to prepare for winter, for example jerrycans, gas burners and power banks. Branches of the DIY chain Dnipro M have also been attacked, where generators are among the items for sale. Ukrainian intelligence services recently obtained Russian plans for attacks on cities such as Kyiv in the coming winter. The documents describe a planned campaign that could have major consequences for the population. This concerns attacks on the power and heating supply, but also on the water supply and sewerage. Deteriorated relationship with the US Meanwhile, the relationship with President Trump has reached a new low in recent weeks. American intelligence needed to warn the population of attacks in time did not get through. This has now been restored. Deliveries of interceptor missiles for Patriot air defence systems from the US are also taking their time. In addition, the use of the Starlink satellite system, crucial for the Ukrainian armed forces, has been restricted. President Zelensky sees all of this as attempts by Trump to pressure Ukraine. Residents of Kyiv are bracing themselves for what could become the harshest winter so far. Especially because Ukraine does not have enough air defence to protect the country against the large-scale, prolonged attacks with ballistic missiles and jet drones. 'Don't just sit still' This means that the Epitsentr stores could be hit at any moment. When the air raid alarm sounds, Sjeremet moves with staff and customers to a shelter bunker next to the department store. A drone has been spotted nearby. "Of course the threat is extremely high", says the operations director. "Every day we get up and get back to work. What is destroyed, we rebuild. We certainly cannot just sit still." Since the start of the large-scale invasion, 23 Epitsentr locations have been destroyed. Mostly shopping centres, but also three logistics hubs and a tile factory of the company. At this moment, 59 branches are still open. In the bunker sits 39-year-old Anna with her little son. She is busy renovating her home, while her husband serves at the front. The apartment has already been prepared for winter with a portable battery for emergency power and a camping gas stove, she says. Anna likes to come to Epitsentr. "There are fewer and fewer of them, unfortunately", she says. "But life goes on. People want to keep building and so do we. If possible, we will keep coming here to shop."

title: Breda woman is world champion in nipple tattooing: 'It is such a valuable profession'
lead: She creates tattoos that almost no one recognises as a tattoo. Mariska de Jong from Breda tattoos nipples on people who have had breast surgery. She does it so well that since yesterday she may call herself the best in the world. Yesterday evening the world championship of the World Universal League of Permanent Makeup, an international organisation that organises competitions and educational congresses for permanent make-up specialists, took place in Turkey. Mariska de Jong works at a skin clinic in Breda and has been making medical tattoos for fifteen years. She specialises in so-called nipple reconstructions, in which she tattoos nipples on people who have had, for example, a mastectomy or treatment for breast cancer. 57 opponents In September she was already crowned champion of the Benelux. That meant she was allowed to go on to the world championship. This week she flew to Turkey, and De Jong was able to show what she can do. "I sat with 57 other participants in two halls. On my table was a piece of latex, which I had to tattoo on", she tells Omroep Brabant. "I had my pigments, but no photo. Normally I do have that. Now I had to do everything from memory. We had one hour. There was a big clock and some people walked around to watch how we were doing it." De Jong says she was not nervous for a moment. "No, I really enjoyed it. It went so well too: it was really my most beautiful work ever." Premonition During the prize ceremonies De Jong soon had a feeling that she was the winner. When her category came up, the third and second places were announced first. "By then I more or less already knew. The number two is a woman I look up to enormously. I thought: if she is second, then I must be number one. And that was the case." De Jong says the prize means a lot to her. "It is such a valuable profession. I have had many operations myself, so I know how it feels when things don't turn out well, but a reconstruction helps you feel like yourself again. I get to pass that on to someone." Besides the pride, the prize brings her something else special. Because of all the attention she already received when she became Benelux champion, hospitals have approached her wanting to work with her. According to De Jong, that cooperation could mean that some health insurers that do not yet do so will start reimbursing her work. "That is of course not sorted out tomorrow, but it would be so nice if that possibility came. That would really be the icing on the cake."

title: Demonstrations in European cities: riots in Tirana, soldiers deployed in Milan
lead: Although the protests in France are receiving the most international attention, today there have also been large demonstrations in several other European cities, including Milan, Madrid, Lisbon, Brussels and Tirana. Italian Prime Minister Meloni today sent 500 soldiers to Milan. Together with thousands of police officers, they must prevent the disorder of last week from being repeated. The demonstrations there are mainly about the rising cost of living. Concerns are especially great in Milan's luxury shopping district. Several well-known fashion stores have boarded up their shop windows as a precaution. Last weekend clothing stores were among the targets of looters. Corriere Della Sera reports that several people have been arrested preventively, including minors. Otherwise, for now it is limited to a few minor incidents, the newspaper reports. Faces left uncovered Security measures were also tightened in Rome. Luxury shopping streets were partly closed off and extra checks took place at various locations. In addition, hundreds of students marched peacefully through the city to make clear that they reject the violence of last week. A separate anti-war demonstration also marched through the centre of Rome. The organizers tried to nip possible disorder in the bud by asking participants to leave their faces uncovered and keep their hands visible. Later this evening, however, there were serious clashes between demonstrators and police. Protesters pelted officers with fireworks, eggs and other objects, after which police deployed water cannons. As a precaution, entrances to Termini station were closed. According to Italian media, 96 demonstrators were taken to the police station. Unrest in Bologna and Turin Elsewhere in Italy it also turned unruly. In Bologna police temporarily deployed tear gas and water cannons to prevent a demonstration from reaching the station. In Turin security forces pushed demonstrators back with shields. Images of various demonstrations: In the Albanian capital Tirana there were again clashes between demonstrators and police. Officers used water cannons against protesters who, among other things, threw objects at the police and set fires. The protests have now lasted more than a week. Pupils and students demand lower study costs, more investment in education and a tougher approach to corruption within education. Part of the demonstrators have joined a broader movement that demands the departure of Prime Minister Rama. The government says it wants to talk with the students, but warns that violence will not be tolerated. Images of the demonstrations in Albania: In the Spanish capital Madrid the demonstrations today passed peacefully. Thousands of people marched through the centre of the Spanish capital to protest against plans that, in their view, put the public pension system under pressure. The protests come shortly before next month's elections. Pensions are an important topic in the campaign. In the Portuguese capital Lisbon demonstrators marched through the city demanding more affordable housing. They oppose government plans that would make it easier to raise rents and to evict tenants with rent arrears. Prime Minister Montenegro has defended the measures, arguing that they must strengthen trust between tenants and landlords and stimulate the rental market. Demonstrators, by contrast, feel the proposals make tenants more vulnerable. Nine arrests in Brussels Also in Brussels there was a demonstration today. According to police, about 400 people came to a gathering announced via social media. During speeches, protest was mainly directed at what activists see as excessive police violence at earlier demonstrations. Among the demonstrators there is also discontent over high housing costs, rising study costs and limited future prospects for young people, the newspaper Het Laatste Nieuws reports. Nine people were arrested, four of them for illegal possession of weapons and incitement to riot. Large-scale disorder did not occur, according to police.

title: 'You cannot censor a free press': thousands of Turks take to the streets for press freedom
lead: Thousands of people, including many journalists, took to the streets in Turkey today for press freedom. Journalist associations and the New Party (an opposition party) had called on people to demonstrate in ten cities across the country. "You cannot censor a free press," the demonstrators chanted. The reason for the demonstrations is censorship, the pressure on journalists and the takeover of several broadcasters by the government, the organizers say. In twenty months at least five broadcasters have been taken over. Not all of them are opposition broadcasters, and the reasons for the takeovers vary. Even so, there are fears that the independence of journalism will come under even more pressure. For example, last week there was a police raid at the popular opposition broadcaster Halk TV. Afterwards the broadcaster was placed under the management of a trustee. Since then, reruns have been broadcast. For a while the broadcaster continued online, but the X account with 3 million followers has been blocked, and for three days no new videos have been uploaded to YouTube. The Turkish Public Prosecution Service suspects the chair of the broadcaster of bribery, money laundering and fraud, but the opposition says the raid is politically motivated and is intended to silence critical voices in the country. 'More police than demonstrators' "There is a culture of fear in Turkey," says a woman who is a member of the New Party and would prefer to remain anonymous. She is afraid that if her name becomes known, she or her family could get into trouble. "Criticism has consequences, we see that. Look around you and see how many police are standing here now. There are more officers than demonstrators." Still, she is determined to take part. In her hands she holds a newspaper. "A journalist from the Turkish newspaper Birgun is in prison because of an article he wrote. With this newspaper in my hands I am calling attention to press freedom in Turkey," she says. She explains that it is precisely now that people in Turkey must stand in solidarity with the press. According to Reporters Without Borders, Turkey is one of the countries with the worst scores on press freedom. Several journalists are also in prison. According to the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), the Turkish government is using the disinformation law to intimidate journalists. That law punishes, among other things, spreading false information concerning domestic and foreign security. This year, according to the organization, sixteen people have been arrested for spreading disinformation. Major stock market scandal Another demonstrator, who is also a journalist, notes that journalists are being suppressed more and more. According to him, Halk TV was taken over because the opposition broadcaster reported on a major stock market scandal. "One of our colleagues is in prison for that," he says, "because he asked about money that was being siphoned away from the people. Because he was doing his job." Last month Turkey was shaken when it became known that 455,000 Turkish savers had lost their savings, while others made tens of millions of dollars in profits. In the media it was compared to a pyramid scheme. People at the top of the ruling AK party, such as the vice chair, were also named. She has since stepped down pending a criminal investigation. Looking to the future Retired journalists also took to the streets today. "I am old, but I stand here for the future, for my young colleagues," says a 70-year-old woman in Istanbul. She is pessimistic about the future because in her view there should have been more people out in the city, which has at least 15 million inhabitants. "Today everyone should, as far as I am concerned, have gone out to support the journalists."

title: Cabinet invites seven opposition parties to negotiations on tax plan
lead: The cabinet has made arrangements on how it wants to meet the opposition halfway and will invite seven parties next week to negotiate further on the tax plan. This is the outcome of a meeting of the top of the cabinet today. These are the parties the cabinet already spoke with earlier: Pro, JA21, BBB, SGP, ChristenUnie, 50Plus and Volt. The cabinet therefore still aims for a broad agreement with both left and right, rather than looking to one side. The tax plan is important for the cabinet, because it sets out how taxes will be arranged in the coming years. This year, for example, the cabinet plans to extend the reduction of the excise duty on petrol and diesel by 1 year, until the end of 2027. It also wants to implement a reduction of the starter's deduction for entrepreneurs. Opposition parties have so far put forward completely different and firm demands in exchange for their support. For example, Pro wants the higher income tax for the coming years to be removed entirely, JA21 wants stricter asylum measures, BBB asks for an adjustment of the nitrogen plans, and SGP wants the cabinet to do more to prevent abortions. Some of these demands are sensitive within the coalition of D66, VVD and CDA. That is why today <entity id="person:rob-jetten">premier Jetten</entity>, deputy prime ministers Yesilgöz and Van den Brink, <entity id="person:eelco-heinen">minister Heinen</entity> and <entity id="person:eelco-eerenberg">staatssecretaris Eerenberg</entity> (both <entity id="org:ministerie-van-financien">Financiën</entity>) discussed how much negotiating room the cabinet has. Asylum, nitrogen and abortions. Next week the opposition parties will negotiate with Prime Minister Jetten and minister Heinen. Other ministers may join, for example minister Van den Brink (<entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-am">Asiel en Migratie</entity>) or <entity id="person:jaimi-van-essen">minister Van Essen</entity> (Agriculture). It appears that the cabinet is therefore still willing to adjust its plans on asylum and nitrogen. Notably, the minister of Health is not on this list. It seems to be a signal from the cabinet that, despite the wish of the SGP, there are no plans to change the abortion laws. 'Serious negotiations'. Ahead of Budget Day, the cabinet has spoken with many opposition parties and included their wishes in the budget. No real negotiations have taken place so far. That changes next week. Pro <entity id="person:jesse-feras-klaver">leider Klaver</entity> already invited himself to Prime Minister Jetten last week to begin "serious negotiations" on the tax plan. He tried in this way to get the cabinet to agree to a single deal on the left. The cabinet did not respond to this and now wants to negotiate with many more parties. Because the <entity id="org:belastingdienst">Belastingdienst</entity> needs time to implement these measures, the tax plan cannot be postponed for too long. On Monday, <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity> will discuss it further. The intention is that it will be put to a vote on 12 November. In addition, a problem regarding the wealth tax (box 3) still persists. A majority of the Tweede Kamer agrees with the plan that minister Heinen has put forward for this. It is only still unclear how it will be paid for. The plan to have smaller savers and investors pay, the cabinet withdrew again after heavy criticism. The cabinet must also find a solution for this. Insiders say the three coalition parties are now more or less in agreement internally, but a majority in the Eerste and Tweede Kamer must still be found for this as well.

title: Nearly 1,000 arrests in France, minister satisfied with how the protests went
lead: French police today arrested nearly a thousand people at demonstrations across the country. This was announced by French Minister of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity> Nuñez. He expects that "this number will rise". According to the minister, 410,000 people took part in demonstrations across France. According to the trade unions, nearly twice as many people, around 800,000, took to the streets today to demonstrate. Nuñez says that thanks to the police intervention, looting was prevented. According to him, police action also prevented public buildings from being attacked, as happened during last weekend's riots. Today the government had also called up around 70,000 extra officers, supported by the army. After the events of last week there was much criticism of Nuñez because the police were not sufficiently prepared for the large number of demonstrators. He acknowledged last week that the authorities had lost control in some cities. He offered his resignation, but President Macron did not accept it. Looting and violence Last Saturday, 385 people were arrested. In several cities, demonstrations later in the evening got seriously out of hand, with large-scale violence and looting. In Limoges the town hall tower collapsed after a fire. The protests in France are directed against government policy, the state of education and the rising cost of living. Large demonstrations also took place today in several other European cities, including Milan, Madrid, Lisbon, Brussels and Tirana. Nuñez expressed satisfaction with how the demonstrations went. Most passed off calmly. There were, however, "as we had expected" some risk groups, he said. "They acted according to a fairly classic pattern. They broke out and tried to commit violence. They were stopped when they tried to reach the city centres." Paris In Paris the protest march largely passed off calmly. The route was changed to avoid places where things got out of hand last week. According to the police, around 110,000 people took part in the march. Ahead of the demonstration, preventive searches were carried out and objects that could be used as weapons were seized: besides knives, batons and fireworks, also a samurai sword and several boules balls. When the demonstrators arrived at Porte Vincennes at the end of the afternoon, riots broke out there and the police used water cannons and tear gas to disperse around 500 rioters. According to the police, the rioters tried to break into a car dealership. Other cities In other French cities too, including Nice, Lyon, Marseille and Lille, the police intervened with tear gas or a water cannon at protests. In Grenoble, riot police were attacked by 400 masked people, and in Bordeaux projectiles were thrown at the police and barricades were erected by demonstrators. Nuñez speaks of "extreme violence by ultra-left groups". In several French cities the police intervened:

title: Daylight saving time is over: tonight the clock went back one hour
lead: Tonight daylight saving time ended. That means the clock was set back one hour and most people can sleep an hour longer. In the morning it gets light earlier, and in the evening it gets dark earlier. Other European countries also switch to 'winter time' tonight. Winter time is the standard time for the Netherlands. Daylight saving time returns on 28 March 2027. Then the clock will go forward an hour again. The mnemonic is: in spring the clock goes forward. Changing the clock In 1916 the Netherlands introduced daylight saving time for the first time. This followed the Germans. They introduced it to save coal during the First World War. Changing the time was abolished in the Netherlands in 1946 but reintroduced in 1977. Changing the clock was meant to save energy during the oil crisis, because in summer time the lights came on an hour later. Discussion Every half year Europe changes time. After years of discussion, the European Commission wanted to stop this in 2018. A European daylight saving time survey showed that a majority of respondents agreed. The main argument for introducing daylight saving time in 1977 was energy saving, but a study showed that only 0.3 percent energy was actually saved. Another argument was that some people have trouble with changing the clock. They are thrown off their rhythm, lie awake the first nights after the change or get cravings for food at odd moments. Although many European countries want to get rid of changing the clock, there is no agreement on which time should then be kept. As a result, the plan to reach one standard time has been shelved again.

title: Ukraine violated Starlink satellite system terms, says Musk
lead: Elon Musk says the Ukrainian army has violated the terms of use of Starlink. On his social media platform X, he writes that it was never permitted to use the satellite system for offensive drone attacks to kill people. "It was never permitted to use the commercial satellite service Starlink, which is intended for civilians, for offensive drone attacks to kill people. That should never be allowed either," Musk writes. According to him, his company SpaceX closed off that possibility last week. Speed restored Musk responded after Ukrainian President Zelensky reported yesterday that the connections of Starlink and the military variant Starshield had been restored. "The speeds are now back to how they should be," Zelensky wrote on X. Ukraine uses both Starlink, the commercial satellite internet service of SpaceX, and Starshield, the military variant intended for governments and defence. On 14 October, the Ukrainian army reported problems with the satellite connections. At certain speeds, the connections dropped, making military drones harder to control. Military missions were also disrupted. The restrictions made it more difficult, among other things, to deploy Ukrainian interceptor drones against Russian attack drones. Tensions The issue has further increased tensions between Kyiv and Washington. The Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday that Musk himself had ordered the speed of the military satellite connections to be limited. Musk has confirmed that SpaceX limited the speed of Starlink. About Starshield, he said that the American government has control over changes to the military system. The problems arose a few days after President Donald Trump had announced that he wanted to buy Russian diesel and had suspended new sanctions against Moscow. He had also called on Ukraine to stop attacking Russian oil refineries.

title: Damage at various locations due to storm Boelo, strong wind again today
lead: The strong wind caused damage or nuisance at various locations last night and overnight, mainly due to fallen trees. Today, the wind caused by low-pressure area Boelo must still be taken into account. Especially in the coastal provinces, severe gusts may occur. For those areas, the <entity id="org:koninklijk-nederlands-meteorologisch-instituut">KNMI</entity> has issued code yellow. In the north, the strong wind will only disappear at night towards Monday. There is a high chance that branches will break off because the trees are still in leaf. This may also cause disruption to traffic. This was already noticeable last night. In Amsterdam-Noord, a moving car was hit and its driver was injured. In Rijnsburg, near Leiden, a house was damaged. In Culemborg, a tree fell onto a parked car. The car is a total loss. Here and there, trees came down onto through roads. The N207 near Alphen aan den Rijn was blocked, and in Nijeveen in Drenthe a residential area was unreachable for some time, until the fire brigade sawed the fallen tree into pieces and removed it. In Gouderak near Gouda, an electricity pole fell across a road. Storm Boelo The Amsterdam Dance Event also suffered from the strong wind. The Into the Woods festival at the NDSM wharf, for example, was ended early as a precaution to prevent dangerous situations. The stormy weather is caused by storm Boelo, which crossed the North Sea from Scotland. In IJmuiden, wind force 9 was measured overnight.

title: Renewed disturbances during Walibi Fright Nights
lead: Fights broke out at the Walibi amusement park in Biddinghuizen last night during the so-called Fright Nights. Footage circulating on social media shows groups of visitors coming to blows. The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> tried to break up the fighting groups. Dogs and batons were deployed. It is not known whether anyone has been arrested. According to Omroep Flevoland, the unrest broke out towards the end of the evening. What the trigger was is still unclear. The Fright Nights were also disrupted by fights last year. Walibi then announced extra measures for this year to tackle unwanted behaviour. Walibi holds special evenings around Halloween in which actors are deployed to frighten people. The event attracts thousands of visitors each year. Earlier, the actors complained that they were hit, groped and harassed by visitors. At that time too, Walibi promised improvement.

title: Thousands of Israelis demand inquiry into 7 October, day before elections
lead: In the Israeli city of Tel Aviv, thousands of people demonstrated on Saturday evening, three days before the Israeli elections, against the government of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The demonstrators demand an independent state inquiry into the failures that preceded the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, which took the country by surprise. Netanyahu refuses such an inquiry. According to the organisers, more than 100.000 people attended the demonstration. The demonstration was held at the so-called Hostages Square, where weekly demonstrations were held during the war calling for the release of the people abducted to Gaza. Many demonstrators want a different government and an inquiry: Among the demonstrators were former hostages and relatives. The father of a man who was murdered in Gaza after his abduction also addressed the crowd. He said that the political leaders have still not decided to uncover the truth about that day. Opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot was also present. He is considered one of Netanyahu's most important challengers. His election programme states that he wants an independent inquiry into the events of 7 October. On Tuesday, Israelis may go to the polls to elect a new parliament. Prior knowledge Netanyahu is faulted in Israel, among other things, for having delayed agreements on the release of hostages, as a result of which they remained captive longer. Last month, journalists from the newspaper Haaretz reported that the prime minister had been warned a week and a half before the Hamas terrorist attack of 7 October 2023 that the terrorist organisation was preparing a major attack on Israel. According to two Israeli journalists, however, Netanyahu did nothing with that information and did not share it with the intelligence services. In the attack of 7 October 2023, about 1200 people were killed. More than 250 people were also abducted and taken to the Gaza Strip. Since then, more than 74.000 Palestinians have been killed by Israel in Gaza in total, including many children. In that period, 175.000 people were also injured.

title: Wake-up call 25/10: Le Pen launches presidential campaign France • PSV-Feyenoord in eredivisie
lead: Good morning! Overnight winter time has begun. The clock went back an hour and most people were able to sleep an hour longer. This is what to expect today: In France Marine Le Pen is launching her campaign for the presidency, and in the eredivisie it is time for the clash PSV-Feyenoord. First the weather: today it is stormy with a strong south to west wind. Clouds and sunny spells alternate. Mostly inland it will rain, sometimes with hail or a thunderclap. Highs range between 12 and 14 degrees. Are you going out today? Here you can find the overview of traffic jams and roadworks, and here you can see the situation on the rail network. What can you expect today? What did you miss? In various places across the country storm Boelo caused disruption, mainly through fallen trees. In Amsterdam-Noord a moving car was hit and the driver was injured. In Rijnsburg, near Leiden, a house was damaged. In Culemborg a tree fell onto a parked car. Here and there trees also came down onto major roads. A festival was also stopped early to prevent dangerous situations. Other news from the night: And finally this: Heavy crowds at a petrol station in Voorst with stunt prices: one hour of fuelling for 1 euro. The petrol station is closing its doors after 38 years and ran a stunt on its last day with fuel prices. Have a great day!

title: Serbian students challenge Vucic in the most tense parliamentary elections in years
lead: Will students in Serbia put an end to twelve years of rule by autocratic leader Aleksandar Vucic? That is the question at stake today in the parliamentary elections in the Balkan country. They are the most tense since Vucic and his Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) came to power, because the Student List has a serious chance. According to polls, the two camps are neck and neck. Vucic stepped down as president in September and wants to become prime minister now, and thus take power with him. But he has never before wavered as he does now. The Student List emerged from two years of mass protests against Vucic. These began when part of the station in the city of Novi Sad collapsed. Sixteen people died. And that happened just after the station had been festively reopened following a renovation. Poorly executed by companies with close ties to the SNS, was the immediate criticism. Smear campaign "Corruption kills!" the students chant, and they start occupying their universities. Initially to force the prosecution of those responsible, but soon they demand an end to corruption and the blockades turn into mass protests. They then want elections to put an end to the rule of the man who calls the shots in their country. Now they have those, and they are taking part with their own list. That today's vote is tense is in itself an achievement of some scale. Vucic has in fact often faced demonstrations. These have almost always been more or less directed against his increasingly suffocating power. Think for example of his grip on prosecutors and judges, the media, state institutions and the economy. But he has always sat out those protests, or managed through a smear campaign to discredit his opponents before they could turn their protest into political capital. Until now. That the Student List will achieve a formidable result is clear. A high turnout in particular could help the students to victory. Part of their success is that their mass demonstrations are always peaceful and they do not respond to provocations, even when the police intervene harshly on a few occasions. Government under the spotlight In addition, they have no open leaders and decide through majority votes in public assemblies. All of this makes it difficult for Vucic to get a grip on them with his propaganda machine. He tries it by portraying the students in the media as troublemakers paid by foreign countries who want to overthrow the Serbian state. But the students do not let themselves be put off: their perseverance, enthusiasm and positivity are infectious, and more and more other Serbs gradually join them. They have no access to major media, so the students must rely on social media and are travelling across the country en masse. The big question is: what will they do if they actually come to power? That is then up to the scientists and other experts on the list, as the students themselves are not on it. The most important programme point is that all government institutions and contracts will be scrutinised. Whoever proves corrupt will be prosecuted. Whoever has enriched themselves with public money will be exposed. Ideas about, for example, better education do exist, but they come second. Whether Serbia should quickly join the EU or instead maintain closer ties with Russia is also something the students are leaving for later. An obvious prime minister does not exist; the number 1 on the list is a relatively unknown cardiologist. Due to the complete lack of political experience, chaos threatens, and that is precisely the biggest Achilles heel of the student list. Fear of fraud Vucic can meanwhile count on many votes from civil servants. Stories have again surfaced in recent weeks of employees of government services being pressured to prove that they vote for the SNS, and with them a part of their friends and family. If not, they lose their job. In addition, the unrelenting propaganda in the media does its work. But there are also Serbs who are not so much affected by Vucic's suffocating grip. Especially in the villages, where they are glad of the economic growth, the building of roads and the stability that Vucic brings to a country with a turbulent recent history. He enters the fight full of self-confidence and says he will accept defeat if it comes. But the students doubt this: they fear that he will, if necessary, try to stay in power through fraud. To prevent this, they call on their supporters to cast their vote right away at 7 am. Long queues at that time must show that Vucic can no longer ignore the students either.

title: Doctors critical of long covid policy of Minister Hermans: 'Disastrous for patient trust'
lead: General practitioners, medical specialists and scientists are tearing apart the plans of health minister Sophie Hermans for patients with long covid and similar conditions such as ME and Q fever. The minister wants to drastically scale back funding for the long covid expertise centres and at the same time largely return responsibility for care to general practitioners. This is far too early, the healthcare sector warns. Scientific research into the various post-acute infectious syndromes (PAIS) is still in its early stages. Doctors only in principle offer care when there is solid evidence for it and medical guidelines have been drawn up; for now there is no such thing. Yet the minister is steering towards doctors in regular care treating patients while there are hardly any guidelines yet. In a letter to Hermans, obtained by the NOS, four major interest organisations on behalf of general practitioners warn that they will then be "confronted with patient expectations that do not match what can be responsibly offered on the basis of available knowledge and professional standards". Unequal care General practitioners fear a breach of trust with their patients. "That risk runs when most healthcare providers can still offer little care," says Hedwig Vos, herself a GP, professor of general practice medicine and board member of the Universitair Netwerk Huisartsengeneeskunde. "Some doctors will already have a bit more knowledge and offer more care, while the majority cannot. Then unequal care arises, and that is disastrous for patient trust." Two years ago expertise centres were therefore opened in the <entity id="org:rwt-academische-ziekenhuizen">academische ziekenhuizen</entity>, thanks to an investment of 27 million euros from <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity>. Not to help all patients, but to test experimental treatments with enrolled patients and collect evidence for guidelines. The idea is that all general practitioners can later treat most patients based on those guidelines. Two years later the minister wants to bring the joint budget for the eight expertise centres back to 1 million euros per year. The doctors behind these centres remain diplomatic towards the minister so as not to complicate consultations on the future of their clinics. But they too confirm that this amount does not provide sufficient resources to fulfil all their core tasks: doing research, providing education to other healthcare providers and supporting doctors with complex cases. "As a system we are stuck," says medical specialist Melvin Lafeber on behalf of the doctors at the expertise centres. "Funding is needed to develop knowledge and treatments, but that funding for care is only available as reimbursed care once effectiveness has already been proven. Otherwise it is against the Health Insurance Act." Researchers and doctors leave Without substantial financial support from the cabinet, developing effective treatments is simply not possible. The last Rutte cabinet invested 40 million euros three years ago in research into long covid. That sounds substantial but is insufficient to take major medical steps. By comparison, Germany is investing half a billion euros in research over the next 10 years. A frequently cited shortcoming of the Dutch approach is the short-term funding of research projects. Although the first research results will be presented next year, the expectation is that the short projects will not yield enough scientific evidence to get treatments into the basic package, according to a survey by the NOS. Scientists want to press on with follow-up research but cannot, because they often can no longer pay their researchers due to expiring funding. The retention of accumulated knowledge is therefore also uncertain, as researchers often leave for other fields. This also applies to doctors in the expertise centres, according to emails in the possession of the NOS. The expertise centre of Amsterdam UMC currently has to cancel new patients out of necessity because staff have left for a job with more security. Both the <entity id="org:gezondheidsraad">Gezondheidsraad</entity> and experts from a ministerial evaluation team recently advised the cabinet to quickly invest heavily in expertise centres and a long-term research programme. Hermans, however, wants ZonMw, the organisation that distributes research grants on behalf of the cabinet, to first explore which research directions are promising before considering substantial funding. Lost time Patients lack urgency with the minister, especially because many of them are getting sicker. With Hermans' approach it will take two to three years before new large studies start. After that it will take years before these studies possibly bring a breakthrough. This is hard for patients to accept because in 2018 the Gezondheidsraad advised opening expertise centres for ME, and that was ignored at the time. "We could have known much more by now," says Carlijn Keijzer. She has ME, a PAIS with much overlap with long covid. Together with fellow sufferers she is organising a demonstration in The Hague today to urge the cabinet to act. "Again!" says Keijzer. She recalls how only four years after the start of the pandemic, the then cabinet, after much wrangling with patient organisations and <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity>, released money for expertise centres. "And barely two years later we have to convince a new cabinet once again of the need for research." Response from the minister Minister Sophie Hermans can say little in response about extra funds for research and expertise centres because the healthcare sector has been tasked with coming up with a proposal on how to organise care for PAIS patients. "That process is ongoing, so I cannot anticipate it."

title: Vehicles of enforcement officers in Waalwijk burned out, police investigating arson
lead: Three vehicles belonging to enforcement officers were burned out at the town hall in Waalwijk. The police are taking the possibility of deliberate action into account, Omroep Brabant reports. The fire broke out last night around quarter to two. The three electric cars were charging. Two vehicles are recognisable as enforcement vehicles; one of the cars has no enforcement logo on the vehicle. The cars were parked in spaces marked as parking spaces for enforcement officers. Presumably the middle car caught fire first, after which the fire is said to have spread to the cars next to it. Photos show that the vehicles have suffered considerable damage. Traces secured The police have started an investigation into how the fire could have started. Traces have been secured and camera footage is being reviewed. According to a journalist on the scene, the emergency services were able to leave the town hall in Waalwijk around half past three last night. A towing company had to come collect the burned-out vehicles later.

title: Fire at car dismantling yard in Zoetermeer, police hold people back
lead: In Zoetermeer a large fire has raged in a car dismantling yard. Residents have been advised via NL Alert to keep windows and doors closed. A lot of smoke is being released and because the wind has shifted, the smoke now hangs over a larger area. Four people have been taken to hospital because they inhaled smoke, the fire brigade says. Fire services from the entire region were called out for the fire on Bleiswijkseweg, which broke out around 06.50. The cause of the fire is not yet clear. Grim atmosphere The car dismantling yard is located next to a caravan park. Houses next to the company were evacuated, and people resisted and the atmosphere turned grim. The police then intervened. Two people have been arrested for insult, and one of them was checked by ambulance staff after being stopped by the police. The police used the baton to keep people at a distance: Residents wanted to go to the company, but were held back because that was too dangerous. A resident tells Omroep West that it is the second time there has been a fire at the company. Last year in February the car dismantling yard went up in flames. It was suspected that this was arson.

title: Looting and arson in Barcelona, over 100 people arrested
lead: At a protest in central Barcelona, about 100 people were arrested after looting and arson. Just over half are minors, Spanish media report. The disturbances continued until deep into the night. The protest was reportedly a reaction to the demonstrations in France. Young people had been called upon via social media to join. Online, the slogan 'institut indignats' circulated, which means 'outraged secondary schools'. TikTok groups started the call, after which people organised themselves in WhatsApp and Telegram channels, the newspaper El País writes. Young people came to Barcelona and vandalised street furniture and bicycles. Shops were also looted and rubbish bins set on fire. Fires were reportedly started in about thirty places. In addition, people reportedly threw stones at the police. More than 220 officers were deployed to bring the situation under control: The regional president of Catalonia, Salvador Illa, condemns the violence. He says that demonstrating is a democratic right, but that attacks, intimidation and vandalism cannot be accepted. The mayor of Barcelona says that people will be punished. He speaks of senseless violence and vandalism. The Catalan police say they are investigating who is behind the protests. They are cooperating with other European police forces, such as the French and Italian. In more European cities protests: Yesterday there were also protests in cities in France and Italy, among others. There was also unrest there. In Italy the demonstrations are mainly about the rising cost of living. Italian prime minister Meloni sent 500 soldiers to Milan. Security measures were also tightened in Rome, among other places. In the evening, clashes broke out between demonstrators and police. Protesters threw fireworks and eggs at officers. Across France, over 400,000 people took part in protest marches yesterday. Around a thousand people were arrested across the country. In Paris, 500 rioters were dispersed with water cannons and tear gas.
